name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: The American dream grows through sharing with newcomers
description: As we continue celebrating 250 years of our nation, we should keep in mind a defining force in our country’s history and growth: immigration. Immigration is a catalyst for America’s demographic survival, economic dominance, and cultural renewal. The story of America at 250 is, as it has always been, the story of the immigrant. As the nation continues […]
text:
"Immigrants make America Great" was the message from this woman and child at a No Kings rally Oct. 18, 2025 at the Iowa State Capitol. (Photo by Joanna Schroeder for Iowa Capital Dispatch)As we continue celebrating 250 years of our nation, we should keep in mind a defining force in our country’s history and growth: immigration.
Immigration is a catalyst for America’s demographic survival, economic dominance, and cultural renewal. The story of America at 250 is, as it has always been, the story of the immigrant. As the nation continues to celebrate its semiquincentennial, the enduring promise of the American experiment relies not just on looking back at our founding principles, but on looking at who continues to build them.
From the construction of 19th-century railroads to the creation of 21st-century artificial intelligence, immigrants have played a great role in the American innovation and with that also have had a big impact in the economy.
Just checking the last 25 years of Nobel Prize recipients, immigrants were awarded 40% of the Nobel Prizes won by Americans in chemistry, medicine and physics.
Foreign-born entrepreneurs started a disproportionate share of American small businesses and Fortune 500 companies. Around 66% of U.S. billion-dollar companies (the so-called “unicorns”) have been founded or cofounded by immigrants or the children of immigrants.
In addition, immigrants fill critical gaps across the economic spectrum, from agriculture and healthcare to construction and engineering. Some of these foreign-born workers are key, especially in rural communities across the country.
Here in Iowa, immigrants contribute in many ways to our communities including with around $1.9 billion paid in taxes annually. My own city, Marshalltown, is a wonderfully diverse community. It is diverse in culture and offers community members so many opportunities to learn and grow, regardless of where they were born.
As the native-born population ages, younger immigrant workers sustain the tax base, funding vital social safety nets like Social Security.
Societies that shut off immigration eventually stagnate. They age, lose economic momentum, and grow cautious. America has largely avoided this trap because immigration acts as a constant injection of youth, ambition, and risk-tolerance. The individuals who leave everything behind to come here possess rare traits: courage and a fierce belief in self-determination. By choice, they embody the very traits of the original revolutionaries of 1776. Immigrants contribute to keeping the nation progressive and future-focused alongside their American neighbors.
Critics often worry that immigration dilutes national identity. History shows the opposite. Immigrants do not dilute American culture; they expand it. The beauty of the American identity is that it is not defined by blood or soil, but by adherence to a shared creed of liberty and opportunity. Each wave of arrivals adds new depth to the cultural landscape while fiercely adopting the core values of their new home.
As the United States marks this historic milestone, the challenge is to reform and modernize an outdated immigration system, not to shutter the gates. To maintain global leadership in the next two and a half centuries, America must remain the world’s premier destination for talent and hope. Securing borders and streamlining legal pathways are not mutually exclusive goals; they are dual requirements for a functional superpower.
Recent polling shows that there is an overwhelming consensus for a fair, restitution-based immigration solution. Everyone can urge Congress for bipartisan work on this topic.
Celebrating the 250th anniversary of the United States means recognizing that the American dream is not a finite resource. It grows larger, the more it is shared. By continuing to welcome those who wish to build a better life, America ensures its greatest chapters are still to be written.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Lawmakers vow to carry on Brown’s and Wallace’s legislative priorities
description: Rep. Price Wallace (left) and Rep. Bo Brown (Rogelio V. Solis/AP)
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
When a lawmaker dies, a district loses more than an elected official. It loses an advocate who understood its communities, built relationships with over years of public service and often became the driving force behind issues that mattered to the people they represented. 
After the deaths of Reps. William “Bo” Brown and Price Wallace last month, fellow legislators say they plan to keep alive the causes each man championed — from criminal justice reform to restoring Mississippi’s ballot initiative process. Because every bill in the Mississippi Legislature must be reintroduced each session, proposals survive only if a lawmaker chooses to sponsor them. Colleagues of Brown and Wallace say they intend to do just that when they return in 2027. 
Carrying on unfinished work 
Although Brown and Wallace focused on different issues, colleagues say they plan to carry forward each man’s legislative priorities. 
Rep. Earle Banks, a Democrat from Jackson, said he plans to reintroduce criminal justice legislation Brown helped champion, including expanding parole eligibility for some incarcerated people. During the 2020 legislative session, Brown, a fellow Democrat who also was from Jackson, and Banks co-sponsored House Bill 361, which sought to broaden parole eligibility for people convicted of certain capital offenses. The bill died in committee. 
State Rep. Earle Banks, D-Jackson, answers a question during a short debate between himself and sitting Mississippi Supreme Court Justice Bill Waller Jr., Monday, Oct. 1, 2012, at the Stennis Luncheon in Jackson, Miss. Waller seeks reelection and Banks, a veteran legislator, wants to unseat him.  (AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)
Banks said Brown viewed the proposal as one step toward addressing disparities in Mississippi’s criminal justice system. 
“There are too many people — Bo felt, and I feel, also — who are incarcerated, who are of no threat to society,” Banks said. 
On the Gulf Coast, Sen. Jeremy England, a Republican from Vancleave, said he plans to revive Wallace’s effort to restore Mississippi’s ballot initiative process. 
The process allowed citizens to place proposed constitutional amendments on the ballot after gathering enough signatures. In 2021, the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled it unconstitutionalbecause the state Constitution still referenced five congressional districts even though Mississippi has had four since 2001. 
Wallace, Republican from Mendenhall, sponsored legislation during the 2025 session to restore the process with additional restrictions. The bill passed the House but died before reaching the Senate floor. 
England said he expects to introduce similar legislation during the 2027 session, although he has acknowledged it still faces significant political hurdles. 
“Until we see someone else take that issue up and move it forward. I don’t know what that’s going to look like coming out of the House,” England said. “But with enough people asking for it, somebody’s going to look at it.” 
Different approaches, shared purpose 
While their priorities differed, colleagues said both elected leaders were driven more by conviction than recognition. 
Banks said Brown, as a representative and former city councilman for Jackson, devoted much of his legislative work to expanding economic opportunities for Black Mississippians while addressing inequities in the criminal justice system. 
“Most of the economic development (in the state) does not happen west of Interstate 55,” Banks said. “We need more economic development in Jackson and Hinds County and in the Second Congressional District so you have better jobs for people.” 
Banks said Brown rarely backed away from a debate and remained engaged throughout his last session. “He believed in what he believed in, and you weren’t going to convince him otherwise,” Banks said. “Once he would get something in his mind, that was what he was going to do.” 
During debate over an education bill in April — Brown’s last appearance in the House — he repeatedly stood to question the legislation despite worsening health. 
“His heart was still there, and his strength was still there to say, ‘Hey, I’m challenging this. I have questions about this and I’m not going to just sit here just arbitrarily vote for something,’” Banks said. 
Sen. Jeremy England, R-Vancleave, asks a question about a bill in the Senate chamber at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson on Wednesday, April 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
England described Wallace as a straightforward lawmaker whose expertise made him one of the Legislature’s leading voices on agriculture. 
A poultry farmer, Wallace was the member colleagues turned to whenever farming legislation came before the House. 
“Price knew that business from the top to the bottom,” England said. Anytime those issues came up, he was ready to fight for the farmer in Mississippi.” England said Wallace also approached legislation collaboratively, often putting policy ahead of personal recognition. 
“He talked to me about his bill on the House side and the work that he had put in, and basically just offered to work with me,” England said. “Price was the kind of guy that it didn’t seem to matter whose name was on the bill. He just wanted to see something get done.” 
Whether either proposal becomes law remains uncertain.
England said restoring the ballot initiative process will likely require additional negotiations before it can gain enough legislative support. Banks said he expects to reintroduce Brown’s criminal justice proposals alongside other legislators who shared Brown’s commitment to the issue.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: State fund helps 911 centers consolidate, with more mergers on the way
description: South Dakota has awarded more than $630,000 in the last year to facilitate three emergency dispatch consolidations, using funds from a statewide fee increase on phone lines that lawmakers approved to support efficiency and equipment upgrades. The consolidations were recommended in a 2025 efficiency report commissioned by the South Dakota 911 Coordination Boa[...]
text:
(Photo illustration by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota has awarded more than $630,000 in the last year to facilitate three emergency dispatch consolidations, using funds from a statewide fee increase on phone lines that lawmakers approved to support efficiency and equipment upgrades.
The consolidations were recommended in a 2025 efficiency report commissioned by the South Dakota 911 Coordination Board. The report recommended the board financially assist consolidation efforts and target consolidations of centers with low call volumes, staffing shortages and high costs per 911 call.
The board created a grant program last year for consolidation costs and equipment upgrades using a portion of funds from a statewide $2 monthly fee on phone lines and 2% tax on prepaid wireless services. State lawmakers raised the fee from $1.25 to $2 in 2024 and made the increase permanent last year.
The board puts $80,000 a month into the 911 efficiency grant fund, which currently has $640,000 in it.
Seven of the state’s 32 dispatch centers were identified as consolidation candidates in the 2025 report. The board has awarded funding for three consolidations so far:

$65,370 for Sanborn County and the Mitchell Police Department in October 2025.
$237,744 for Miner County and Lake County in October 2025.
$327,121 for Lawrence County and Spearfish this month.

The other centers identified as consolidation candidates are in Spink, Moody, Fall River and Butte counties.
Spearfish and the Lawrence County dispatch center in Deadwood are 15 miles apart in the Black Hills. The two plan to merge by January, with Lawrence County’s dispatch center absorbing Spearfish’s center and one of its dispatchers. The move will cut two dispatch positions.
Jamie Pesicka Olson, with the Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office, told board members the consolidation would ensure Lawrence County residents receive dependable emergency communications.
“It improves coordination and operability and efficiency,” Pesicka Olson said.
Michelle DeNeui, a state 911 board member who recused herself from the award decision because she works for Spearfish, said the county is an “oddball” because it had two dispatch centers. Most dispatch centers serve multiple counties.
A map of South Dakota dispatch center locations and their coverage areas prior to recently approved consolidations. (Courtesy of South Dakota Department of Public Safety)
The grants can help county commissions get past the initial hurdle of short-term consolidation costs, said Jason Husby, the state’s 911 coordinator.
“This is where previous consolidations fell: Two agencies wanted to join, they see this initial cost and then they back out of it,” Husby said.
Perkins County Sheriff Kelly Serr, who chairs the 911 board and the subcommittee that reviews applications before they come to the board, said the Spearfish-Lawrence County merger would pay for itself within nine years.
The Miner-Lake consolidation should be wrapped up by the end of the year, said April Denholm, director of Lake County 911 Communications. Radio equipment and software still need to be installed and tested. The grant primarily covered those costs.
Consolidation makes sense for smaller, rural counties, Denholm said. While the average Miner County resident likely won’t notice much change, it can mean faster response times and cost savings for the county.
“With Miner being a much less populated county, running a full-time dispatch center is a drain. Running a dispatch center is a drain for any county, but making sure you have someone there 24/7 is more difficult with a smaller county,” Denholm said.
Before the Miner-Lake consolidation, Miner County Dispatch had also covered Sanborn County’s emergency calls. Denholm said her center couldn’t absorb Sanborn’s needs, which is why Sanborn merged with the Mitchell Police Department dispatch.
Crow Creek Sioux Tribe and Buffalo County dispatch centers, in central South Dakota, are working to merge with the Winner Police Department dispatch, according to the Department of Public Safety. The board has not yet received a funding request for that consolidation.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Okefenokee Swamp clinches World Heritage status, officially joining ranks of top natural wonders
description: The Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge is now a World Heritage site.  The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization’s World Heritage committee approved the addition around midnight Saturday morning in Georgia time and about 1 p.m. in Busan, South Korea, where the meeting was held. The decision was reached without debate from the inter[...]
text:
Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge has been named a UNESCO World Heritage site. Larry Woodward/U.S. Fish and Wildlife ServiceThe Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge is now a World Heritage site. 
The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization’s World Heritage committee approved the addition around midnight Saturday morning in Georgia time and about 1 p.m. in Busan, South Korea, where the meeting was held. The decision was reached without debate from the international committee set up to recognize sites of universal environmental or cultural importance, but the effort to join that coterie was more than four decades in the making.
“The Okefenokee is a place where nature still reigns,” Kim Bednarek, executive director of Okefenokee Swamp Park and Adventures, said in an acceptance speech. “Across more than 400,000 acres, water, fire, peat and time continue to shape an intact wetland, reminding us that conservation is about protecting the natural systems that sustain life itself.” 
Georgia Rivers Executive Director Rena Peck described the celebration in a phone call from Busan with a lot of clapping and cheering in the background.
Kim Bednarek, executive director of Okefenokee Swamp Park and Adventures, in Busan, South Korea, with a stuffed gator. Rena Peck/Georgia Rivers
“Everyone’s just thrilled,” she said. “People from all countries are coming up to congratulate us. It’s just a vision of world peace. You have all these different nations caring about protecting their treasures and sharing those treasures with the world, and the world is recognizing the Okefenokee.”
In a phone call after the hearing, Bednarek said the crowd of international diplomats and cultural experts were going crazy for a particular swampy souvenir – plush Okefenokee alligators.
“I’m going to tell you, the plush gators have been the biggest hit,” she said with a laugh. “Everyone loves the plush alligator. American alligators are the iconic charismatic megafauna for the Okefenokee. In the Okefenokee, we know them as swamp puppies, and here, the little plushies are being handed out as swamp puppies, and everyone is absolutely loving them and it’s a great way for them to get excited and to learn about the Okefenokee.” 
A boon for tourism and education
A lot more of those plush swamp puppies could soon be on store shelves in south Georgia, along with gator keychains, magnets, hats and more.
A 2024 Conservation Fund report found that the number of people visiting the Okefenokee each year could double from 800,000 to 1.6 million by 2035 if it were to become a World Heritage site. 
Some local residents have been wary of what the increased attention might mean for the swamp and the neighboring communities. But Gov. Brian Kemp celebrated the World Heritage designation as a win for those communities in a statement.
“An important part of our state’s heritage and economy, this is a fitting recognition for the Okefenokee that will further strengthen rural communities that surround it,” Kemp said.
In recommending the Okefenokee be added to the list, UNESCO praised the U.S. Department of Fish and Wildlife for its effective management of the land, but noted that it is vulnerable to a variety of threats, including climate change, water management, mining interests and “the projected increase in tourism.”
An increase in tourism at natural wonders like the Okefenokee sometimes means an increase in dangerous or damaging behavior, but Bednarek said the swamp is protected in that regard by its size and remoteness.
“We have 120 miles of water trails in the Okefenokee, which means you can really only access about 2% of the entire national wildlife refuge on those trails,” she said. “So there’s not an opportunity to harm the swamp because you can’t access it. The real opportunity is in the communities, in the gateway communities of Charlton County and Ware County and Clinch County in Georgia, and in Baker County in Florida to really see an uptick in tourism and have pride in this incredible place.”
Larry Winslett, the endangered species issue leader for the Sierra Club Georgia Chapter, agreed.
“In the future, somebody might slap some big hotels next door or something like that, I suppose it could happen with that,” he said. “But there’s more of a concern on that issue at places like Stone Mountain, Jekyll Island, Arabia Mountain, places like that that do get a tremendous amount of visitors.”
Ancestral lands
Speaking from Busan, where she addressed the UNESCO committee, Tracie Revis said she hopes the new designation will encourage people to learn about the Muscogee (Creek) Nation, which she is a member of. The Muscogee and other Native American communities lived in and around the swamp for thousands of years until they were forcibly removed in the 1800s.
The name Okefenokee comes from the Muscogee language and means “land of the trembling earth,” Revis said, a reference to the way the thick peat moves on top of the water.
“It is our ancestral lands,” she said. “It’s lands that we lost after 1814 after the Treaty of Fort Jackson, but it served as a refuge, it served as a homeland, it served as a place that had a lot of meaning for us.”
“We believe culturally that the trees are older, the water is older, and it remembers our stories and our voices,” she added. “So for us to be able to be a part of this celebration and everything moving forward, it creates a healing for our community.”
The park contains information on Native American culture and linguistics, and Revis said work is underway for more educational experiences.
‘A shooting star’
The Okefenokee now joins natural wonders like the Grand Canyon and Yellowstone National Park.
Its biodiversity helped the swamp win the day in Busan. It’s one of the world’s largest naturally driven freshwater ecosystems and home to at least 856 plant species, 48 mammal species and 238 bird species, 39 fish species and 90 reptile and amphibian species, according to UNESCO. 
Last year, Alabama-based Twin Pines Minerals abandoned plans to mine valuable minerals near the refuge. The new designation does not prevent any kind of nearby development, but Bednarek said she feels optimistic that the new honor will help ensure the land surrounding the park will be protected.
“The direction is – it’s a shooting star,” she said. “And I think it’s game over for talking about the Okefenokee and having to talk about a mine at the same time.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont expands housing investment program
description:
The investments will allow new projects to move forward at a more affordable price, according to the state treasurer. The financing is available through the treasurer’s Invest in Vermont program.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont expands housing investment program.
text:
Vermont State Treasurer Mike Pieciak chats before a groundbreaking ceremony at the Cambrian Way housing complex in Burlington in August 2025. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Chris Mays was first published in the Brattleboro Reformer on July 21, 2026.
BERLIN — An additional $25 million is now available in low-interest financing to help spur new housing, job creation and affordability across Vermont. 
“Our state continues to be in desperate need of more housing,” Vermont Treasurer Mike Pieciak said Tuesday at a news conference. “Housing in Vermont is simply too expensive, whether you are a renter, whether you’re a first-time homebuyer, or whether you’re somebody that’s lived in your home for 30 years and is trying to maintain the home and trying to keep up with property taxes.”
The financing is available through the treasurer’s Invest in Vermont program, which uses 12.5% of the state’s average daily cash balance to provide low-interest loans for housing and economic development projects without spending tax dollars.
A request for proposals went out Tuesday. Proposals are due Sept. 4. 
The program was formerly called “10% in VT.” The Legislature recently expanded the program’s lending capacity by 2.5 percentage points in this year’s major housing bill, S.328. Now, the program has been renamed Invest in Vermont. 
To date, the program has been used to invest more than $130 million into housing and other initiatives across Vermont, according to an announcement. 
“Without spending a single tax dollar, those investments have leveraged over $600 million in outside capital, supporting nearly 1,700 units of high-quality housing for Vermonters of all kinds, including working families, seniors, and those exiting homelessness,” the announcement states.
The funding is also credited with creating nearly 200 permanent, good-paying jobs. 
When Pieciak was first elected treasurer 3½ years ago, his office looked at what tools are available to confront the housing issue. He said his team knows that “there is so much more that we need to do.”
“We went to the Legislature and asked if they would consider giving us even more authority to expand our 10% in Vermont program to 12.5%, and that is exactly what they did,” he said. “We want to thank the Legislature for their support and their confidence in us to invest this money wisely.”
Pieciak said the investments allow projects to move forward at a more affordable price. In March, he announced The Village at Winston Prouty in Brattleboro would receive $4 million in financing through the program. 
Alex Farrell, the commissioner of housing and community development, said the governor is “extremely grateful to the treasurer and his whole team for the partnership that they have displayed, not only with Invest in Vermont and really focusing these funds on housing, but also on some of our initiatives to create more innovative ways to deliver housing.”
“We are going to continue to push on the front to find new ways that large and small projects can have a fast track through the regulatory process,” he said, “because it’s so important that residential construction can happen in rural Vermont.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont expands housing investment program.

name: Missouri Independent
title: ‘E pluribus unum’ is not a slogan. It’s a choice
description: Like two sides of a coin imprinted with the nation’s motto, “e pluribus unum” — out of many, one — America’s political factions are cast in opposition, but they are intrinsically bound together as parts of a larger whole. From the beginning, the United States has aspired to build a more perfect union. When our founders […]
text:
The 2026 NCSL Legislative Summit will bring together state lawmakers and legislative staff from the 50 states and U.S. territories from July 27-29 in Chicago. (Leontura/Getty Images).Like two sides of a coin imprinted with the nation’s motto, “e pluribus unum” — out of many, one — America’s political factions are cast in opposition, but they are intrinsically bound together as parts of a larger whole.
From the beginning, the United States has aspired to build a more perfect union. When our founders convened the Constitutional Convention in 1787, they disagreed about the structure of government, the balance of power and the protection of individual versus collective rights. But when they debated — and they often did, with great conviction and intensity — they honed their arguments on what they thought was best for the entire country, guided by the shared vision of a new nation established on the ideals of individual freedom, equality and opportunity.
Today, that shared commitment to America’s founding creed is under strain.
Most Americans feel exhausted by politics, and a growing number are unhappy with the way the political system is working. Worse, this unhappiness is showing up in unhealthy ways, with low trust in government and each other — a sense that the other side is the problem.
We are painfully aware that partisanship and distrust have grown. We see this too often, when people are reduced to disparaging labels, states are cast as simply red or blue, and the hostility in our politics produces no progress, leaving us all no better off, or worse than before. Our political parties appear deadlocked in a struggle for power, forgetting that they are inseparable sides of the nation’s democratic system, which depends not on who wins but on a shared commitment to the common good. Central to that commitment is a willingness to listen to opposing views, not simply to respond but to understand.
Disagreeing is one thing — it is rooted in our pluralist republic. But when we cannot find ways to work together, it becomes impossible to solve our problems. The founders understood this. They argued passionately, but they shared a deeper allegiance to the nation’s success and its posterity, and they were partners in creating and safeguarding a system that we all continue to rely on.
Whether we choose to engage in political warfare or civil debate is up to each of us. That’s as true in statehouses and city councils as it is at the family dinner table, in the community center, on the debate stage, or standing on opposite sides of a free speech zone. In each of these venues, we can choose to practice democracy by engaging in debate that is spirited, healthy and rooted in strong arguments rather than name calling — or worse, heeding the impulse to withdraw from political engagement altogether.
There are glimmers of hope.
Here in Chicago, as part of the nation’s largest public policy gathering of state legislators and staff from all 50 states and U.S. territories, our organizations, the National Conference of State Legislatures and The Pew Charitable Trusts, are working together to build connections across the political spectrum and share policy ideas and best practices that strengthen legislatures and serve communities nationwide. This follows a series of events held around the country, including a February “America at 250 Forum,” to bring people with opposing views together to discuss issues that matter to everyone. All of the events demonstrate a serious commitment to strengthening our democratic muscles at this historic moment for the country.
Legislators from different parties sitting together to discuss not only their politics but also their human connection and shared belief in the country demonstrates that, despite the spotlight on our divisions, the time is ripe to unite for a common cause. We need to see more unity from our leaders — and be willing to try it ourselves.
Today, Americans must recognize that our political differences are not inevitably divisive, because our futures are fundamentally connected. Politics are difficult, yes, but they do not need to be ugly. Finding common ground is welcome, but at a minimum, Americans need to find the space to connect with one another and the courage to engage in healthy and substantive discussion. We can do that by building up state and local institutions where individuals get to know each other personally and by overcoming the silos and sides we’ve allowed to define us. A far better approach is to deal with people face-to-face and with respect, even when we profoundly disagree.
In a time when polarization and mistrust are treated as inevitable, we encourage all Americans to recommit to the principles and institutions that bind us together: a common belief in individual rights and equality, the rule of law, the legitimacy of representative democracy and our shared pursuit of national prosperity.
As America honors its 250th anniversary, it’s important to say, unequivocally and collectively, that we’re grateful to our country’s founders for starting this great experiment. We care about each other, and we want our fellow citizens to be successful. And we are proud to be part of this diverse, complicated and hopeful country.
Shared beliefs like these are central to the American experiment. E pluribus unum — out of many, one — if we so choose.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Gretchen Whitmer quickly becomes Haley Stevens’s most prominent ally after a late game endorsement
description: DETROIT — Just hours after Gov. Gretchen Whitmer announced that she was endorsing U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Birmingham in her fight to win the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate race, the pair appeared at Teamsters hall in the Motor City to flex a bit. At a small meet and greet event with supporters […]
text:
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer speaks at a meet and greet event for U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens just hours after endorsing her bid for the Democratic U.S. Senate nomination at a Teamsters hall in Detroit, Mich. Also pictured: U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. July 24, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan AdvanceDETROIT — Just hours after Gov. Gretchen Whitmer announced that she was endorsing U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Birmingham in her fight to win the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate race, the pair appeared at Teamsters hall in the Motor City to flex a bit.
At a small meet and greet event with supporters and surrogates at the Michigan Conference of Teamsters Welfare Fund hall in Detroit, the energy in the room was palpable, and gave Whitmer a chance to add some major fire to Stevens’ campaign in the final stretch of the August primary.
“You’ve got to be willing to go everywhere, talk to everyone and stay focused on what Michiganders actually need to get ahead,” Whitmer said with Stevens and U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-South Carolina) standing beside her. “You’ve got to put solutions first, and politics last. And you gotta get shit done. I know Haley’s got what it takes to win.”
Whitmer officially endorsed Stevens on Friday. The nod brings new enthusiasm to Stevens’ campaign as she faces a tough election Aug. 4 against the progressive Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, who commands an army of energetic young followers and a broad coalition of Democrats looking for a change.
U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (center) speaks at meet and greet event in Detroit with Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (right) and U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina (left). July 24, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
Stevens had long been the frontrunner for most of the race, but ceded some ground to El-Sayed and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow of Royal Oak. As voters became more intrigued by McMorrow and El-Sayed, Stevens fell in the polls and has been fighting back to regain her position in the race.
A big opportunity came when McMorrow exited the race earlier this month, as both Stevens and El-Sayed began vying for McMorrow’s voters. It appears, however, that neither candidate grabbed a more than 50% share of McMorrow’s supporters, especially after McMorrow decided to not endorse Stevens or El-Sayed, saying only that she would wholeheartedly back the winner of the contest.
U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (center) meets with supporters after an event in Detroit with Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, who endorsed her as the U.S. Senate primary winds down. July 24, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
A finding in that same poll showed at least 34% of undecided Democratic primary voters would be swayed by Whitmer’s endorsement if she decided to throw her political capital behind one of the candidates.
On Friday, Whitmer chose Stevens. Within a few hours, Stevens’ campaign announced a meet and greet event with Teamsters and other supporters, which also featured Clyburn. Prior to the governor’s inclusion on the bill, Clyburn could have been labeled as her most prominent supporter at the function, but Whitmer stole the show.
“If you want to send a fighter to Washington D.C., and you’re ready to take back the U.S. Senate; if you’re ready to show the rest of the country how Michigan gets the job done, vote for Haley Stevens on Aug. 4,” Whitmer said.
Clyburn still used his might as a longtime representative to make the case for Stevens, who recent polling shows is ahead in the predominantly Black city of Detroit.
“I made it known months ago where I stood on this race,” Clyburn said. “This may be the third time I’ve been here, and each time, I took steps to go places and make it known my support for Haley Stevens.”
U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina speaks at a meet and greet event for U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens just hours after Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer endorsed her bid for the Democratic U.S. Senate nomination at a Teamsters hall in Detroit, Mich. July 24, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
With so much on the line in 2026 — control of Congress but also Michigan’s executive offices and the state Legislature — Clyburn said destiny was now in the voters’ hands.
Stevens has long made the argument that she is the better candidate to face Republican former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers of White Lake in the general election. Rogers’ campaign and national Republican outfits have also signaled that they would likely feel better about facing El-Sayed in the general election due to his more progressive beliefs, which they have labeled as communist, with the GOP is banking on the fact that they can use that against him.
Either way, Clyburn said all the rhetoric or flashy campaigning in the world won’t win the election, it’s going to take getting Detroiters to the polls.
“We’ve got to do what’s necessary to put candidates forward who understand what it is to represent the dreams and aspirations of working men and women,” Clyburn said. “That’s why we’re in this place, because we’re here to honor the dreams and the aspirations of people who work every day, trying to make ends meet, trying to do what is necessary to prepare a future for their children and grandchildren.”
“Haley has done that,” Clyburn said.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Vermilion Parish senator wants to join the ‘new space race’
description: Around 200 Vermilion Parish residents packed the Abbeville Rotary Club’s largest meeting in its 90-year history Wednesday, hoping to have their questions answered and learn new details on a rumored aerospace company land deal on the parish’s coast They received some answers and plenty of reassurances from their representative in the Louisiana Senate, Bob Hen[...]
text:
The SpaceX Starship V3 is seen docked at a launch pad at Starbase on May 22, 2026, in Boca Chica Beach, Texas. (Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images)Around 200 Vermilion Parish residents packed the Abbeville Rotary Club’s largest meeting in its 90-year history Wednesday, hoping to have their questions answered and learn new details on a rumored aerospace company land deal on the parish’s coast
They received some answers and plenty of reassurances from their representative in the Louisiana Senate, Bob Hensgens.
The possible project would be part of a “new space race,” he told the assembled crowd at the Erath Community Center, one its residents would do well not to be left behind in.
“We can run from tomorrow, but tomorrow is coming, so we better face it with strong, safe hearts,” he said.
Vermilion Parish would also need to strengthen its infrastructure and school system to withstand the sudden influx of new residents such a project may bring, he noted.
The senator called a question about the long-term impact on families already living nearby “a tough one,” acknowledging that along with new jobs, rising property values and new resources for schools, there would be costs as well.
“We have to admit there will be challenges: short-term construction traffic, noise, and some pressure on housing and services in the growth areas.” But, he added, “we have time to prepare.”
The key, Hensgens said, would be “minimizing the downsides, while maximizing the upsides.”
That’s if the project comes to fruition at all.
Hensgens repeatedly emphasized that he was not aware of any deal having been closed on a land purchase in Vermilion Parish by SpaceX or any other aerospace company: “Like all of you, I’ve heard nothing but rumors since March.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a previous interview, Hensgens told The Current he believes his declining to sign an NDA, a new practice by the state’s economic development agency, Louisiana Economic Development, for major industrial development projects, may be the reason he has been kept out of the loop.
“That’s probably why I don’t have the details for some of these questions,” he told The Current earlier this month.
Still, Hensgens said he’s “taking the possibility serious.”
“The fundamentals of the parish line up extremely well,” he said Wednesday, adding that he anticipates a net benefit should the project come to pass.
“This possible project would diversify our economy,” he said. “Our beloved oil and gas, farming and fishing, our ports along the Gulf and coastal waterways, Freshwater Bayou will all become vital corridors for rocket commerce. UL Lafayette, our public school system, regional universities will gain powerful new avenues.”
While making comparisons to projects such as SpaceX’s facility near Brownsville, Texas, and Meta’s massive data center project currently under construction in Richland Parish with regards to the potential economic impact of such a project in Vermilion Parish, Hensgens didn’t address related environmental concerns.
In Texas, 58 households are currently embroiled in a lawsuit with SpaceX over alleged sonic-boom damages from the company’s launches. New Louisiana laws passed during the most recent legislative session would prevent Vermilion Parish residents from filing such lawsuits in case of damages to their homes or any quality of life impacts, should the company set up shop here.
State and federal regulators have also documented multiple environmental violations at the company’s Texas facility, which is located directly next to the Boca Chica Wildlife Refuge.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
In 2024, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality found SpaceX had discharged industrial wastewater without a permit four times at its Boca Chica facility, after the EPA separately warned the company of Clean Water Act violations. Ultimately leading to SpaceX agreeing to pay a $3,750 penalty without admitting wrongdoing.
Meta’s Richland Parish project, while not yet completed, has also drawn environmental and cost-of-living concerns, especially with regards to its projected energy and water use.
Meanwhile, the company is currently fighting a court order to disclose data on that anticipated energy use as well as the number of jobs it actually projects to create in the area.
None of the questions related to these issues, despite being posed in response to the club’s request for Q&A input on Facebook, were selected for discussion at the meeting. No additional questions were allowed at the event. Hensgens, flanked by a police escort, left the event without answering any additional questions from press outside of the venue.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Omaha moviemaker says state-funded venture paralyzed as DED stretches suspension of $5M grant
description: OMAHA — Randy J. Goodwin sits alone these days at Fallen Giant Films headquarters, a space rented with state dollars that stretches across much of the 11th floor of a trendy midtown Omaha highrise.  Eight months ago he was surrounded by interns, office workers and a crew that shot and processed movie segments. Since December, […]
text:
Founder Randy J. Goodwin stands in Fallen Giant Films Omaha headquarters. He wrote a script for “The Father’s Fight” movie about  a mixed martial artist who lost everything. Goodwin, shown in the poster, would have a star role but he said the project stalled along with a $5 million state grant to the company.  (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — Randy J. Goodwin sits alone these days at Fallen Giant Films headquarters, a space rented with state dollars that stretches across much of the 11th floor of a trendy midtown Omaha highrise. 
Eight months ago he was surrounded by interns, office workers and a crew that shot and processed movie segments. Since December, not even Goodwin shows up regularly.
Fallen Giant Film production offices span much of the 11th floor of the Blackstone Plaza building. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
“We can’t work. We can’t do post production. We haven’t been able to pay anybody — we are still in suspension,” said Goodwin, an Omaha-born actor and director whose Fallen Giant company was awarded a $5 million slice of the $235 million North and South Omaha Recovery Grant program. 
So far, the state over two years has paid Goodwin’s venture nearly $3.4 million. Seen in television series such as “Vampire Diaries” and “Dynasty,” his goal was to build a Hollywood-esque industry in his hometown. More specifically, the contract with the Nebraska Department of Economic Development called for creation of at least three Nebraska film and TV projects in qualified low-income census tracts to help prove the viability of a local film sector. It  called for a focus on retaining youth and growing the economy and community.
 ‘Sweating us out’ 

The Nebraska Examiner first reported on the Fallen Giant funding freeze earlier this year. In response to questions about a status update, DED said that Fallen Giant had produced three film projects, per the terms of its contract. But the state agency cites Fallen Giant’s alleged “significant noncompliance with respect to the financial management of its grant funds.”
“Do not touch” sign points to files stacked in Fallen Giant offices that Randy J. Goodwin said contain receipts and records the state is reviewing. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
During suspension, the state said, it has authorized payments for what DED believes is “reasonable compensation” for Fallen Giant staff to answer compliance questions and for “core operating expenses.”
Goodwin, who disagrees with the DED assessment overall, said his operation is paralyzed. He said the state since December has frozen funding, save for roughly $60,000. He said his team has produced receipts and answers but that the state officials keep adding demands. Noting the state’s own growing budget deficit, Goodwin believes DED is “sweating us out” until Fallen Giant “walks away” from remaining grant dollars.
DED, in a statement last week, said it has spent a “considerable amount of resources” working with Fallen Giant and that the group’s expenses continue to be evaluated to ensure they were “reasonable, allowable and allocable.” That includes a November gala at the downtown Omaha Holland Center that Goodwin said cost about $31,000 and drew an estimated 600 guests, including various public officials. 
“What we brought was Hollywood,” said Goodwin. “Everything we have to do has to be on a level not seen in Nebraska, and we’re doing it on a shoestring budget.”
Randy J. Goodwin, founder and CEO, and Chaysen Beacham, head of productions, during a Fallen Giant event at the Holland Center in Omaha. (Courtesy of Bryce Johnson and Zach Wagner)
Both sides say they continue to work toward a resolution that could include resuming award payments. But the DED said a possible remedy also includes asking for a return of funds already distributed. 
The situation has prompted Goodwin to seek legal counsel. Attorney Bill McGinn argues that DED guidance to grant awardees was lacking and that expenses incurred by Fallen Giant are allowable under Internal Revenue Service rules. He believes it is the state that is not complying with contractual obligations.
“They say you need ABC. We give them ABC and they say now we need D, E and F,” said McGinn. 
 Unprecedented grant program

The conflict marks another in a complicated, unprecedented state grant program rooted originally in pandemic recovery funds intended to revive North and South Omaha and marked at various times over the past four years by controversy, community complaints and celebration. The funding source later was swapped for state general funds to, as lawmakers said at the time, allow more time for multi-year projects to develop. Dollars are to be expended before 2027 wraps up.
Movie posters adorn the Blackstone Plaza Fallen Giant Films office space, which has a view of urban Omaha. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
DED confirmed that it has placed another North-South grant recipient’s funding under suspension and has placed multiple others on “corrective action plans” to address areas of noncompliance. 
To date, the agency said that DED has terminated four contracts with small businesses that had been awarded North-South grants but were unable to begin their projects.
Another dozen awardees in the “small business support” category never entered into an official contract with the DED, the agency said, though each had been selected to receive a $50,000 award. 
In all, roughly 130 groups and businesses were announced as DED choices for the $235 million grant program during back-to-back press conferences in January 2024 that were led by Gov. Jim Pillen and Omaha’s mayor in both North and South Omaha.
Originally, 367 applications were vetted.
Award amounts ranged, on the high end, from $39 million to a South Omaha coalition that has launched multiple projects to rejuvenate the Q Street corridor to, on the lower end, $50,000 awarded to entrepreneurs. About 80 small business ventures originally were announced as winners of a $50,000 award.
Then-DED director K.C. Belitz said that over a five-year period he expected 9,250 new jobs in North and South Omaha to materialize as a result of the slate of projects and their “ripple effect.”
 Does dream die? 

Randy J. Goodwin talks about a documentary his company produced on the ascension of a football program at Omaha Westview High. Post-production efforts have stopped, he said. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
On a recent visit to Fallen Giant, Goodwin was the lone person in the grantee’s Blackstone Plaza headquarters where he said he is behind on rent that runs about $10,000 a month. Files sat piled on tables. Hollywood film posters decorated the walls.  A hallway was lined with tall banners featuring movie projects that Goodwin said were started as part of the grant but not released.
“When I’m here I’m still working, pumping out scripts…”
Goodwin said three of 11 team members, including himself, technically remain with the company but aren’t currently being paid. He said the DED “forbade us to do any work that would be construed as part of the (grant).”
Among expenses being challenged, Goodwin said, are meal reimbursements at 88 Tactical, which he once represented as brand ambassador. Goodwin said that relationship ended when he got the grant so he believes there should be no conflict. He also said the meal prices for Fallen Giant guests there were more reasonably priced than other options.
Asked about private investors, Goodwin said some potential funders have gone cold, considering his situation “too murky.”
Randy J. Goodwin in part of Blackstone Plaza’s 11th floor. Goodwin said the landlord allowed use of this space for production, as it was not yet leased. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
He said he has turned some of his attention toward an unrelated real estate venture in Oklahoma, where he also has a cabin to stay. He said most of his original team members have moved on, unable to pay their Omaha rent.
Goodwin said he is pursuing a meeting with Pillen. 
Sometimes, Goodwin said, he questions whether to continue to pursue his dream to build a piece of Hollywood in Omaha. 
“If home is going to treat me like this, I’ll go build it somewhere else,” Goodwin said. Then he adds: “But I think the people want me here.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: DACA recipients did everything right, yet 14 years later they are more vulnerable than ever
description: Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, hailed as the most successful immigrant integration policy ever, gets weaker daily as the Trump administration chips away at it, write Christina Getrich and Giani Garcia, which is why a permanent fix is needed.
text:
Supporters of the DACA program rally outside the U.S. Supreme Court in 2020. (Photo by Robin Bravender/States Newsroom)As the 14th anniversary of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program passes, recipients’ futures are deeply uncertain. Once lauded by scholars as “the most successful policy of immigrant integration,” many recipients are now abruptly losing gains they experienced with DACA, raising alarm about the possibility of downward mobility. 
Giani is a public health professional who, with the benefit of DACA, earned degrees from prestigious Ivy League universities and worked as a health analyst, contributed to COVID-19 response efforts, and supported community health initiatives in the D.C. metropolitan region.
“I [Giani] was enrolled in a doctorate program when I submitted my DACA renewal to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services within the recommended four- to five-month window prior to my work permit’s expiration.  Like many other recipients, I did everything right: I had carefully followed every renewal requirement since getting DACA in 2013 and never experienced a significant delay–not even during the pandemic. 
“However, this time, I waited anxiously for several months, checking every day to see if my renewal was approved, before my work authorization expired in March. Instead, I received an email notifying me that my university position was being terminated effective immediately since my work authorization expired. 




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




“As a result, I became unemployed and uninsured, and faced tuition bills, uncertainty regarding my academic future, and the potential loss of opportunities for which I had worked for years. The most challenging aspect of this experience was that it did not result from any failure to comply with requirements, but from delays beyond my control.”
Giani is unfortunately not alone—thousands of the 500,000+ DACA recipients nationwide are experiencing similar renewal delays after more than a decade of increased stability with DACA. 
DACA was created by executive order in 2012 as a stop-gap measure to address the legal situation of undocumented immigrant youth. Recipients are employed across all sectors of the U.S. economy, though DACA protections only last for two years, requiring regular renewal. Since President Donald Trump’s initial attempt to terminate DACA in 2017, recipients have experienced ongoing legal uncertainty, described as “a non-stop roller coaster,” as courts assess the program’s legality and future.
Fourteen years later, recipients are well into adulthood — they are an average age of 31 — and focused on building careers and families. This reality raises the stakes of these renewal delays. Health care professionals like physicians and nurses can no longer care for patients while educators worry about the impact of their abrupt departure on students. Recipients are losing homes that required years of effort to purchase and many are exhausting savings accounts, facing mounting debt, and defaulting on loans.
Additionally, they encounter difficulties renewing driver’s licenses, depending on state requirements, restricting their ability to drive legally and safely. Many are also canceling travel plans out of fear. This livelihood disruption is also cascading to their mixed-status families since about 240,000 U.S. citizen children have at least one recipient parent. These delays are also taking a major emotional toll on recipients. 
Simultaneously, recipients’ protection from deportation has diminished. By mid-2025, Trump administration officials asserted that recipients were not automatically protected from deportation and urged them to self-deport. By the end of 2025, 174 DACA recipients had indeed been deported. In April 2026, the Justice Department published a new precedent decision further weakening recipients’ deportation protections. Meanwhile, in April, a new father in Texas was detained while delivering milk to his daughter in the NICU and in May, an Arizona resident was aggressively removed from her home without justification. 
 Yet the United States continues to benefit substantially from recipients, who have contributed tens of billions to the economy and paid a cumulative $40 billion in taxes. Terminating DACA would result in the loss of an estimated 440,000 employees from the workforce, upending industries and pushing families into poverty. The total economic loss could reach up to $1 trillion. Beyond economic contributions, recipients bolster the wellbeing of family members and make important everyday contributions to their communities.
These threats to recipients’ livelihoods are not incidental, but rather demonstrate how the Trump administration is actively “chipping away” at DACA. Yet the majority of Americans have long supported providing recipients with a pathway to citizenship. As May’s Senate Spotlight Forum underscored, there is new urgency in passing the bipartisan DREAM Act.
As the limitations of temporary measures like DACA become clearer with every passing day of the second Trump administration, it is beyond time for Congress to give recipients like Giani the permanent solution they have earned.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Most school systems will hit base $60,000 teacher pay, after some ‘difficult’ decisions
description: The majority of Maryland’s 24 public school systems met a July 1 deadline to boost their starting teachers' pay to a minimum salary of $60,000, but for some smaller districts the higher salaries came at the cost of cuts elsewhere in their budgets.
text:
Front cover of Blueprint for Maryland's Future implementation plan.The majority of Maryland’s 24 public school systems met a July 1 deadline to boost their starting teachers’ pay to a minimum salary of $60,000, but for some smaller districts the higher salaries came at the cost of cuts elsewhere in their budgets.
The salary deadline is part of the state’s multiyear, multibillion-dollar education reform plan known as the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future. It’s also a mandate for which there is little wiggle room for local districts: At a legislative hearing in March, an official with the Accountability and Implementation Board, which oversees the Blueprint, said the July 1 date was firm and there was no waiver.
But some local school officials said it wasn’t easy to meet that July 1 deadline.
Denise Sopa, chief financial officer for Cecil County Public Schools, said in an email Tuesday that a first-year, 10-month teacher will receive a starting salary of $60,086 for the 2026-27 school year. But “in order to meet the state requirement and balance the budget in general, we needed to reduce 104 positions,” she said, including 60 teachers, 30 support staff and 14 administrators.
Jodi Colman, assistant superintendent for academics and student services in Dorchester County, said some restructuring had to be done to hit the salary mark and balance the system’s 2026-27 budget. One of the results: an increase in classes sizes – possibly from 18 to 22 – because the school system wasn’t able to fund as many teacher positions.
Colman said Dorchester schools, which have about 4,500 students, also had to resort to a reduction in force “in order to make sure we were funding the classroom positions because we wanted to have the least impact on the schools as possible.”
Colman acknowledged the work on this year’s budget “was difficult. We don’t have a lot of extras around here.”
House Ways and Means Committee Vice Chair Del. Jessica Feldmark (D-Howard), right, and Del. Eric Ebersole (D-Baltimore County) at a Feb. 4, 2026, hearing. (Photo by Joe Wicke/Maryland Matters)
But legislators who support the Blueprint, such as Del. Jessica Feldmark (D-Howard), said Friday the salary increase is an investment that helps not only the education profession, but also the students.
“Within the context of whatever budget challenges we’re facing, we have to remember that this is about investing in our children and in our future, investing in the future of our workforce, our economy, our democracy, and that investment is something we have to take seriously,” said Feldmark, vice chair of the House Ways and Means Committee.
“If we want to have great schools, we need to be able to recruit and retain great educators, and recognizing their value and paying them a fair salary is a critical piece of that,” she said.
When AIB Executive Director Rachel Hise told a House subcommittee in March that there would be no waivers on the minimum salary requirement, just half of the state’s 24 school districts met the threshold: Allegany, Anne Arundel, Baltimore City, Baltimore County, Calvert, Carroll, Charles, Howard, Montgomery, Prince George’s, St. Mary’s and Washington counties. Starting salaries for those systems ranged from $60,000 even in Allegany and Carroll counties to $64,591 in Montgomery.
Since then, officials with Cecil, Dorchester, Frederick, Garrett, Harford, Queen Anne’s and Talbot counties said they have met the minimum salary requirement. The remaining counties either did not respond or said they are still working on it.
One of the penalties for failing to hit the deadline is that the AIB can withhold a certain amount of funding from a district until the $60,000 salary gets approved.
At least one school district continues to work on it: Somerset County, which had the state’s highest percentage of people living in poverty, at 20.3% in 2025, according to the U.S. Census.
Somerset schools remain in negotiations with their bargaining units, Superintendent W. David Bromwell said in an email Thursday. Bromwell said the district is aware of the $60,000 minimum salary requirement.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“Any budgetary item/mandate, can be difficult to complete for any MD Public School system, especially the smaller districts,” he wrote in his email.
Somerset officials have time on their side because they’ll have until Sept. 1 to send an attestation to the AIB to confirm the $60,000 minimum teacher salary has been met. That must also be done by all other school districts.
While some school systems struggled, or continue to struggle, officials in Frederick County said it was simply a matter of doing what had to be done.
“It was a requirement under the law. We did it. I hope everybody else did the same,” said Sarah Sirgo, chief of staff for Frederick County Public Schools.
Other school districts may have focused on the challenge to work on their budgets this year due to the salary mandate, but  Sirgo said she and her colleagues in Frederick don’t view it that way.
“We’re not like, ‘Oh well, if we’re going to pay teachers more, we can’t do X, Y, or Z,’” said Sirgo, who also serves as the district’s Blueprint coordinator. “When we build our budget, we have our strategic plan. We make sure that our budget is advancing the goals that we’re after.”
