name: Rhode Island Current
title: Quonset Business Park’s latest tenant: renters who already work there
description: For the first time in more than 50 years, a former U.S. Navy base turned industrial park in North Kingstown will feature housing under a lease agreement between Quonset Development Corporation and Moran Properties. The 60-year ground lease announced Wednesday authorizes a 140-unit workforce housing project on a roughly 7-acre property at the business park […[...]
text:
Workforce housing is coming to Quonset Business Park under a lease agreement between the Quonset Development Corporation and local developer, Moran Properties. (Photo by Laura Paton/Rhode Island Current)For the first time in more than 50 years, a former U.S. Navy base turned industrial park in North Kingstown will feature housing under a lease agreement between Quonset Development Corporation and Moran Properties.
The 60-year ground lease announced Wednesday authorizes a 140-unit workforce housing project on a roughly 7-acre property at the business park entrance on Gate Road off Route 1. 
The agreement marks the first residential component within the peninsula overlooking Narragansett Bay since the U.S. Naval Air Station was decommissioned and shut down in the mid-1970s, displacing the military members and their families who lived there. The land was repurposed in 2004 as an industrial park, managed by the quasi-public Quonset Development Corporation, and now boasts more than 260 companies with a combined 15,000 workers.
The residential development was the result of a competitive solicitation process meant to alleviate the state housing shortage, while providing a convenient and affordable option for business park employees and their families to live, said Steven King, Quonset managing director.
“With the high levels of need, the Park’s projected growth, and the influx of funding available to construct housing that is affordable for Rhode Island’s workforce, now is the time to consider the development of rental workforce housing within the Quonset Business Park,” King wrote in a December 2022 letter to the North Kingstown Planning Commission.
The 6.8-acre property sits across from a grocery store and other retail shops, with convenient access to public transportation via the Rhode Island Public Transit Authority, according to Quonset. 
While Quonset’s appointed board of directors has sole authority over commercial and industrial lease agreements and development in the business park, housing is not expressly listed as a permitted use — meaning that adding residential development requires a variance approved by both the board of directors and the town Planning Commission. The latter gave its blessing to the broad strokes of a residential plan in April 2023, following a series of four public hearings, according to meeting minutes published on the town website. It wasn’t until July 9, 2026, that Quonset’s board finalized the term sheet with the developer, following a complicated solicitation process in which a separate company submitted, then rescinded, its development proposal.
Steven Moran, president of Moran Properties, was not available for comment on Friday.
The final lease agreement requires that at least 40% of the one and two-bedroom units be designated as workforce housing, reserved for renters who earn no more than 120% of area median income — $96,120 for one-person, or $137,160 for a family of four, based on fiscal 2025 federal limits. And, those renters will pay more than 30% of their income on rent.
Another 10% of units will be designated as “low and moderate income housing,” reserved for renters who earn no more than 80% of area median income, as defined by state law.
Preference will be given to people who work in the business park or a 25-mile radius; federal, state or local government employees; and healthcare workers.
Town officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment Friday. 
A 6.8-acre property at the entrance of Quonset Business Park on Gate Road is slated to host a 140-unit workforce housing development. (Courtesy of Quonset Development Corp.)
It all comes back to sludge 
North Kingstown has historically maintained a strong relationship with the Quonset agency, receiving economic benefits including revenue from the industrial park’s development. But tensions emerged this spring amid allegations of lack of transparency by Quonset’s governing board, and concerns about how heavy industrial projects were affecting the health and safety of nearby residents.
A preliminary lease agreement allowing a renewable energy developer to build a sludge processing plant in the West Davisville section of the park, less than one mile from homes and schools, became a top point of contention between residents, town officials, and Quonset leaders, spawning a pair of lawsuits and a series of policy protections by the Rhode Island General Assembly. The lease remains on hold, awaiting results of a joint legislative study commission in June 2027 on the broader shortage of sewage treatment options in Rhode Island, but public trust remains shaky.
Jim Sheehan, a Democratic candidate for Rhode Island’s open House District 31 seat whose campaign centers on reforming Quonset’s operations and relationship to its host community, worried that the new workforce housing project would again present problems of health and safety for renters living near heavy industrial operations.
“I think it’s a good idea in concept, but I’m not certain it’s suitable unless they tend to the environmental needs, and health and welfare of the people who would be residents,” Sheehan, a former state senator, said in an interview Friday. “There’s such a need for affordable housing, that you might not want to live in proximity to emissions and other potential health hazards, but you might not have much of a choice.”
Neighborhood impacts, including pollutants, are one of the considerations the town considered in reviewing and approving the variance required to allow residential development in Quonset Business Park. The proposed development site also sits next to a hotel, in a section known as the “Gateway District” which was “intentionally and thoughtfully planned and zoned” to blend with the commercial areas along Post Road, said Chelsea Siefert, Quonset’s chief operating officer. 
“We do not have concerns about this location,” Siefert said in an email Friday. “Housing is a logical next step to building out this section of the Business Park and helps us deliver affordable housing opportunities to Rhode Islanders.”
The lease includes the options for three, 10-year-apiece extensions and one, nine-year extension, with a $150,000 annual rent, though payment is deferred under a separate, sublease agreement for the building itself. There is also a sub-sublease for a management agency to oversee daily operations of the housing project, with rent paid upon the first certificate of occupancy for the first building.
The total project cost has not been determined, nor has the expected completion date.
Construction is expected to begin in late 2027, pending approval by Quonset’s technical review committee and state permitting regulators. Once finished, the project is expected to generate another $270,000 in revenue for the town under a payment-in-lieu of taxes agreement.

title: Iowa sales tax holiday is Aug. 7-8
description: Iowa’s Annual Sales Tax Holiday will take place Aug. 7-8, exempting clothing and footwear purchases under $100 from the state’s 6% sales tax and 1% local option sales taxes. The annual holiday — a feature in 20 other states — gives consumers some relief from sales taxes. Proponents of the holiday argue that it helps […]
text:
Iowa shoppers will not owe sales taxes on certain clothing and footwear purchases during the state's annual sales tax holiday Aug. 7-8. (Stock photo by Thanasis/Getty Images)Iowa’s Annual Sales Tax Holiday will take place Aug. 7-8, exempting clothing and footwear purchases under $100 from the state’s 6% sales tax and 1% local option sales taxes.
The annual holiday — a feature in 20 other states — gives consumers some relief from sales taxes. Proponents of the holiday argue that it helps economic growth because it increases retail activity.
Opponents of the holiday point to a study that says it does not help economic growth because consumers would have shopped at different times.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Kathrien Loughead, the vice president of State Tax Policy, said sales tax holidays suggest policymakers recognize that state sales taxes can discourage economic activity.

More information
See the list of items exempt from taxes, as well as items that will be taxable, and other information about Iowa’s Annual Sales Tax Holiday here.

“The prevalence of sales tax holidays points to deeper structural weaknesses in state tax codes: their existence reveals that the sales tax is overly burdensome throughout the rest of the year,” Loughead said in a news release. “If policymakers believe that suspending the sales tax for a single week, for example, can stimulate economic growth, they are implicitly acknowledging that the tax suppresses economic growth for the other 51 weeks.” 
Loughead added that state revenue losses from sales tax holidays are small and she believes revenue would have to be generated from elsewhere to make up for the losses, which would result in the state losing revenue.
“They inject unnecessary instability into government and business revenue streams; create administrative and compliance costs for businesses, governments, and consumers; and do not promote long-term economic growth,” Loughead said.
Iowa’s tax holiday is shorter than those in some other states, where exemptions can last up to a week and cover a broader range of consumer items.

name: VTDigger
title: Protesters again block access to ICE surveillance hub in Williston, prompting arrests
description:
Organizers said about a dozen people were arrested Friday morning at ICE’s National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Protesters again block access to ICE surveillance hub in Williston, prompting arrests.
text:
A person is carried to a vehicle by four Vermont State Troopers after being arrested for blocking the entrance to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center in Williston on Friday, July 24, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
WILLISTON — Police arrested a group of protesters at a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement surveillance office in Williston on Friday morning. The group intended to block ICE employees from accessing the facility by sitting or standing in front of its entrances, according to protest organizers. 
Julie Macuga, one of the organizers, said 13 people were taken into custody, most of whom came to the demonstration expecting to be arrested. State and local police carried several protesters out of an east-facing entrance to the building around 10 a.m.
Macuga said demonstrators gathered at the office, which has been the site of similar demonstrations and arrests, around 7:30 a.m. Friday. 

Protesters block the exterior entrance to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center in Williston on Friday, July 24, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Vermont State Police had not publicly identified those arrested as of midday Friday or what charges they might be facing. Macuga and other organizers described the protest as a response, among other reasons, to the shooting deaths by ICE agents earlier this month in Maine and Texas. 
The Williston facility, which is in the White Cap Business Park off Industrial Avenue, houses ICE’s National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center. Data collected at the office from publicly available sources, such as social media feeds, help ICE officers throughout the eastern U.S. know whom to arrest, according to federal records.
Several demonstrators Friday said that in addition to hindering the office’s operations, they wanted to draw more public attention to that work.
“I just find it reprehensible that this is in our town,” said Moki Fox of Williston, who was holding a hand-drawn poster of a large eyeball. “It’s just wrong. If I don’t stand up, who will? Everybody should be standing up.” 

 
A person is carried to a vehicle by three Vermont State Troopers after being arrested for blocking the entrance to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center in Williston on Friday, July 24, 2026. Video by Shaun Robinson/VTDigger

While protesters were brought out in handcuffs, Fox and about a dozen others stood in the building’s parking lot holding banners and signs and chanting “shame” at police. They also yelled, “You are not alone!” as protesters, who spanned a range of ages, were guided or carried out and put into state or Williston police cruisers. Some were driven off in a black van that did not appear to have any markings on the outside.
The facility is one of several U.S. Department of Homeland Security offices in and around Williston, many if not all of which have been the focus of anti-ICE demonstrations over the past year.

title: Evers pushes Trump to speed up DACA renewals
description: Gov. Tony Evers sent a letter Thursday to President Donald Trump and Wisconsin’s congressional delegation urging the White House to resolve delays in the processing of applications for the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program.  The DACA program has existed since the administration of President Barack Obama and allows people who were brought to the[...]
text:
DACA supporters rally outside the U.S. Supreme Court in 2019. (Photo by Robin Bravender/States Newsroom)Gov. Tony Evers sent a letter Thursday to President Donald Trump and Wisconsin’s congressional delegation urging the White House to resolve delays in the processing of applications for the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program. 
The DACA program has existed since the administration of President Barack Obama and allows people who were brought to the country as children without documentation to live and work in the U.S. 
There are 500,000 DACA recipients across the country and more than 5,000 in Wisconsin. The Trump administration has put their renewal applications on “processing holds.” For some of the program’s participants, those holds have now pushed their renewal beyond the deadline, putting their ability to obtain work permits and driver’s licenses at risk. 
Since its inception in 2012, the DACA program has been broadly popular among Democrats and Republicans. Earlier this year, Evers signed into law a bipartisan bill that allows DACA recipients to obtain occupational licenses from the state. 
But Trump attempted to end the program during his first term and amid his administration’s harsh crackdown on immigration, DACA recipients have been detained and deported despite their legal status. The delays in application processing have put even more people in legal limbo. 
“Mr. President, I urge you to end this harmful practice by your administration and resume expeditious processing and renewal of DACA applications,” Evers wrote. “And to Wisconsin’s Republican congressional delegation, I urge you to stand up for Wisconsin’s Dreamers, who will be or are up for renewals, and join me in demanding that the Trump Administration immediately identify and resolve the source of these unconscionable delays and resume processing and renewal of DACA applications, as Senator Baldwin, Congressman Pocan, and Congresswoman Moore have done. These hardworking members of our community should not endure the consequences of the Trump Administration’s failure to uphold the DACA program to basic standards.”

name: National
title: Measles cases have reached a 35-year high
description: Measles cases this year have surpassed all of 2025 to become the worst since the disease was declared eliminated in 2000, with cases now in 44 states and the District of Columbia, according to a federal report released Friday.  There were 2,318 confirmed cases as of July 23, compared with 2,289 in all of 2025, […]
text:
A nurse vaccinates a child at the Latino Community Development Agency on July 9, 2026, in Oklahoma City. As vaccination rates decline nationwide, measles cases have surpassed 2025 to the highest since the disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)Measles cases this year have surpassed all of 2025 to become the worst since the disease was declared eliminated in 2000, with cases now in 44 states and the District of Columbia, according to a federal report released Friday.  
There were 2,318 confirmed cases as of July 23, compared with 2,289 in all of 2025, with 93% of cases for both years being among unvaccinated people, mostly younger than 20. 
There have been fewer hospitalizations this year, 151 compared with 243 last year, and no deaths yet, compared with three in 2025. The highest number of new cases was in mid-January 2026, when there were almost 300 new cases. 
The largest number of current cases are in South Carolina (670), Utah (522), Texas (188), Virginia (176) and Pennsylvania (134). Except for Virginia, all those states have childhood vaccination rates below the 95% level considered necessary to prevent outbreaks among unvaccinated people as of the 2024-25 school year. 
Measles, whooping cough spike amid low vaccination rates

Virginia’s statewide rate was 95.6%, but the measles outbreak was in two rural counties west of Richmond where measles vaccination rates are less than 75%. 
The last time national cases were higher than 2025 and 2026 was in the 1990s as national vaccinations were still ramping up, with 9,643 cases in 1991 and almost 28,000 in 1990. 
Most states now have childhood vaccination rates below the 95% level considered necessary to prevent outbreaks among unvaccinated people, including people who choose not to be vaccinated and small children too young for the shots. 
Oklahoma has a low childhood vaccination rate of 88.7% and saw 20 cases last year, but only one so far this year. A foundation has sent a mobile health van around the state to vaccinate thousands of children. 
Delaware declared a new outbreak this week. The state’s first measles cases in a decade climbed to five cases in a few days. The state’s child vaccination rate is 94.1%. 
“High vaccination coverage has protected even the unvaccinated and undervaccinated because of herd protection, keeping measles at bay for the past few decades,”  said Dr. William Moss, director of the International Vaccine Access Center at Johns Hopkins University, in a published statement. 
“But in communities with pockets of susceptible individuals across a broad age range, measles has been able to take hold, infecting those who are susceptible and spreading rapidly,” he said.
The center used its own measles tracker to declare more cases in 2026 than last year as of July 21. 
The Pan American Health Organization is scheduled to review the U.S. measles status in November and consider revoking “elimination” status as it did for Canada last year.  
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Trump makes if official and endorses Jackson in race for Georgia governor
description: When President Donald Trump departed Georgia after his Cobb County rally Wednesday, he left something behind: fresh endorsements for governor nominee Rick Jackson and other aspiring GOP leaders who will be on the ballot in November. The president invited Jackson to join him on the stage, calling the Republican healthcare executive “a true champion for […]
text:
President Donald Trump and GOP governor candidate Rick Jackson share the stage at a White House event at Cobb County's Wheeler High School. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderWhen President Donald Trump departed Georgia after his Cobb County rally Wednesday, he left something behind: fresh endorsements for governor nominee Rick Jackson and other aspiring GOP leaders who will be on the ballot in November.
The president invited Jackson to join him on the stage, calling the Republican healthcare executive “a true champion for the people.”
Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who is running for governor, at a rally for her and U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff in Atlanta on May 31, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Jackson will face former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms to become the state’s next chief executive. Republican Gov. Brian Kemp has served two terms and is barred from seeking reelection.
Trump endorsed Jackson’s opponent, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, during the GOP primary, but he said Wednesday he had also been impressed by Jackson. Late Thursday, he followed up with a string of endorsements for Jackson and other Georgia Republican candidates on his social media website.
Sen. Greg Dolezal, a Cumming Republican and 2026 candidate for Georgia lieutenant governor speaks at a Trump rally near Marietta. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
“I watched this man run and he’s really phenomenal actually,” Trump said. “Because I liked the other side too. I was a big fan of the other side too. Two good men, frankly, but I watched him run and it was amazing what he was able to do. Very, very successful guy, and he decided he wanted to be governor because he thought he could do some really incredible things for the state, more so than have been done.”
Jones has not yet endorsed in the governor’s race. In an episode of the Atlanta Journal-Constitution’s “Politically Georgia” podcast, Jones said “We’ll see” when asked whether he would vote for Jackson, adding that he wants to keep Georgia under Republican leadership. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment Friday.
Sen. Brian Strickland, the Republican candidate for Georgia attorney general, speaks at an event with President Donald Trump at Wheeler High School. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Jackson, who grew up in the foster care system, has made his triumph over a difficult childhood a centerpiece of his campaign. Standing beside the president, he compared the new Trump savings accounts for children to help he had received as a child. If elected, Jackson said he would urge the state Legislature to match the federal government’s contribution toward the accounts, and if they don’t he pledged to pay for the match out of his own pocket.
State Rep. Tim Fleming, the Republican nominee for Georgia secretary of state, speaks at an event with President Donald Trump in Cobb County. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Children born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028 are eligible for a $1,000 pilot contribution from the federal government.
“I’m going to make sure that Georgia’s the best place to do business and reduce affordability to the lowest it’s ever been, and I’m going to be this man’s favorite governor,” Jackson said on stage Wednesday, pointing at Trump.
In a statement following the rally, Bottoms appeared to welcome the association between Jackson and Trump. Polling from data analytics firm Civiqs finds Trump’s approval rating 21 points underwater in Georgia, although he remains popular among Republicans.
“There’s a clear choice in this election: Rick Jackson would work for Donald Trump, I will work for Georgians,” Bottoms said. “As Governor, I’ll take action to lower costs, expand Medicaid, and make pre-K accessible for every Georgia family. I will also stand up to anyone — including Donald Trump — if their policies hurt Georgians.”
Trump also gave his support to GOP candidates Sen. Greg Dolezal, who is running for lieutenant governor against Democratic Sen. Josh McLaurin; Sen. Brian Strickland, who is running for attorney general against state Rep. Tanya Miller; and Rep. Tim Fleming, who is running for secretary of state against Judge Penny Brown Reynolds.
Rick Jackson, the Republican nominee for Georgia governor, speaks at a Donald Trump rally near Marietta, Georgia. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Trump called the men “true warriors.”
Kennesaw State University political science professor and former Cobb County GOP chairman Jason Shepherd said Trump’s endorsement helps unify the Republican base, which will need to turn out in high numbers in November if the party wants to win.
“Democrats will try to use it to drive a wedge between the GOP ticket and swing voters, and to fire up their own base by casting these nominees as proxies for a vote against the President,” he said. “But the real effect is at the margins. We’ve seen candidates run on a Trump endorsement and little else and lose spectacularly, and we’ve seen candidates with strong platforms treat it as value-added and win.”
“Democrats are already motivated, they would be in any midterm under a Republican president,” he added. “Whichever side makes the endorsement the centerpiece of its campaign, instead of the issues voters actually care about, is likely to find itself more than a few votes short in November.”

title: Moscow churches team up to keep Idaho kids fed on weekends all summer
description: This story was first published by FāVS News on July 22, 2026. MOSCOW, Idaho — In late 2012, Moscow’s League of Women Voters published a study of local poverty, which pointed to food insecurity for children as one of its most serious effects. St. Mark’s Episcopal Church took note, and in the summer of 2014 debuted […]
text:
At present, Food for Kids distributes bags of food to over 200 local children each Friday from 11 a.m. until noon at Lena Whitmore Elementary School throughout the summer. (Courtesy photo)This story was first published by FāVS News on July 22, 2026.
MOSCOW, Idaho — In late 2012, Moscow’s League of Women Voters published a study of local poverty, which pointed to food insecurity for children as one of its most serious effects.
A perfect storm for Boise’s unsheltered neighbors — and how you can help

St. Mark’s Episcopal Church took note, and in the summer of 2014 debuted what is now known as its Food for Kids initiative — a privately-funded complement to the Moscow School District’s weekday Summer Food Program. A year later, the Unitarian Universalist Church of the Palouse stepped in to partner with St. Mark’s, and the two houses of worship have maintained the effort ever since.
At present, Food for Kids distributes bags of food to over 200 local children from 11 a.m. until noon each Friday at Lena Whitmore Elementary School throughout the summer. The program is all-volunteer, and relies on individual donations and recurring fundraising efforts.
 How the Food for Kids program works

“We basically try to give them enough food for the whole weekend,” said St. Mark’s parishioner Lois Clifton, who has been involved almost since the beginning and is the most senior volunteer currently with the team. “Canned pasta, canned chili, canned vegetables, chocolate milk, juice pouches, apple sauce cups, macaroni and cheese cups, instant oatmeal, pop tarts, snack foods, fruit snacks, granola bars.”
Mary Jo Hamilton organizes the UUCP side of Weekend Food for Kids. Volunteers purchase and pack food on Thursdays at the churches before taking them to Lena Whitmore on Fridays for distribution.
“I have a few friends around here that have good fruit trees, so I’m able to pick cherries or plums or something like that and give that to kids,” Hamilton added.
To receive the food, children need only to show up, and do not have to apply or register in any way.
 Meeting the food program’s expenses

The program saw a fundraising bump of thousands of dollars early this year when longtime Moscow resident and Food for Kids volunteer Joanne Sutton made it her dying wish that others would contribute in her memory. Her family put out the word in her obituary, published in the Moscow-Pullman Daily News this January, that “in lieu of flowers and in honor of (Sutton’s) service to both students and the food bank,” donations should be made via checks payable to St. Mark’s with “Food for Kids” written along the bottom left line.
Two months later, the UUCP hosted a benefit concert for the charity starring the local band Gefilte Trout.
“We’re going to be doing this program for a long time,” Hamilton said. “Food prices have gone up so high, it’s amazing how much more we’re spending on food — but we do have people that give us money to buy food. As long as they’re willing to give us money to buy food, we’ll keep doing it.
“This is one of the more important things we could be doing for kids in the summer, and I know we have a lot of adults that are very, very grateful to get those bags of food.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: National Weather Service confirms three tornadoes touched down in West Virginia Tuesday
description: The National Weather Service has confirmed at least three tornadoes touched down in West Virginia during Tuesday’s storms.
text:
Flood waters cover vehicles on E Main Street in Buckhannon, West Virginia on Thursday, July 24, 2026, two days after severe storms hit the state. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey)The National Weather Service has confirmed at least three tornadoes touched down in West Virginia during Tuesday’s storms. 
One confirmed tornado went from St. Marys in Pleasants County into Doddridge County, said Simone Lewis, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Charleston, West Virginia.
Another tornado that originated in Washington County, Ohio is believed to have also dropped down in Pleasants County, West Virginia on Tuesday, but that has not been confirmed, Lewis said.
In the state’s Eastern Panhandle, a tornado touched down in Lehew, an unincorporated area in Hampshire County, according to meteorologist Luiz Rosa, with the National Weather Service in Sterling, Virginia. Another tornado touched down in Seneca Rocks, Pendleton County, Rosa said. 
The storms brought damaging winds and 5 to 6 inches of rain to parts of West Virginia on Tuesday, leading to flash flooding and landslides. 
Gov. Patrick Morrisey declared a state of emergency Tuesday evening for all 55 counties in the state because of the storms.
Upshur, Lewis and Pleasants counties in North Central West Virginia were among the hardest hit. About 500 members of the West Virginia National Guard have been deployed to assist with flood response. 
Straight-line winds estimated at between 70 and 80 miles per hour were confirmed in Lewis County, Lewis said. 
Two people have died as a result of the storms, a spokesman for the governor confirmed on Friday. He did not clarify if they were the two people from Upshur County who Morrisey said were still unaccounted for on Thursday. Officials had located a vehicle believed to be associated with the missing people, but had not been able to access it because of flood debris.
The storms and flash flooding on Tuesday damaged about 1,000 homes and businesses, said Jim Seward, adjutant general of the West Virginia National Guard.

name: National
title: Crime continues historic decline as homicide rates approach century lows
description: Crime rates continued falling across a sample of large U.S. cities in the first half of 2026, with homicide rates dropping enough to put the nation on track for another historic low in killings. A new analysis from the nonpartisan think tank Council on Criminal Justice found that nine of 13 crime categories tracked in […]
text:
Police block off a road in downtown Minneapolis after a police pursuit of a man on suspicion of homicide. Last year’s decline in the homicide rate among more than 30 cities was widespread but not universal; Minneapolis was among four cities with rates above their 2019 levels, according to a recent report. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)Crime rates continued falling across a sample of large U.S. cities in the first half of 2026, with homicide rates dropping enough to put the nation on track for another historic low in killings.
A new analysis from the nonpartisan think tank Council on Criminal Justice found that nine of 13 crime categories tracked in 36 cities declined compared with the first six months of 2025. Homicides fell 18% in the first half of the year, with 215 fewer killings among the 30 cities that reported data for the offense.
The decline builds on a trend that began in late 2022 after homicide rates surged during the COVID-19 pandemic. The council’s previous analysis estimated that the national homicide rate in 2025 was likely the lowest in more than a century, since at least 1900, based on preliminary data. Final national figures from the FBI are expected later this fall. The group’s latest findings suggest homicide rates could fall further in 2026.
But the researchers cautioned that the data do not reveal what’s driving the decline, nor do they support crediting any single policy or intervention.
Preliminary FBI data shows a sharp drop in violent crime

“There is no single or easy explanation for these historic lows,” the report’s authors wrote, though they pointed to possible influences, including changes in criminal justice operations, technology, and broader social and cultural shifts.
The continued decline has occurred across cities with different political leadership, policing strategies and economic conditions, said Adam Gelb, the council’s president and CEO, in a news release. 
“Local policies and programs surely matter, but the striking consistency of the decline suggests that macro-level forces are exerting enormous influence as well,” Gelb said.
The report examined monthly crime data from 36 cities that have consistently published incident-level figures over the past nine years, including Baltimore, Chicago, New York City, Philadelphia, San Francisco and Washington, D.C. The cities are not necessarily representative of all U.S. cities, and the researchers noted that the figures may change as local agencies update their data.
Homicide was among the offenses with the steepest decline. The average homicide rate in the first half of 2026 was 51% lower than its peak in 2022 and 31% lower than the first half of 2019, before the pandemic-era increase in violence.
Last year’s decline was widespread but not universal. Homicides fell in 21 of the 30 cities with available data, including declines of more than 50% in Rochester, New York; Little Rock, Arkansas; Arlington, Texas; and Colorado Springs, Colorado. Four cities — Austin, Texas; Minneapolis; Norfolk, Virginia; and Pittsburgh — had homicide rates above their 2019 levels.
Other violent crimes also generally declined. Reported robberies dropped 17% compared with the first half of 2025, gun assaults fell 6%, and carjackings declined 47%. The report found the rate of serious violent crimes ending in death, known as lethality, fell 23% compared with the same period last year.
Property crime also continued to trend downward. Motor vehicle theft declined 20% compared with the first half of 2025, while residential burglaries fell 13% and larcenies dropped 6%.
Still, not every category moved in the same direction.
Drug offenses rose 12% compared with the first half of 2025, and reported domestic violence incidents increased 8%. Shoplifting was the only offense tracked that remained higher than before the pandemic, with rates 5% above first-half 2019 levels.
Researchers said those differences highlight the difficulty of identifying a single explanation for the overall decline. Homicides, for example, have fallen much faster than aggravated assaults, which were only 3% lower than 2019 levels.
That gap suggests the forces reducing lethal violence may not be the same as those affecting other forms of crime, according to the report.

title: Maine ends another year with revenue surplus
description: Maine ended another year with a general fund surplus, allowing the state’s rainy day fund to again reach its statutory cap and helping to fill a transportation funding gap that had halted projects earlier this summer.  Gov. Janet Mills’ administration announced Friday that the state concluded the 2026 fiscal year with an excess of more […]
text:
Gov. Janet Mills gives her final State of the State address on Jan. 27, 2026. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)Maine ended another year with a general fund surplus, allowing the state’s rainy day fund to again reach its statutory cap and helping to fill a transportation funding gap that had halted projects earlier this summer. 
Gov. Janet Mills’ administration announced Friday that the state concluded the 2026 fiscal year with an excess of more than $148 million. That’s slightly less than the $152.2 million general fund surplus in 2025, which had grown by nearly $60 million compared with 2024. This marks the fifth consecutive year the state has had a surplus. 
Because of the higher-than-expected revenue, the state’s Budget Stabilization Fund, also known as the rainy day fund, has returned to its statutory maximum $1.056 billion, or 18% of the prior year’s general fund revenues. 
Budget squeezes through after battle over Gov. Mills’ affordability checks

Mills and the Legislature’s Democratic majority had pulled $292 million from the rainy day fund — over the objection of Republicans and some Democrats — to pay for policy priorities last session, including $155.2 million for relief checks that certain Mainers are expected to start receiving early next month.
The reported surplus comes after Mills and the state financial office have repeatedly warned against major spending in recent years amid projected revenue shortfalls and uncertainty from federal funding cuts under President Donald Trump’s administration.
The higher than expected year-end revenues are first transferred to certain priorities outlined by state law through what’s called the “cascade.” But then the remaining surplus is divided, with 80% slated for the rainy day fund (amounting to $26.2 million this year before the fund reaches its cap) and the remainder going to the highway and bridge capital fund ($115.7 million this year). 
Additionally, the Maine Department of Transportation will receive another $20.26 million, which will help address a funding gap that led the department to cut up to $400 million from its planned projects earlier this year. 
“Thanks to these year end transfers, many of the projects MaineDOT initially had to put on hold can get rescheduled, and we look forward to thoughtfully, reasonably, and expeditiously processing them in the weeks ahead,” Maine DOT Commissioner Dale Doughty said in a statement Friday.
However, Doughty added that the short-term funding boost does not solve the state’s perpetual challenge with funding transportation projects. 
The state’s highway fund, which is separate from the general fund, has long been a point of struggle for lawmakers. Lawmakers have attempted, though unsuccessfully, to combine the funds. A few years back the state diverted various sales taxes that had previously funneled into the general fund to help boost the highway fund. But those taxes are now down and the outlook for the highway fund for the coming years is broadly negative.
The other transfers to be made through the cascade process as a result of the surplus include $1 million to governor’s contingency account, $1 million to Finance Authority of Maine’s loan insurance reserve, $2.5 million to reserve for operating capital, and $2 million to retiree health insurance.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Researchers identify thousands more Iowa livestock facilities than state database shows
description: Iowa’s official database of animal feeding operations, which serves as the state’s primary regulatory inventory of livestock facilities, does not include thousands of facilities that researchers say contribute to the state’s growing manure burden and potential water pollution.  After spending about a year reviewing aerial photographs, satellite imagery and s[...]
text:
A typical pen format for swine in many Iowa animal feeding operations. (Photo by Kent Becker, United States Geological Survey)Iowa’s official database of animal feeding operations, which serves as the state’s primary regulatory inventory of livestock facilities, does not include thousands of facilities that researchers say contribute to the state’s growing manure burden and potential water pollution. 
After spending about a year reviewing aerial photographs, satellite imagery and state records, researchers with the Environmental Working Group (EWG), an environmental advocacy organization, identified 15,309 livestock facilities across Iowa using data current through July 2025, more than 4,000 additional operations beyond the roughly 11,000 listed in the Iowa Department of Natural Resources database. 
The difference does not necessarily mean Iowa has overlooked thousands of regulated livestock facilities. Instead, the two inventories measure different things.

In an email, the Iowa Department of Natural Resources said its animal feeding operation database, which is updated daily, was developed to administer state and federal regulations and “does not include all animal feeding operations in the state.” The database does not include small confinement operations and open lots that are not subject to state or federal regulations, the agency said. 
The Environmental Working Group’s inventory, by contrast, sought to identify every active livestock facility the researchers could verify using aerial imagery and public records, including many operations that fall outside the state’s regulatory database. The study authors said their analysis included facilities with at least 50 animal units, while the DNR data file generally includes facilities with more than 300 animal units.
For the analysis, the researchers classified facilities using the Environmental Protection Agency’s animal-unit thresholds. Operations with fewer than 300 animal units were classified as small, those with 300 to 999 as medium-sized and those with 1,000 or more as large. An animal unit represents 1,000 pounds of live weight — the equivalent of one beef cow, about 2.5 hogs or 125 chickens.
The researchers included livestock facilities of every size, not just those subject to state regulation, arguing that even smaller operations contribute to Iowa’s manure load and potential water pollution.
Anne Schechinger is senior director of agriculture and climate research at the Environmental Working Group. (Courtesy photo)
“We really thought it was vital to know where all animal feeding operations are located in Iowa and where manure is likely being produced in order to understand the full view of the impacts of this manure on water quality and public health,” said Anne Schechinger, senior director of agriculture and climate research at EWG and one of the study’s authors.
The mapping also documents the continued consolidation of Iowa’s livestock industry.
The researchers identified 4,444 large facilities in 2025, a 12.9% increase from the 3,936 they documented in a similar statewide analysis in 2019. Schechinger said the study documented an increase in the number of large livestock facilities but did not track whether existing facilities had expanded. That, she said, would require additional analysis.
Researchers have observed similar trends in other major livestock-producing states, including Minnesota and North Carolina, but Iowa stands apart because of the sheer concentration of hog production.
“There’s really nothing like the number of hog facilities in the state of Iowa, and the concentration in that northwest part of the state,” Schechinger said. “There’s just a lot of facilities up there.”
Five counties with the largest number of livestock facilities— Sioux, Lyon, Plymouth, O’Brien and Washington — contained 3,095 operations, or about one in every five livestock facilities identified statewide, according to the study.
Nitrate exposure associated with health risks 
The study also offers a new estimate of the waste these facilities produce. Using industry-standard and the estimated number and type of animals at each operation, the study concluded that Iowa livestock operations generated 107.6 million tons of manure in 2025, equivalent to about 33 tons per Iowa resident each year.
The estimate includes manure from hogs, cattle, chickens and turkeys raised at confinement operations and open feedlots.

Hogs accounted for about 66% of the livestock facilities identified in the study, reflecting Iowa’s position as the nation’s largest pork-producing state.
The study found that manure production is increasingly concentrated among the state’s largest operations. Facilities with at least 1,000 animal units represented 29% of all livestock facilities identified by the researchers but generated about 60% of Iowa’s manure, according to the report.
“The largest facilities producing the most manure are growing in over time, more concentration to the largest facilities,” Schechinger said.
The researchers say the scale of manure production matters because most livestock waste is applied to nearby cropland as fertilizer. While manure supplies crops with nitrogen, phosphorus and other nutrients, those same nutrients can become pollutants when they leave farm fields.
Elevated nitrate concentrations in drinking water are a potential cause of methemoglobinemia, or “blue baby syndrome,” a potentially life-threatening condition that reduces the blood’s ability to carry oxygen in infants. 
Studies have also associated nitrate exposure with an increased risk of certain cancers, including colorectal cancer, although the strength of the evidence varies across health outcomes. 
Schechinger said the purpose of creating a more complete inventory was not simply to count facilities but to better understand where manure is generated and the cumulative pressures those operations can place on surrounding landscapes.
“You know that the public health implications are really important for this amount of manure that’s being produced,” she said. 
According to the Iowa DNR’s 2025 Public Drinking Water Program Annual Compliance Report, nitrate concentrations above the Environmental Protection Agency’s drinking water standard were the most common health-based violations among Iowa public water systems. 
The report documented 36 nitrate violations at 13 water systems, affecting 2,479 customers. Nitrate violations accounted for 41% of the 87 health-based drinking water standard violations recorded that year.
High nitrate concentrations have also strained central Iowa’s drinking water supply. During the summer of 2025, nitrate levels in the Des Moines and Raccoon rivers reached near-record highs, prompting the first-ever lawn watering ban in the Des Moines metropolitan area.
Elevated concentrations persisted through the winter, requiring Central Iowa Water Works to operate its nitrate removal facility in January this year before issuing another temporary lawn watering ban this summer.
Reining in Iowa’s industry pollution 
The study is likely to add momentum to an ongoing debate over whether Iowa’s oversight of livestock operations adequately reflects the industry’s size and environmental footprint.
State Sen. Art Staed is a Democrat from Cedar Rapids. (Courtesy photo)
State Sen. Art Staed, a Cedar Rapids Democrat who has introduced legislation aimed at strengthening water-quality protections in at least the past two legislative sessions, said the new inventory highlights the need for better information about where manure is produced and applied.
“There’s more and more research on the correlation between the cancers and the toxins in our water,” Staed said.
Staed said previous proposals to strengthen oversight of livestock operations, including a moratorium on new large livestock facilities until Iowa improves its water quality, have failed to gain traction in the Republican-controlled Legislature.
“There are a lot of things that can be done,” he said. “There could be better fines, better regulation.”
Among his priorities, Staed said, are stronger manure management requirements and better public records showing where manure is applied.
“Manure management, for sure, and keeping track of where the manure spreads,” he said. “We need to have the records, and people can see where it’s being spread and how much is being produced.”
Tarah Heinzen, legal director for Food & Water Watch, said Iowa’s current regulatory framework fails to adequately oversee factory farms and called for stronger water-quality protections.
“Iowa’s deliberate head-in-the-sand approach to factory farm regulation is failing public health and the environment,” Heinzen said..
She said the group supports requiring factory farms to obtain Clean Water Act permits, mandating best management practices at animal and row crop operations, and permanently funding statewide water quality monitoring.
“Even as Iowans experience a worsening water pollution crisis, with agricultural nitrate contamination at its center, Iowa legislators and regulators are failing to adopt even the simplest of regulatory frameworks to rein in this industry’s pollution,” Heinzen said.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee’s biggest drag show is the 6th District Republican primary
description: If you’re bummed that the most recent season of RuPaul’s Drag Race ended back in April and you’re looking for your next drag fix, check out the 6th Congressional District Republican primary. The leading candidates, former U.S. Rep. Van Hilleary and state Rep. Johnny Garrett’s ads will give you quite a show.  Garrett posts a […]
text:
Campaign ads from two Republican candidates for Congress in Tennessee's 6th District have exposed more Middle Tennesseans than events like Pride parades, including Nashville's 2025 parade featuring Mystique, pictured here, ever could. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout) 
If you’re bummed that the most recent season of RuPaul’s Drag Race ended back in April and you’re looking for your next drag fix, check out the 6th Congressional District Republican primary. The leading candidates, former U.S. Rep. Van Hilleary and state Rep. Johnny Garrett’s ads will give you quite a show. 
Garrett posts a capable drag queen playing basketball to show his support of women’s sports, while Hilleary’s ad features an image of a deep-fake “woke” Garrett surrounded by a bevy of elegant AI queens.
I have so many questions.
The obvious question for both of them is this: do they realize that by including drag queens in their campaign ads, they have broadcast drag to more youth in Middle Tennessee than anyone? “Not around the kids” is one of the big anti-drag talking points, isn’t it? 
Now, they’ve probably even made more than a few adults drag-curious. Because these are commercials, they pop up unannounced, whether someone is looking for drag or not. Seeing drag, of course, doesn’t hurt anyone. But it’s sad to see it weaponized like this. 
Now let’s move to the individual critiques. What a lost opportunity for Hilleary! He used AI drag queens when there are perfectly good Tennessee queens who could have performed in his video.
How are we going to believe he’ll create jobs for Tennesseans when he won’t even hire them? And I have to say that if he is trying to sully the reputation of his opponent, that ad made Garrett look way cooler than he could have done on his own. That is to say nothing, of course, of the ethical issues involving deep-fakes and the environmental cost of AI. 
Moving on to Garrett’s ad, I’m guessing he paid the real-life drag performer in his commercial. If he did, I have to wonder whether he is the first congressional candidate in Tennessee to pay someone to do drag. I don’t know how that plays out with the Republican base, but it is noteworthy and merits further research for historical purposes, of course. And why not spend our time that way since we’re discussing this instead of measures like increasing the minimum wage?
As for the sports issue, I know Garrett’s point is to try to present himself as some big protector of women’s sports from the few trans athletes who have tried to compete when what we should be doing is finding a path for everyone to play.  
But how is he going to explain to women athletes that spokespersons for the Heritage Foundation, who will most likely try to influence Congress on these issues, are now suggesting that Title IX — the 1972 civil rights measure requiring equality in men’s and women’s sports, among other issues — is bad because they believe women’s sports might hurt fertility and make women less feminine and graceful? Is he really ready to carry the banner of women’s sports all the way?
I know, I know. It’s more fun to dream up drag sports skits and create AI Pride parades than it is to deal with the affordability issues Tennesseans are facing. But this gay man is asking these candidates to step out of Rainbow Land long enough to leave us alone and talk about the issues we all care about.

name: VTDigger
title: Owen Foster stepping down as chair of state’s most powerful healthcare regulator
description:
His tenure has been defined by a harder line on reining in hospital budgets and insurance premium increases. He plans to stay on as a board member.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Owen Foster stepping down as chair of state’s most powerful healthcare regulator .
text:
Owen Foster, chair of the Green Mountain Care board, speaks during roundtable on health care costs hosted by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont, in Burlington on Friday, May 31, 2024.  Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
The chair of the regulatory board that decides hospital budgets and health insurance premium increases in Vermont is stepping down at the end of September, Gov. Phil Scott announced Friday. 
Scott appointed Owen Foster as the Green Mountain Care Board’s chair in 2022 and reappointed him to serve through September 2030. But Foster has decided to cut that term short, saying he wants to spend more time with his children and focus on other professional pursuits. He intends to remain on the board as one of the four regular members, filling a vacancy created by the departure of board member Jess Holmes, whose term ends this year.
The decision was “entirely mine,” he told VTDigger in an interview. “I have young children. I’m a lawyer. I want a chance to focus on my family and my other professional interests a little bit more too.”
In a press release posted Friday, Scott wrote “I appreciate Owen’s willingness to continue serving the people of Vermont. He’s been an effective leader as we work to make healthcare more affordable for Vermonters, and I believe he’ll continue to be a valuable member of the board in this new role.”
Under Foster’s leadership, the board has taken a tougher stance on reining in hospital budgets and insurance premium increases. He leaves his post as hospitals across the state struggle to stay out of the red and Vermonters pay some of the highest rates in the country for Affordable Care Act marketplace plans.
The Green Mountain Care Board was created in 2011 as part of Vermont’s effort to create state-funded healthcare for all. It is an independent government regulator tasked with approving hospitals’ annual budgets and ACA marketplace plans’ annual rate changes, among other authorities.
The board’s hospital budget review for the coming fiscal year begins Aug. 3. Foster intends to remain as chair through the whole budget process, until the end of September. The board is already reviewing next year’s rates for the two insurers that sell plans on Vermont’s ACA marketplace — BlueCross BlueShield of Vermont and MVP. This year, Foster has recused himself from participating in the board’s review of BlueCross BlueShield’s rates, citing personal reasons, though he declined to provide more details when the state’s healthcare advocate requested an explanation.
Under Foster’s tenure the board has shifted from being a body that largely rubber-stamped hospitals’ and insurers’ requests to one that put serious pressure on both to reduce expenses.
Mike Fisher, the state’s health care advocate, has watched the evolution of the board since its early days: the original idea to combine the regulatory authority of approving hospital budgets and insurers’ premium increases came from a need to make sure that the costs of hospitals’ healthcare services stayed in-line with the amount of money insurers raise through premiums to pay out those claims.  
“That hasn’t always happened,” Fisher said. “More and more in recent years, the board has responsibly aligned both the spending and revenue side.”
He also sees this moment of Foster’s tenure as one of much more urgency, one that the board has met “responsibly.”
In an interview, Foster said that one of the board’s defining points of progress under his leadership has been a push to move care into less-expensive settings if it does not need to occur in a hospital — for example, outpatient surgery, imaging or lab work. 
During his tenure, he said, the board has also brought a high level of scrutiny to how much Vermonters are paying for administrative services in healthcare.  
“Since I’ve been here, (the board has) very, very much focused on ‘let’s stop spending on healthcare administration and let’s start spending on the fundamentals of a good healthcare system,’” he said. 
When Vermont ran its all-payer model of healthcare funding, the care board also regulated the Accountable Care Organization responsible for coordinating those payers and payments.  
In his early days as chair, Foster brought a similar skepticism to the ACO’s budget and its executives’ compensation that he has brought to the state’s largest hospital group in recent years.
“When we cut (the ACO’s) budgets, what we did was we redirected the money from spending on healthcare bureaucracy at an ineffective ACO, and we literally took the dollars and said, ‘Give this to primary care,’” he said. 
In the early days of Foster’s tenure, when the state still had the all-payer model, Vermont saw itself as more of a leader in innovative healthcare, even as costs mounted and health outcomes plateaued for many Vermonters, Foster said.
“When I started, it was not widely understood or accepted how fragile and distressed our healthcare system was,” he said. “I do think a big part of what the staff and the board has done the last four years has focused on educating the Legislature, (the Agency of Human Services), the governor’s office and the public, that we are in a tough situation, and we need to make changes. And now I think everyone really recognizes that.” 
But he suggested that the biggest changes ahead for healthcare need to come not from the care board, but from hospitals, the state, and private and public insurers working together to take a serious look at how hospitals can cut spending without cutting services for Vermonters who need them.  
“There are different leaders for different moments,” Foster said. “And I do think my role as a leader was to look hard at what we’re doing and evaluate if it was working. The next stage is a different stage.”
This story will be updated.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming congressional candidates talk paying for their campaigns, roadless rule, keeping Trump in check
description:
Eight prospective U.S. House members pitched their candidacies to a Casper audience during a nearly two-hour-long forum Thursday night. 
The post Wyoming congressional candidates talk paying for their campaigns, roadless rule, keeping Trump in check appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
CASPER—One of the spicier moments of Thursday night’s U.S. House of Representatives forum came when the eight-person panel was asked about the record-breaking sums of personal and family cash that candidates were throwing into the race — and what that trend forecasts for access to office in Wyoming.
Instructions were to keep the discourse civil: Panelists who sat on stage in Casper College’s Durham Auditorium were told explicitly to avoid personal attacks on other candidates, and to address the audience, not one another.
Current Secretary of State Chuck Gray, among the candidates dipping into the family piggy bank, used the question to address fellow big spender Reid Rasner, alleging that he’d spent “hundreds of thousands of dollars in false attacks.” Then Gray, the Wyoming Republican Party’s pick for the seat, turned to yet another heir of a family fortune, Steve Friess, who’s written the largest check to his own campaign, $2 million, so far.
“I’m not spending as much as Mr. Friess over here, with the Jackson element,” Gray said.
He was cut short for breaking the rules. 
Republican primary candidate Chuck Gray talks a forum on Thursday, July 23, 2026, at Casper College. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)
Candidates who haven’t benefited as much from their own wealth and family largesse bemoaned the trend in Wyoming politics. 
“We’re creating a situation where millionaires and billionaires can buy their way into office,” said Kevin Christensen, a Bureau of Land Management retiree whose campaign has brought in about $13,000. “That circumvents our democracy in Wyoming. We as voters need to be aware of where that money is coming from and why people are spending that kind of money for a $174K job in D.C.” 
Candidate Bo Biteman, the Wyoming state Senate president, called the campaign spending trend “unnerving.” He’s raised about $94,000, almost all from individual contributions.
“Candidate quality used to be the thing. Retail politics used to be the thing,” Biteman said. “Hopefully, the voters ultimately have the final say. The voters will be able to go to the election booth and make their choice based on who they think is best to represent them, not based on who spends money on mailers and ads and billboards.” 
Republican primary candidate for U.S. House of Representatives Bo Biteman talks during a forum on Thursday, July 23, 2026, at Casper College. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)
Divisions among the crowded pool of GOP candidates weren’t always easy to come by. None, for example, openly supported disposing of federal lands.
The day of the forum, the crowded field became less crowded. Frank Chapman, a Jackson Hole businessman who’d loaned his own campaign over $1 million, announced that he was dropping out that morning. That leaves nine still vying for the seat. Candidate Keith Goodenough did not attend the forum. 
Over the course of the nearly two-hour-long forum, the candidates had just one minute to answer questions that were sometimes about convoluted policies. Asked about the Trump administration and U.S. House Rep. Harriet Hageman’s efforts to rescind the Roadless Rule, the candidates were mostly on the same page in their desire to get rid of the environmental protections. 
“The roadless rule was a Clinton-driven, left-driven attempt to hurt our public lands,” Gray said of a policy that comment-writing Westerners overwhelmingly want to keep. “Some of these agencies are almost like the Joker: It’s almost like they want it to burn,” he said, referencing an argument that roads are needed to defend national forests from wildfires.
Some candidates struck a more nuanced tone.
“It’s hard to say ‘always yes’ or ‘never no’ to something like the Roadless Rule,” Balow said. “It depends on the location, it depends on the use.”
Republican primary candidate for U.S. House of Representatives Jillian Balow talks during a forum on Thursday, July 23, 2026, at Casper College. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)
Only Christensen clearly wanted to retain the policy, which has been in place for a quarter century.
“Modify, but do not rescind the Roadless Rule,” he said. “Wyoming people love to go into these areas. That’s where I go to hunt. Out-of-state people love to go on their roads.”
Asked if Congress is fulfilling its role as a check on executive power, the field was somewhat split. Most stated plainly that the U.S. government’s legislative branch needed to do more, but most candidates were leery of criticizing President Donald Trump, who’s retained 64% approval in Wyoming — the highest rate of any state.
Friess, who calls himself a “Trump Republican,” used the question to argue that Congress should do more to support the president. 
“It is important to lock down many of the advances President Trump has made,” Friess said, “so they aren’t reversed by the next liberal administration.” 
Candidate Richard Dodson, an actor and singer, made a quip out of the question: “If I were an orthopedic surgeon,” he said, “I would very much be in the business of spine transplants.” 
Congress “needs a lot of help” finding their spines, Dodson said. 
Christensen, a U.S. Army veteran, was the only candidate who cited an example of what he felt was an overstep by the Trump administration. 
“We have no further to look than the current conflict in Iran,” Christensen said, calling the war “untenable, unclear, and unwinnable.” 
“Members of Congress have the responsibility to ask those tough questions,” he added. “I’ll have a personal conversation with Pete Hegseth on the first week.” 
Organized by the League of Women Voters of Wyoming, Wyoming Public Media and WyoFile, Thursday’s forum was the last of five statewide candidate forums for the 2026 primary election. Footage of each is available on YouTube.  
Wyoming’s primary election is Aug. 18. Early voting is underway.
For more information about candidates in Wyoming’s federal, state and legislative races, check out WyoFile’s 2026 Election Guide.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri congressional incumbents flush with cash heading into primary election
description: Missouri congressional incumbents seeking reelection hold a huge cash advantage over their leading challengers, final preprimary campaign finance reports show. The seven incumbents seeking reelection held $13.6 million in their campaign accounts on July 15, filings with the Federal Election Commission show. Challengers held $1.9 million. Republicans hold six[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, D-Kansas City, files for re-election Feb. 24 in the 5th Congressional District. The district is at the center of a fight over a gerrymandered map intended to flip the district to Republicans. (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent)Missouri congressional incumbents seeking reelection hold a huge cash advantage over their leading challengers, final preprimary campaign finance reports show.
The seven incumbents seeking reelection held $13.6 million in their campaign accounts on July 15, filings with the Federal Election Commission show. Challengers held $1.9 million.
Republicans hold six of Missouri’s eight seats in the U.S. House of Representatives. Last year, the Republican-led majority in the General Assembly forced through a gerrymandered redistricting plan intended to flip the 5th District, currently held by Democratic U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver of Kansas City.
Cleaver’s campaign had $1.1 million on hand as he awaits the winner of the Republican primary.
Among the six Republicans competing for the nomination to oppose Cleaver, Taylor Burks of Boone County held the most cash on July 15, the final day of the reporting period. Burks was sitting on $718,631, mainly because he loaned his campaign $900,000 when he launched it.
State Sen. Rick Brattin of Harrisonville held $222,510 in his campaign account.
Brett Hueffmeier, a one-time staff member for U.S. Sens. John Ashcroft and Kit Bond who now works in commercial real estate, loaned his campaign $275,000 but repaid $100,000 during the period and had $492 on hand.
None of the other candidates have raised more than $8,000. 
Outside groups seeking to help Burks or Brattin in the primary have spent $3.5 million.
The only incumbent facing a strong primary challenge on Aug.4 is U.S. Rep. Wesley Bell in the 1st District in St. Louis. Former U.S. Rep. Cori Bush is seeking to regain the seat she lost two years ago. 
Bush has raised $1.3 million but had only $98,433 on hand on July 15, the final day of the reporting period. Bell has raised $3.6 million and had $1.1 million on hand.
Outside spending in the primary has surpassed spending by both candidates. The United Democracy Project, funded by the American-Israel Political Action Committee, has spent $2.5 million and the New Democrat Majority PAC has spent $1.1 million, both to support Bell.
No other incumbent faces a well-funded primary opponent.
The congressional district map for the Aug. 4 primary was drawn Missouri Republicans during a 2025 special session. The GOP’s goal with the changes from 2022 is to win the 5th District seat currently held by U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, a Kansas City Democrat (Screenshot from Missouri House website).
Among the other six incumbents, U.S. Rep. Jason Smith of Cape Girardeau, who represents the 8th District, held the most cash, just over $5 million. Smith’s best-funded Democratic challenger is former state Sen. Frank Barnitz of Lake Spring, who has raised $48,420 and had $19,800 on hand on July 15.
A primary opponent, Gordon Heslop of Rolla, has raised $70,606 as he seeks to replace Smith on the Republican ballot.
U.S. Rep. Ann Wagner of St. Louis County, who represents the 2nd District, was sitting on $4.2 million. She faces the best-funded general election challenger, with Democratic candidate Fred Wellman holding $242,217 after raising $1.2 million.
Both Wagner and Wellman have primary opponents but no one else in the race has raised $10,000 in the six-county district of eastern Missouri.
Other incumbents, and their best-funded opponents, are:

U.S. Rep. Bob Onder of Lake Saint Louis, in the 3rd District. Onder’s campaign fund held $471,459, while Bethany Mann of St. Peters, making her third run for Congress, had $2,776.
U.S. Rep. Mark Alford of Kansas City, in the 4th District. Alford had $747,401 on hand, while Hartzell Gray III of Lee’s Summit had $44,969.
U.S. Rep. Eric Burlison of Springfield in the 7th District. Burilson had $953,675 in the bank on July 15. Missi Hesketh of Forsyth is the only Democrat running and had $33,543 on hand.

In the 6th District, where U.S. Rep. Sam Graves of Tarkio is the only incumbent not seeking reelection, the two Republican candidates with the most successful fundraising have collected almost identical amounts.
