title: Southfield advocates emphasize community support while protesting GSA lease tied to ICE
description: A U.S. General Services Administration lease for a Southfield office being used by the Office of the Principal Legal Advisor, ICE’s legal wing, has drawn protest and criticism from the surrounding community since plans were first reported in February. At a panel hosted on Wednesday night, community organizers gathered to emphasize the importance of neighborh[...]
text:
Elida Reyes, founder of Community Action for Empowerment, or CAFE, tearfully tells the story of the detention and deportation of a young Venezuelan girl who she had housed and cared for. July 22, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. A U.S. General Services Administration lease for a Southfield office being used by the Office of the Principal Legal Advisor, ICE’s legal wing, has drawn protest and criticism from the surrounding community since plans were first reported in February. At a panel hosted on Wednesday night, community organizers gathered to emphasize the importance of neighborhood solidarity in the face of ICE activity in the region.
Lauren Fink, who, along with her husband Cameron, started the Southfield Neighbors Action Committee in response to the news of the Southfield office, told the crowd that, following news that a proposed detention facility in Romulus would be sold by ICE, resistance to the agency’s presence in Southfield remains important — and the win in Romulus shows that they can be pushed out. 
“People need to be just as disgusted by what is happening in REDICO building at One Towne Square as they are by the idea of a detention center in Romulus, and we should be just as disgusted by what is happening in that office building, because it is disgusting,” Fink said, referring to the building owners. “What is happening in that office building is what enables these detention centers.”
The event, titled “What Does It Mean to Be a Good Neighbor When ICE Moves In?” focused on how the local community can react and respond to immigration enforcement. 
Beyond the regular protests hosted by Fink and her colleagues, panelists emphasized the need to support the broader community — especially those at risk of becoming targets of ICE themselves.
Lauren Fink (left) and Dr. Patricia Talley (right) speak on community responses to ICE’s in Southfield and metro Detroit. July 22, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Elida Reyes founded Community Action for Empowerment, or CAFE, to advocate for immigrants in Oakland County and to provide direct support for those most impacted — volunteers document arrests, deliver food to affected families, and transport them to court appointments. 
At Wednesday’s event, she told the story of Vera, a young Venezuelan immigrant who arrived in Pontiac knowing no one, having fled the regime of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Reyes took her in after she came to her church looking for a place to stay.
“I treated her as if she was my granddaughter, and I put her through the school,” Reyes said. “And no one can say she didn’t have papers because we paid for the attorney. We made sure she had all her papers.”
But after leaving Michigan to visit a friend in Florida, she was stopped by ICE, detained in Louisiana, and was eventually deported to Venezuela — and Reyes has not been able to reach her since earthquakes devastated the country in June. 
She has continued her work through CAFE, accompanying people to court hearings and doctor’s appointments where they fear they or their loved ones might be detained by ICE. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I started this a year ago,” Reyes said. “I’d like to end it, but we can’t until it’s done.”
She further urged those in the room to similarly look out for their neighbors, offering support in times of need. 
“I’ve got grandkids, and I don’t want them to go through this. I’ve got grandkids, and I worry about their future every single day,” she said. “I don’t know what our future looks like, but if we don’t change it, it’s not good. It’s really not good.”
Dr. Patricia Talley, attending the panel as part of the Afro-Mexican advocacy organization Mexico Negro, A.C., similarly emphasized the need for community support in the face of ICE’s presence in Michigan. 
“We are all good neighbors,” she said. “We want to live in a beloved community, one where everyone is respecting their basic humanity.”
Talley’s mother, Barbara Talley, was a trailblazer for the civil rights movement in Michigan — she was the first Black member of Southfield’s city council, first elected in 1983. Throughout the event, she referenced the King Center’s work on nonviolence to inspire the community response to immigration enforcement — contacting elected officials, telling stories of immigrants, and attending town halls like the one held on Wednesday.
“We’ve been so culturalized to accept these things,” she added. “We become complacent.”
REDICO, which owns the One Towne Square building with the GSA lease in question, was invited to participate in the panel, according to organizers — a seat was reserved for the company’s CEO, Dale Watchowski. 
Asked why Watchowski did not attend, Fink said, “We sent them an invitation. We would love to have conversations with them. We have had conversations with REDICO in private. We have attempted many times to have conversations with REDICO in public. It has not been successful. I think the answer is because they don’t want to be here.”
Organizers for a community panel on responding to ICE presence left a seat for the CEO of REDICO, the building with a U.S. General Services Administration lease currently used by ICE’s legal team. July 22, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
A statement from REDICO said that Watchowski “was out of town traveling on business and has no record of receiving an invitation to this meeting.”
The statement continued on to say that REDICO has engaged consistently with local officials and community members on the GSA lease.
“The terms of the lease explicitly prohibit any law enforcement, detention or similar activities from occurring at the property,” the statement continued. “REDICO is prepared to fully enforce the agreement if the terms of the lease are violated. We have been observing the usage closely. REDICO cannot unilaterally cancel a legally binding lease with the GSA, or any tenant, unless the terms of the lease are in default. To date, government usage of the space has been for office purposes only, which is well within the terms of the lease.”
U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Detroit), whose district includes Southfield, also spoke at the event remotely. 
“When ICE comes into one community and violates people’s civil rights or uses weapons, excessive force, it is a violation of all of our civil rights,” she said. “These are real human beings, real lives that are being impacted, but it’s being done in a very dehumanizing, very aggressive way that it really doesn’t create a fair, just immigration system.” 
Emphasizing local organizations working to provide support and legal representation to those facing immigration detention, Tlaib also emphasized her concerns about federal law enforcement activity on Election Day — and how those are directly tied to the current immigration enforcement regime.  
“You all think about ways you can obviously uplift and show what ICE is doing with the billions of dollars that the Trump administration has been pouring in there,” she said. “It’s important to understand the impact of what the Trump administration is doing, using these law enforcement agencies or these extensions of agencies that are supposed to be keeping us safe. They’re actually not doing that.”

title: Wisconsin’s chaotic primary for governor highlights Democrats’ identity crisis
description: Small wonder nearly half of voters haven’t decided who to back in the Democratic primary for Wisconsin’s next governor. If you sent in your ballot early, you might have voted for the candidate who won the straw poll at the Democratic party convention only to flail her way through a dramatic public scandal, run out […]
text:
State Rep. Francesca Hong speaks during a forum for Democrats seeking the party's nomination to run for governor. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)Small wonder nearly half of voters haven’t decided who to back in the Democratic primary for Wisconsin’s next governor. If you sent in your ballot early, you might have voted for the candidate who won the straw poll at the Democratic party convention only to flail her way through a dramatic public scandal, run out of money and quit. The latest Marquette Law School poll, released this week, still had her name as a candidate, but didn’t include the candidate who dropped out two weeks ago before getting back in the race with Gov. Tony Evers’ endorsement. 
Meanwhile, the frontrunner in poll after poll, as Baylor Spears reports, is Francesca Hong. 
Some Democrats are so sure Hong, as a democratic socialist, will lose in a general-election matchup with Republican Tom Tiffany they’re desperately hopping from horse to horse, searching for an alternative. One of those horses, Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez, stumbled badly and collapsed. Now we’ve got Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, whose late endorsement by Evers generated a backlash against the “Democratic establishment.”
Whoever’s running the “establishment’ might be overbearing, but they sure don’t seem to be adept at picking winners. Days after his reentry, Crowley is struggling with negative stories about crude posts to an old Twitter account.
The problem Democrats in Wisconsin face is less about party bosses behind the scenes calling the shots than it is lack of any organization. A little leadership from Evers earlier in the process might have staved off disaster.
At a minimum, he could have made up his mind to back Crowley before Crowley dropped out. He could have had painful but necessary conversations with Joel Brennan, Sara Rodriguez and Missy Hughes, the other members of his administration who campaigned at least partly on their association with him. “Look, I see a bright future for you in politics, but I’ve decided to go with Crowley in this race,” he might have said. Then Crowley (or whoever Evers decided to support) could have built some strength over the course of the campaign.
Instead, we have the current mess.
Wisconsin’s messy primary is also a symptom of Democrats’ general disarray. Unable to come up with a plan to effectively counter the frightening power of a violent, kleptocratic regime in Washington, they are waffling between trying not to alienate swing voters by sounding too radical versus tapping into the energy and outrage of the anti-Trump electorate.
Looking over their shoulders at the Republicans, several Democratic campaigns point to the millions of dollars in TV ads the Republican Governors Association bought featuring light criticism of Hong. The ads appear to be a transparent effort to boost Hong in the primary, since Republicans think they can beat her in the general election. So what? Hong appears to be winning the primary anyway, with or without the RGA boost, through her straight talk, superb social media strategy, grassroots ground game and the enthusiasm she’s generating, especially from young voters who don’t trust normal politicians and institutional Democratic party politics. 
That doesn’t mean she’s the best candidate to beat Tiffany. But instead of buying into the Republican political analysis, or as one Democrat did, running an ominous attack ad trumpeting that Hong is a “proud socialist!” (the horror!), Democrats should be trying to steal a page from Hong. That ugly ad, featuring photos of the three candidates of color, labeling them all unelectable, and then toggling to Joel Brennan, the only white guy in the race, is a good example of what Democratic primary voters want to reject.
It’s no surprise Hong is catching fire. People like candidates who say what they mean and aren’t afraid to be themselves, as opposed to candidates who seem to be trying to tell them what they want to hear or pretending to be just like them. They want to see courage and conviction in the face of bullying and corruption. They do not particularly like seeing Democrats tearing each other apart — especially not by drawing on the kinds of smug, bigoted attacks made by the other side. 
Imagine a Democratic party that includes democratic socialists and more middle-of-the-road candidates, promoting an uplifting message about protecting a decent society, functional government and human rights. 
That’s the vision people are hungry for. Wisconsin Democrats should not be afraid to serve it up.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio renters need to earn at least $23.82 an hour to afford two-bedroom rental, new report shows
description: A full-time Ohio worker needs to be making at least $23.82 an hour to be able to afford a “modest” two-bedroom apartment, according to a new report released this week.  This is slightly more than a 5% increase from last year — which was $22.51, according to National Low Income Housing Coalition and the Coalition […]
text:
A for-rent sign. (Photo by Marisa Demarco, States Newsroom.)A full-time Ohio worker needs to be making at least $23.82 an hour to be able to afford a “modest” two-bedroom apartment, according to a new report released this week. 
This is slightly more than a 5% increase from last year — which was $22.51, according to National Low Income Housing Coalition and the Coalition on Homelessness and Housing in Ohio’s annual Out of Reach report. 
The Housing Wage is an estimate of the hourly wage full-time workers must make to afford a rental home at HUD’s Fair Market Rent without spending more than 30% of their income. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ohio’s Fair Market Rent for a two-bedroom apartment is $1,238, meaning a household must earn $49,537 annually to cover rent and utilities, according to the report. 
The state’s Fair Market Rent for a one-bedroom apartment is $996, according to the report. Ohio has nearly 1.6 million renter households. 
The report showed the average Ohio renter earns $19.59 an hour, $4.23 less than what they need to be making to afford a two-bedroom apartment. 
The Housing Wage gap was $1.57 an hour in 2020, meaning the Housing Wage has increased by 169% in the past six years, the report said. 
“Renters’ incomes shot up in the early 2020s, but then rent increases eventually swamped the wage gains,” COHHIO Executive Director Amy Riegel said in a statement. 
“And it’s not just housing. The cost of food, transportation, healthcare, childcare, and education is continuing to rise while people working in low wage jobs are getting squeezed.” 
Of the 10 most common jobs in Ohio, only general operations managers and registered nurses pay more than $23.82 an hour, according to the report. 
Fast food workers, retail salespeople, stockers, laborers, home health aides, and cashiers earn a median hourly wage less than $20 an hour, according to the report. 
Ohio’s minimum wage is $11 an hour for non-tipped workers — meaning a minimum wage worker would have to work 87 hours per week to afford a two-bedroom rental and 70 hours to afford a one-bedroom rental. 
Economic Policy Institute modeling shows 616,700 Ohio workers would get a raise due to a state minimum wage increase of $15 an hour by 2030, according to a report by Policy Matters Ohio published earlier this year. 
Union County had the highest Housing Wage, where full-time workers need to make at least $27.56 an hour, the report showed. 
Urban areas in the state were not far behind. The Housing Wage is $27.50 an hour in Columbus, $26.02 in Cincinnati, $24.60 in Cleveland, and $24.48 in Dayton. 
Ohio has a shortage of 266,000 affordable and available rental units, according to the 2026 Gap Report by the National Low Income Housing Coalition and COHHIO. 
“While we’re helping many families get stably housed, even more are falling into homelessness every day,” Fred Berry, president and CEO of Humility of Mary Housing in Akron, said in a statement. 
“The lack of affordable housing is increasing the risk of homelessness and making it harder to get out of homelessness.” 
There were 12,196 people experiencing homelessness in Ohio last year, according to HUD’s annual Homelessness Assessment Report. 
Only one in four eligible households receives federal housing assistance, NLIHC President and CEO Renee M. Willis said. 
“To meaningfully address the affordable housing crisis, the federal government must adequately fund housing programs in a way that would expand rental assistance and both preserve and increase the supply of deeply affordable homes for those with the lowest incomes,” she said in a statement. 
“We have the resources to invest in expanding housing solutions that provide stable homes for the lowest-income people in our country. We just need the political will to do so.”

title: Poll: Americans don’t think recipients are ripping off Medicaid
description: As some Republican leaders are pushing allegations that Medicaid recipients and their families are defrauding Medicaid, a new poll indicates that most Americans believe they’re far from the main culprit. Most respondents also said they thought the overall Medicaid-fraud push was just politics. In addition, the poll indicated that when it comes to defrauding[...]
text:
A patient has blood drawn as he receives a free HIV test from a medical assistant in Miami. The giant tax and spending bill under consideration in the U.S. Senate would bar clinics that provide abortions — which tend to be testing sites for sexually transmitted infections — from accepting Medicaid. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

As some Republican leaders are pushing allegations that Medicaid recipients and their families are defrauding Medicaid, a new poll indicates that most Americans believe they’re far from the main culprit. Most respondents also said they thought the overall Medicaid-fraud push was just politics.
In addition, the poll indicated that when it comes to defrauding the government, Medicaid wasn’t respondent’s top concern — it was taxes.
The poll, by the nonpartisan health-research organization KFF, was published July 16. The combination online/phone poll was conducted between June 25 and 30 among a nationally representative sample of 1,321 U.S. adults.
It comes after President Donald Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill” last year cut almost$1 trillion from Medicaid over 10 years while giving massive tax cuts to the richest Americans. Congressional Republicans also allowed subsidies to buy health coverage on Affordable Care Act exchanges to expire. 
Since then, Ohio has seen the steepest drop in coverage purchased on the exchanges. Almost a third, or 161,000, have dropped coverage as their premiums doubled.
Amid an overall affordability crisis, Americans’ are still most worried about healthcare, the KFF poll found. Sixty-two percent said they were very or somewhat worried about affording healthcare, while 38% were not too worried or not worried at all.
Healthcare was followed by gas prices, then housing costs, then food expenses and then utilities in respondents’ affordability concerns.
As the public and Medicaid administrators brace for the brunt of Medicaid cuts to take effect Jan. 1, the Trump administration and Ohio officials have been highlighting what they say is rampant fraud in the system. 
In early June, acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and other administration officials gathered on a stage in Whitehall with Ohio Republicans to decry alleged Medicaid fraud — particularly home health programs it funds. But the dollar figures they threw out also included allegations of undelivered behavioral-health services and alleged fraud in federal programs unrelated to Medicaid.
The KFF poll said the administration has also been playing up Medicaid fraud in other states. It said a big majority of respondents think it’s not a genuine anti-fraud effort, merely election-year politics.
“The Trump administration has recently deferred federal Medicaid payments in a few states with claims that these actions will save money and root out fraud,” it said. “But voters are skeptical: fewer than half say these deferrals are ‘very’ or ‘somewhat likely’ to save taxpayers money (43%) or that it is likely to lower health care costs for people like them (31%). However, most voters — including majorities across partisans — say the deferrals are likely to cause eligible low-income people to lose access to care they rely on. About two-thirds of voters (65%) believe this approach is mostly motivated by politics, though most Republican voters say it is mostly motivated by a genuine effort to reduce fraud and protect Medicaid (69%).”
When it comes to fraud, respondents placed other suspects higher on their list.
A whopping 92% said the federal tax system was subject to a lot or some fraud. That was followed by defense contracting (87%), foreign aid (79%), Medicaid (78%), Medicare (75%), Social Security (72%) and ACA marketplaces (70%).
Respondents also don’t appear to be buying what some Republican officials are selling in terms of Medicaid fraud — that recipients and their families are bilking the system. 
Keith Faber is Ohio auditor and the Republican nominee for state attorney general. On a May 5 appearance on Cincinnati’s WLW radio, Faber said that family members paid by Ohio Medicaid are bilking a program to provide home care. 
“The problem is that it’s very difficult to catch the abuse because grandma’s never going to rat out granddaughter or daughter who’s supposed to be taking care of her, but she’s sitting there playing on her cell phone all day,” Faber said at the 1:16:18 mark of the “Sunday Nights With Bill Cunningham” show. “So that’s the problem you get into and, candidly, why the legislature probably needs to get out of that waiver and get back to the… eliminate these programs.”
In other words, Faber was accusing an elderly Ohioan of being complicit as family members denied her care that taxpayers were financing. When Faber’s campaign was asked for a documented example of that happening, it didn’t provide one.
Respondents to the KFF poll didn’t think such alleged scams were much of a problem.
Just 13% thought that Medicaid or Medicare fraud was carried out by individual patients. Another 53% said it was carried out by providers, including doctors’ offices and hospital systems. The remainder were unsure.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Primary results for federal, statewide races officially certified
description: It's official: The Maryland State Board of Canvassers certified the results Thursday of last month's primary election in state and federal races. There were no surprises, with most winners chalking up wide margins of victory.
text:
A basket of “I Voted” stickers sits on a table at a polling location in St. Luke’s Methodist Church in Oklahoma City in this 2024 file photo. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)It’s official: The Maryland State Board of Canvassers certified the results Thursday of last month’s primary election in state and federal races.
The certification was announced by State Elections Administrator Jared DeMarinis at Thursday’s meeting of the State Board of Elections. The final results can be found here.
The final results held no surprises, with some races uncontested and others won by comfortable margins. In the U.S. House races, all the incumbents were easily renominated and will all face challengers in November. In the race for the only open seat, to replace longtime Rep. Steny Hoyer (D-5th), Del. Adrian Boafo (D-Prince George’s), backed by Hoyer, easily defeated a field of two dozen Democrats to win the nomination. He will faceRepublican Chris Chaffee in the Nov. 3 general election for the seat.
Maryland Green Party announces its general election nominees

The state-run primary on June 23 featured only Republican and Democratic candidates. Other parties choose their nominees through party-run primaries or conventions.
DeMarinis said during the Board of Elections meeting that this year’s election marked the first time local boards of election used risk-limiting audits of ballots statewide. Those audits use statistical science to audit and confirm results reported by tabulators. It became in effect last year due to the passage of Senate Bill 313 and House Bill 426.
“I thank the Board of Canvassers for their careful oversight of the certification process,” DeMarinis said in a statement. “This step of public certification and independent oversight ensures that every eligible vote is accounted for and that the public can have confidence in the integrity of our elections.”
The Board of Canvassers is made up of the state’s attorney general, the comptroller, the secretary of state, the state treasurer and the clerk of the Supreme Court of Maryland.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Advocates, regulators both call for reforms at power grid operator PJM
description: As federal energy officials met Thursday for a daylong conference on PJM Interconnection, Maryland legislators and advocates rallied outside the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to express concerns about the multistate grid operator.
text:
Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery), with microphone, and Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery) call for changes to management of PJM, the multistate electric grid operator, at a rally Thursday outside the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. (Photo by Mayah Nachman/Maryland Matters)As federal energy officials met Thursday for a daylong conference on PJM Interconnection, Maryland legislators and advocates rallied outside the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to express concerns about the multistate grid operator.
“PJM has lost sight of who its customers are,” said Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery).
“Every decision they make affects the 67 million ratepayers, yet PJM’s governance is primarily accountable to its market participants, those who have a financial stake in the outcome, not the people who are paying those residential bills,” she told a small crowd outside FERC headquarters.
Inside the packed conference, FERC officials appeared sympathetic to the need for change at PJM, the nation’s largest regional power grid operator, calling for improved transparency, faster decision-making and affordability for customers.
“Frustrations are mounting,” said commission Chair Laura Swett. “Put plainly, market participants have lost confidence in PJM’s decision-making abilities.”
FERC put on the conference in response to growing frustrations over PJM’s governing structure, which lawmakers and advocates say gives unfair voting power to companies, including utilities, that have a financial stake in the outcomes of its decisions. 
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission headquarters in Washington. (Photo by Mayah Nachman/Maryland Matters)
Maryland lawmakers, and Gov. Wes Moore (D), have been among those pushing for state officials to have a greater say at PJM, as their constituents grapple with ever-increasing utility bills. PJM, the nation’s largest electricity grid, includes all or part of 13 states and the District of Columbia.
Hester, who is leading a bipartisan, multistate coalition of legislators pushing for reform at PJM, was joined Thursday by Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery), Pennsylvania Rep. Joe Webster (D-Montgomery) and environmental advocates. 
Fry Hester submitted a proposal on behalf of the coalition, outlining ways in which PJM should overhaul its governing structure. They call for ensuring PJM prioritizes affordability and reliability, formalizing states’ roles in decision making and strengthening transparency. They also recommend creating ways to speed up decision-making process and strengthening board independence and accountability, including by requiring FERC to evaluate PJM using specific performance markers.
Charkoudian said PJM’s slow decision-making process and governance structure have undermined states.  
“When we look at each of these areas where states are trying to move policy forward on reliability, on decarbonization and on affordability, and where PJM has overridden our ability to do that, we have to ask the question of who is calling the shots,” Charkoudian said. “The people calling the shots are the folks who have money to make when each of these solutions do not succeed.” 
Both Fry Hester and Charkoudian thanked the FERC for convening the conference, with Fry Hester noting that she heard commissioners express views that aligned with the collaborative’s recommendations.
Many of the concerns stem back to an energy auction that PJM held in 2024, which ended with a record clearing price an astounding 800% higher than a year before. The reason was an imbalance between energy supply and energy demand, caused in part by massive amounts of demand projected to come from data centers. The auction increased Maryland customers’ bills by varying amounts, with BGE customers faring the worst, with a $21 monthly increase in 2025.
After the auction, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) sued PJM, backed by Moore, and a January 2025 settlement established a new price cap for the auction, which has been extended several times. Each subsequent auction has hit the cap, and consumers are estimated to have saved tens of billions. At the auction for 2028 and 2029, held earlier this month, PJM also wound up securing less energy from suppliers than it had hoped, leaving it with slimmer energy reserves should an emergency affect the grid.
PJM Interconnection electricity price hits cap again in latest auction

Critics have long complained about PJM’s clogged interconnection queue that keeps new projects from connecting to the grid expeditiously. PJM’s procedures were built for a time when a smaller number of large power plants were coming online. These days, with renewable energy projects like solar, wind and battery storage facilities, a much larger quantity of small projects want to come online.
PJM is governed by a board of managers with nine voting members and the PJM CEO, currently David E. Mills. The members must have expertise in various areas, including corporate leadership and transmission systems, but they cannot have any relationship with or financial stake in a member company.
PJM’s more than 1,000 members include transmission owners, generation owners, electricity distributors and others. Consumer advocates from PJM states are ex officio members with voting rights on certain committees. But otherwise, state leaders have no formal role, though they can participate in stakeholder processes and at the Organization of PJM States, or OPSI.
In a comment document prepared by PJM officials for Thursday’s FERC conference, the grid operator notes that when PJM formed, the states chose not to be members, “so as to not be placed in a position to vote or otherwise opine on matters that may subsequently come before them in their role as state commissioners.”
“More recently, the energy politics in each of the PJM states has become more complex,” reads the document. “Within individual states, PJM may hear from governors, utility commissioners, legislators, consumer advocates and other public officials who each hold diverging views. The range of diverse voices speaking for each of the states can make it difficult for PJM to determine how best to incorporate any given state’s view into its decision-making.”
PJM said it has shown “great deference” to the states, including by agreeing to the settlement establishing a price cap for its auctions.
“PJM is open to discussions around how PJM can enhance opportunities for state participation and better define roles and responsibilities,” the document reads. “But such proposals should be paired with an appropriate level of responsibility and accountability based upon our states’ very important role – especially in maintaining resource adequacy for the region.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Democrats Annette Taddeo and Earle Ford compete to face CFO Blaise Ingoglia in November
description: An interesting point in discussing the Democratic primary election for chief financial officer (CFO), one of the most powerful positions in Florida government, is that there almost wasn’t one. For months, it appeared the Florida Democratic Party would strike out in fielding a candidate to oppose GOP incumbent Blaise Ingoglia, appointed to the position a […]
text:
Annette Taddeo and Earle Ford are the Democratic candidate for CFO. They were photographed at the FDP's Leadership Blue conference on July 18, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)An interesting point in discussing the Democratic primary election for chief financial officer (CFO), one of the most powerful positions in Florida government, is that there almost wasn’t one.
For months, it appeared the Florida Democratic Party would strike out in fielding a candidate to oppose GOP incumbent Blaise Ingoglia, appointed to the position a year ago by Gov. Ron DeSantis.
Then, just two weeks before the qualifying deadline, Earle Ford, a former assistant state attorney and federal investigator for the Internal Revenue Service, dropped out of his race for Congress in Florida’s 13th District and announced he was running for CFO.
Former Miami-Dade County state Sen. Annette Taddeo joined him, entering the contest just days before the June 12 qualifying deadline.
The CFO heads the Department of Financial Services, which includes the Office of Insurance Regulation and the Office of Financial Regulation. Those offices have oversight over the insurance and financial  services industry, which includes banks and credit unions.
In interviews during the Florida Democratic Party’s Leadership Blue conference last weekend, the two candidates discussed why they’re running.
Name recognition 
Taddeo, 59, says she was recruited by Ruth’s List Florida, the political group that recruits, trains, and campaigns for Democratic pro-choice women candidates.
She is critical of Ingoglia’s high-profile campaign-like visits to cities with his DOGE and later FAFO (short for Florida Agency for Fiscal Oversight) auditors who have determined that every local government in the state they trained their focus on is guilty of excessive and wasteful spending, “because we can’t figure out where the numbers are coming from or how they’re coming up with them.”
“I do think that of course you can probably find waste and abuse in lots of levels in government,” Taddeo said, but she questions why he is isn’t looking at state spending — or overspending.
“You have $1.2 billion for Alligator Alcatraz,” she said, referring to the immigration detention facility built in the middle of the Everglades that recently shut down.
“No-bid contracts. No audits. By law in statute, he’s supposed to do that and he’s not doing it. Maybe he’s doing this to get his name recognition up, but also partly to not look at where the real waste and abuse is. When he came here to Orlando and said, ‘Oh, look, $6,000 was given to the poet laureate,’ I’m like, ‘Are you serious ?‘ Are we supposed to be worried about that when you have Doodie Calls being given millions and millions of dollars?”
(The Phoenix has reported that the state made nine payments to Doodie Calls, a portable toilet provider, totaling more than $92 million, as part of efforts to fight undocumented immigration).
“If you were to describe what is the one job of the CFO, it is to be the watchdog for our money,” she added. “Our resources. Not to be the lapdog for whoever is the governor at the time, or whoever is lining up for your political campaign. That is not okay.”
Over the past decade plus, Taddeo has run for public office several times, giving her more name recognition than Ford. In addition to her time representing a part of Miami-Dade County as a state senator from 2017 to 2022, she was Charlie Crist’s running mate on the 2014 Democratic gubernatorial ticket, which lost by a single point to Rick Scott.
If elected, she says, she can be an independent voice representing the public.
“I think both parties go wrong all the time and people are fed up with it,” Taddeo said. “I’m somebody who has criticized my own party [and] voted against my own party when it wasn’t in the best interests of the people I represent. You can never forget that. You get there to do good and to move the agenda forward to really, really deliver for people, and the CFO position, you have the opportunity on the Cabinet to be that watchdog. That person that can ask the questions like I always did, even of the Democrats on things that were questionable, and I think that it’s really important to have that independent voice, and right now we have a lapdog for the governor,” a reference to Ingoglia.
Army veteran
Ford, 40, is a U.S. Army veteran who served for a year as assistant state attorney in Florida’s Ninth Judicial Circuit in Orange and Osceola County in 2019. In 2021, he became an estate and gift tax specialist with the Internal Revenue Service until 2025.
“I’m proud of my experience with the IRS. They’re good at what they do for a reason,” Ford told the Phoenix.
“And I think that’s one of the things that pulled me to the CFO position, because I’m a Floridian at the end of the day,” he said. “I hate to see the waste of taxpayer money. That’s not a Republican or a Democratic issue. People want their government to be efficient. They also want it to be transparent. And they also want accountability. A lot of businesses in local communities rely on government to be on the up and up so that they can compete for contracts, and that’s what I want to bring.”
Ford calls Ingoglia’s high-profile attacks on local governments for their spending habits “disappointing” and says the CFO’s office can be more aggressive in taking the property insurance industry straight on. He calls the campaign for property tax reduction an attack on local government “in order to unify power in Tallahassee,” and says the whole exercise has been “a distraction.”
Insurance crisis
Ford and Taddeo argue lowering property insurance rates, not property taxes, is the policy demand they hear most about from Floridians on the campaign trail. Florida remains the most expensive state in the nation for homeowners’ insurance, reaching an annual average cost of $8,292 last year, according to Insurify.
Florida GOP lawmakers have said that the home insurance market is on the rebound. They note how more than a dozen new insurance companies have entered Florida, dozens of others have requested rate reductions, and that the number of policies held by Citizens Property Insurance Corp., the state’s insurer of last resort, have dropped to their lowest level in 14 years.
The state did so by making it harder to sue insurance companies alleged to have shortchanged claims.
“I know that they’re proud of tort reform, and we know that litigation drives up costs, but you also have to balance that out,” Ford said about the recently enacted legislation regarding property insurance in the state. “I want to make sure that I’m working with consumers.”
He added: “I’m not trying to go to war with the insurance industry, I just want to level the playing field. Because when we have a level playing field, businesses that also deal with the insurance industry, they’re going to thrive, but we’re also going to have a healthy market as well.”
The winner of the Aug. 18 Democratic primary will face Ingoglia. The sitting CFO does have a primary opponent in Frank W. Collige.
The chief financial officer of Florida is one of three Cabinet positions in state government, along with the attorney general and agriculture commissioner, and goes up for election every four years. Together, Cabinet officers help the governor administer a number of state agencies.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Congress has given states new housing tools. CT is ready to make them work
description: Increasing production and protecting our most vulnerable residents are not competing priorities. A healthy housing system requires both.
text:
For years, housing has been one of the few issues everyone seemed to agree was a problem but no one could quite agree on how to solve. Enter the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. 
The new legislation represents one of the most significant federal housing reforms in decades, bringing together Republicans and Democrats around reality: the United States isn’t building enough homes, and the shortage is affecting families, employers, and communities in every corner of the country. 
The bill won’t solve the housing crisis in Connecticut or anywhere else overnight. It wasn’t designed to. But it provides states like us with a stronger set of tools to increase housing production, better utilize federal housing programs, preserve more affordable housing, and reduce some of the barriers that have made it harder to build the homes our communities need. 
That’s good news for Connecticut. For years, we have watched housing costs outpace wages, homeownership become increasingly out of reach, and employers struggle to recruit workers because people simply can’t find homes they can afford. Chances are you live in a community where young adults are struggling to find a home they can afford. Older residents are finding it difficult to downsize. Families are spending more of their income on housing, leaving less for childcare, healthcare, education, and retirement. Many of us have grown to almost accept this as the norm. 
But these things aren’t normal. They’re symptoms of a housing market that hasn’t kept pace with demand.  
This new federal legislation recognizes that reality. Among its most important provisions are long-overdue improvements to the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, the primary financing tool for affordable housing development in the United States. By increasing available tax credits and making financing more flexible, Congress has made it easier for affordable housing developments to move from concept to construction. 
The legislation also invests in reducing unnecessary barriers to housing production. It encourages communities to modernize planning and permitting processes, supports adaptive reuse of existing buildings, expands opportunities for manufactured housing, and strengthens tools that help local governments plan for their future housing needs. 
These may not be the provisions that generate headlines, but they are exactly the kinds of policy changes that can make a meaningful difference over time. 
And they align with the conversations and efforts already taking place across our state among local officials, nonprofit organizations, developers, business leaders, lenders, and residents that recognize that housing isn’t simply a social issue. Communities that cannot produce enough housing struggle to attract employers. Businesses struggle to recruit workers. Families spend more of their income on housing and less in their local economies. Young people leave for places where homeownership feels attainable. These challenges affect every municipality, regardless of size or geography. 
The federal government has now provided additional tools to address those challenges. 
The question is whether states will use them. Connecticut has an opportunity to do exactly that. 
Many communities across the state are actively working to remove barriers to housing production. Federal support can help accelerate that work by providing new financing opportunities, encouraging innovation, and rewarding the communities that are willing to meet the housing needs of residents. 
At the same time, we cannot mistake increased housing production as the complete solution. 
Building more homes is essential. Without significantly increasing supply, affordability will continue to worsen. But many Connecticut residents will continue to need housing that the private market alone cannot provide. Older adults living on fixed incomes, people with disabilities, households experiencing homelessness, and families with the lowest incomes will still depend on rental assistance, supportive housing, and existing deeply affordable homes. Those investments remain every bit as important as increasing overall housing supply. 
Increasing production and protecting our most vulnerable residents are not competing priorities. They are complementary ones. A healthy housing system requires both. 
As Connecticut continues shaping its housing future, our goal shouldn’t simply be to build more homes. It should be to create a housing system that gives young adults the opportunity to stay in Connecticut, allows older residents to age in their communities, provides working families with affordable options close to jobs and schools, and ensures that people facing the greatest housing challenges are not left behind. 
The passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act is worth celebrating. It reflects years of advocacy from organizations across the country, including our partners at the National Low Income Housing Coalition and colleagues throughout the New England Housing Network, who worked to elevate the experiences of states like Connecticut and demonstrate why comprehensive housing reform was needed. 
Now the focus shifts from Congress to states and local communities. That work belongs to all of us. If Connecticut embraces the opportunities this legislation creates while continuing to invest in the people and communities who need housing the most, we’ll be well positioned to build a stronger housing future and more competitive state for generations to come. 
Chelsea Ross is Executive Director of the Partnership for Strong Communities.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Without Olmstead rule protection, God help the disabled
description: People with disabilities are at risk of losing their community services if the Olmstead decision of 1999 is set aside.
text:
I am EXHAUSTED…..WHY you may ask? Again people with disabilities have to gear up for battle. 
We just saved Community First Choice so we can continue to have services in the community instead of the nursing home. Now the Olmstead decision of 1999 is in danger. On June 22, 1999, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that states are required to provide community-based services when appropriate rather than institutional care. It was a landmark ruling celebrated by people with all disabilities because it compelled states to funnel Medicaid funds from institutions to community programs.
Then almost exactly 27 years later, on June 18, 2026, Deputy Assistant Attorney General Lanora Pettit released an opinion that attempts to undermine the Olmstead Promise. This opinion could potentially lead to a domino effect causing states to no longer fund community programs. President Trump has been clear that he thinks states should limit the use of Medicaid funds to institutions and not community programs.


This is absolutely terrifying to me. I was born with a physical disability Arthrogryposis. Unfortunately in my later years I also developed spinal stenosis and diabetes. I lived in New Haven for over 30 years with daily assistance from personal care assistants. 
In March 2024 my family and I made the difficult decision for me to enter a nursing home due to some financial issues and all the physical problems I was having.
My goal was to return to the community as soon as possible. It took over two years to be able to return to my home city of New Haven. While the staff at the nursing home was good, it also had many challenges. Their were numerous staff shortages and call outs. Patients would wait sometimes over an hour to be cleaned from bathroom accidents. The CNAs typically had 10 to 15 residents to care for which is allowed by the state but many of the patients were total care either physically or mentally due to dementia. 
My roommate, who I grew to love, also grew worse mentally. Honestly there were many times if I had not been there to watch her I don’t know what would have happened to her. I would hear residents hollering on a daily basis. It was difficult to deal with. When the weather allowed I would sit outside and listen to music or go on walks with my sister to escape. The home was sold to another company and services worsened, like food, and there were cuts across the board.
My day of freedom was June 3. My new apartment is small but with the assistance of my personal care assistants I am getting settled in and it is feeling like home. I’m getting to know my neighborhood and looking forward to using transit to get around.
People think placing their relatives in a nursing home will keep them safe because they will have 24-hour care. Trust me I was there. It’s a lie. They are not going to be safer. The other day the home I was in posted to Facebook they are at 100 percent capacity. The administrators posed happily with balloons in celebration. I did not see any CNAs in the picture. I’m sure they were too busy. The post made me sad because I know what’s happening on the unit. Patients are not getting the care they need and CNAs being overwhelmed.
If Olmstead gets set aside, God help us. 
Remember any of us can become disabled due to accident, illness or age. If we lose Olmstead we all could end up in an institution. I encourage you to watch a documentary about Willowbrook.  It’s an institution in New York that Geraldo Rivera investigated. What you will see is absolutely horrific. Do we really want to reverse history and go back to this?
Sandra Roberts lives in New Haven.

text:
Kansas Reflector columnist Max McCoy, right, and editor Sherman Smith pose for a photo Thursday night at Radius Brewing Co. in Emporia after learning McCoy had received a first-place national award. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)EMPORIA — Kansas Reflector columnist Max McCoy won a first-place National Society of Newspaper Columnists award for the second year in a row, claiming the top prize for humor writing.
The annual awards were announced Thursday evening, with winners in eight categories drawn from more than 80 publications. McCoy won first place for online humor writing and an honorable mention for crisis commentary. Kansas Reflector opinion editor Clay Wirestone placed third in crisis commentary.
This is the third time McCoy has won a National Society of Newspaper Columnists award since he began writing his Sunday column for Kansas Reflector after the publication launched in July 2020.
Last year, he won first place in the online general interest category. He also won first place for online humor writing in 2021, and second place for online general interest in 2023.
This year’s first-place award was based on two columns McCoy wrote last year:

“When night comes, we might all be listening for Radio Free Kansas.” (March 30, 2025)
“A theocrat’s prayer to end democracy.” (April 20, 2025)

“We live in absurd times so it is appropriate that two of my columns, dealing with the deadly serious business of authoritarianism and theocracy, should be chosen as winners in the humor category in a national contest,” McCoy said. “How else to get a serious message across except with some wit? I’m pleased to be recognized by the NSNC and am grateful for the opportunity to be published by the Reflector. I’m most thankful, however, to my first and best reader, my wife Kim, and to all of those who check in with me every Sunday.”
Wirestone previously won an honorable mention for crisis commentary in 2024.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: State-contracted report shows broad access to higher education in Iowa
description: Iowa’s community colleges told lawmakers this year that portions of Iowa are lacking access to a higher education and one solution to eliminate “education deserts” is to offer bachelor’s degrees at their institutions. Private colleges pushed back against this premise, disagreeing about the perceived need. A state-commissioned study received by the Iowa Depar[...]
text:
The Iowa Department of Education contracted with NCHEMS to develop a report on Iowa's higher education field and workforce alignment. (Photo by Kathie Obradovich/Iowa Capital Dispatch, Report title and logo from NCHEMS "Higher Education and Workforce Alignment in Iowa: Final Report")Iowa’s community colleges told lawmakers this year that portions of Iowa are lacking access to a higher education and one solution to eliminate “education deserts” is to offer bachelor’s degrees at their institutions. Private colleges pushed back against this premise, disagreeing about the perceived need.
A state-commissioned study received by the Iowa Department of Education last month, but not released until now, says the vast majority of the state is in reach of higher education resources, and that Iowa’s colleges and universities are rising to meet student and workforce needs. The study attributes workforce shortages to the business climate, not the higher education system. But community colleges argue the study misidentifies higher education deserts and says the state could still benefit from four-year degree programs at their schools.
Parties on opposite sides of the debate on whether Iowa’s higher education institutions are adequately meeting student and workforce demand had different takeaways from the report that maps out degree demand and access, though both agree the public and state officials would benefit from seeing it and adapting its recommendations.
“Higher Education and Workforce Alignment in Iowa: Final Report” was prepared for the department of education by the National Center for Higher Education Management Systems (NCHEMS) after the department contracted the nonprofit consulting organization in December, according to the report. It is dated March 6. The Iowa Capital Dispatch obtained the report Thursday through a public records request.
Iowa Department of Education Communications Director Heather Doe said in an email the department, governor’s office and Iowa Board of Regents received the report on June 25, and its aim is to give an overview of Iowa’s current higher education and workforce landscapes and “help inform continuous state systems improvement.”
“As we continue to partner with education and workforce leaders across Iowa, these findings and recommendations inform our collective work to ensure students get a strong return on their investment and employers have the skilled talent pipelines they need to grow and innovate,” Doe said in her email. “Our work to prepare learners for high-demand, high-skill and high-wage careers here in our state will continue to benefit from our improved data and alignment efforts across PK-12, higher education and workforce.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Neither the department of education or the governor’s office responded to questions about why the report wasn’t released before now.
The 119-page report details Iowa’s higher education landscape, its accessibility, student outcomes, the state’s population and groups potentially seeking a postsecondary education, demands of the state’s labor market and recommendations to improve improve access, align programs with workforce needs and “clarify the roles and missions of different types of institutions in meeting those needs.” The state requested NCHEMS “produce findings and recommendations to support data-driven policy and funding decisions.”
However, a lack of data was one of the concerns brought up in the report, and the report’s first recommendation is to “improve the state’s capacity for gathering and analyzing data about the linkages between educational supply and workforce demand.”
Other recommendations include strengthening the state’s ability to coordinate individual and collaborative work by higher education institutions and putting policies in place to “promote the creation of institutional capacity to deliver programs to remote sites on an as-needed basis” to meet specific needs of that area.
Private, community colleges disagree on definition of ‘deserts’
Gary Steinke, president of the Iowa Association of Independent Colleges and Universities, said the report states what he and other private institution officials have been saying throughout this year — there are no education deserts in Iowa, and private colleges and universities are providing high-quality services to students.
“That was our expectation, and I’m frankly quite happy with the conclusions and with the data now finally all being in one place,” Steinke said.
Community Colleges for Iowa Executive Director Emily Shields disagreed, saying the report’s definition of education deserts doesn’t fit into reality and it identified areas of Iowa where in-person higher education is sparse, partnered with stakeholders expressing dissatisfaction with online education.
Iowa lawmakers, community colleges cite benefits of offering bachelor’s degrees

“We had a pretty significant conversation about community college bachelor’s degrees this legislative session, and one of my frustrations is that we were seemingly not on the same page about whether there was even a problem with educational access to bachelor’s degrees, and I think this report demonstrates that there is,” Shields said. “There are people who don’t have access to bachelor’s degrees and other educational opportunities, and I think that is a problem worth solving.”
Report shows education access, areas of improvement
The report states that its analysis and findings are mostly based on quantitative, public data, supplemented with stakeholder interviews and submitted information.
From this work, the NCHEMS team found that the current higher education offerings in Iowa have capacity to meet state college-educated workforce needs, both current and future, and current data on degree and credential attainment “more than adequately meets the state’s needs.”
Iowa tops 42 other states for the number of higher education institutions per 100,000 people, the report stated, and college and university main campuses, branch locations and Iowa State University Extension and Outreach create “postsecondary access point(s)” that are spread across the state and could be used to expand educational reach.
Rather than educational capacity, the report stated that “troubling population and migration trends” are a more likely cause of “workforce misalignment” and other problems Iowa faces. While the state brings in more college students than it sees leave, it also sees more college graduates leave than move here or stay here. Wages in certain parts of Iowa are lower than those in surrounding states, drawing people outside of Iowa to work.
According to the report, 40% of Iowa public university graduates and 60% of community college graduates are employed in Iowa five years after program completion, with graduates of baccalaureate education programs and associate-level health care programs more likely to remain in the state.
Iowans are also getting older, with only eastern and central Iowa expected to see growth in their populations of people aged 25 to 44. Iowa’s unemployment rate is below the national average, leading more recent high school graduates to be recruited by employers “eager to hire workers directly out of high school” and opening up potential opportunities for upskilling employees through higher education, the report states.



Quotation







“I think the conversation is not necessarily about community college bachelor's degrees; it's about a lack of access in some parts of the state. And community college bachelor's degrees may not be the right solution, but I would love to talk about other ones then, because we do have an issue, and it is worth addressing.”


– Emily Shields


Working adults are a potential source for enrollment that could offset decreasing numbers of traditional collegegoers, the report stated, especially as postsecondary credentials become required in more and more job fields. Another area of Iowa’s “education-to-work pipeline” that could be strengthened, the report stated, is transfers from community colleges to four-year institutions, something public and private areas of higher education have devoted resources to.
Issues like a lack of college graduates to hire in certain areas were generally found in specific occupations, the report stated, such as nursing, and “real challenges” identified in stakeholder interviews and data had a higher chance of being specialized to that locality.
“The primary education and workforce challenges from a statewide perspective, therefore, are not how to produce more college graduates, or how to align programs with occupations better, but instead how to motivate college graduates to stay in Iowa, how to retain workers, and how to provide working adults with continuing education and upskilling while they remain employed,” the report stated.
Education deserts versus broad access
Shields and Steinke differed in their opinion on how the report categorizes “education deserts” and how access to higher education is spread across the state as shown in the report. Researchers noted that the areas where degree attainment is consistently below the state average can be found in western Iowa along Interstate 80 and in the southwest corner of the state.
A report by Community Colleges for Iowa exploring the feasibility of having bachelor degree programs at community colleges used a smaller measurement for education deserts than the report — citing a 30-mile drive rather than the report’s 60-minute drive.
The deserts identified by Community Colleges for Iowa were one point toward a lack of access for certain placebound Iowans, but Shields said that’s not the only factor that must be considered. Affordability must be brought into the question as well, she said, and the report stated that while higher education costs differ widely between different institutions, private colleges and universities were on average more expensive than other avenues to education.
A map of higher education access in Iowa. (Map from NCHEMS “Higher Education and Workforce Alignment in Iowa: Final Report”)
“I think that 60 minutes is not supported if you talk to actual human beings about their abilities to get places,” Shields said. “One thing the report didn’t do was that — you know, talk to actual people who live in Iowa who might be looking for additional education.”
Other concerns she had with the report was its inclusion of Iowa State University Extension and Outreach offices as entities that provide educational access at the level the report is discussing, as well as a lack of evidence showing how retirements will impact the number of needed employees with bachelor’s degrees.
Steinke said the report concluded that anywhere in the state with internet access is an “education-rich environment as a result” due to online offerings from private and public higher education. The report stated that the stakeholders researchers interviewed were dissatisfied by online education delivery, and encouraged institutions to create “more effective and creative student supports for online learners” in addition to strengthening transfers.
Report recommends better coordination, data gathering
Included in the report were three recommendations, which the executive summary lists as:

Improve the state’s capacity for gathering and analyzing relevant data for use in designing and evaluating policy, but also to help institutions align programs to demonstrable needs.
Consider enhancing the state’s ability to plan and coordinate how its higher education  assets work separately and together to achieve state priorities.
Develop policies that promote the creation of capacity to deliver programs to remote sites on an as-needed basis.

Shields said many of the recommendations are “spot on” for what Iowa needs to do and what is happening across the U.S., specifically with better data collection. Part of that work needs to be done on the workforce development side of operations, she said, like getting enhanced wage records.
She added that greater coordination at the state level would be helpful as some duties and responsibilities have been separated between the state’s workforce development and education departments, and she is “obviously very interested in increasing community college capacity to deliver programs at remote sites.”
“One of my biggest takeaways from this report is we’re doing a lot of things well, but we need to do a better job of reaching adult students,” Shields said. “I think we do a good job with recent high school grads who know what they want to go do, but if you start college and stop, or you get an associate degree and then you want to continue later, or you don’t go right into higher ed but decide you want to later, I don’t think we’re meeting those people’s needs very well, and that is something the community colleges do a lot of, but with targeted resources could do even better.”
While he believes private colleges and universities “do a pretty darn good job of” data gathering and sharing, Steinke said he doesn’t disagree with the recommendation that universities provide more data for statewide tracking. However, some data held by private institutions is “proprietary” as they work to keep a competitive edge over other colleges and universities, public or private.
Data on graduate outcomes like employment and residency are “the most difficult types of data to provide,” he said, as students are often relied on to respond to surveys and not everyone can be followed after they receive their degree.
One area of the recommendations Steinke said he “absolutely” disagrees with is tying increased data collection and reporting to eligibility for the Iowa Tuition Grant program, a move private colleges have opposed in the Statehouse for years.
Iowa private university leaders see bills as harmful to their institutions

“Never, ever, should a student’s financial aid depend upon what it is an institution feels that it can or cannot provide in the way of data or in anything else,” Steinke said. “You know, this is a financial aid program, it’s not a hammer that you hang over students’ heads in order to get private institutions to do what you want to do.”
Looking back and moving ahead
Steinke said “all three sectors” of higher education interacted with NCHEMS in its work to compile the study, and he joined Zoom calls with the researchers in January. He was told that they were trying to get the report completed as soon as possible but he didn’t expect to see it during the legislative session, which ended in May. Shields herself was not involved in this process, she said, but community college officials were, and no one was provided a timeline.
Josh Lehman, senior communications director for the Iowa Board of Regents, said in an email the board provided requested data to the report and “a few Board members participated in a focus group.”
“We are carefully reviewing the report and its findings now and hope it can help inform future work on the value of higher education and the Regent universities in preparing Iowa’s workforce,” Lehman said in his email.
Steinke said it would have been nice to have the report in January for the legislative session, where discussions of academic alignment with workforce needs and issues of access were prevalent.



Quotation







“Never, ever, should a student's financial aid depend upon what it is an institution feels that it can or cannot provide in the way of data or in anything else. You know, this is a financial aid program, it's not a hammer that you hang over students' heads in order to get private institutions to do what you want to do.”


– Gary Steinke


Iowa lawmakers introduced a number of bills aimed at expanding certain programs, changing curriculum and providing funding to the state and its initiatives, including bills to pilot bachelor’s degrees at community colleges and require certain university endowments to be taxed.
Private universities were also urged to conform to changes in general education requirements and core curriculum that were signed into law this summer.
Both Steinke and Shields said they’re sharing the report with institution heads across the state with the goal of going through it and identifying areas where they can improve and apply the included recommendations.
What the report showed Steinke about Iowa’s current higher education climate and where it’s headed is that the state has “three wonderful, quality sectors of higher education” that each serve students’ particular needs “as long as everybody stays in their lane.”
Shields said she wouldn’t take away from the report that “we have no room for improvement,” and she hopes the rest of Iowa’s higher education industry will use the report to find ways to improve like Community Colleges for Iowa does. She supports the idea of further exploring community college bachelor’s degrees, but said efforts from them and the state should span farther than that.
“I think the conversation is not necessarily about community college bachelor’s degrees; it’s about a lack of access in some parts of the state,” Shields said. “And community college bachelor’s degrees may not be the right solution, but I would love to talk about other ones then, because we do have an issue, and it is worth addressing.”

title: Former Louisiana golf champ Sydney Moss wins State Am in playoff
description: Sydney Moss
text:

PEARL – Mississippi Christian University golfer Sydney Moss has added the 2026 Mississippi Women’s Amateur championship at Patrick Farms Golf Club to her growing list of accomplishments.
Moss, a Shreveport native and daughter of former LSU All American and PGA Tour player Perry Moss, had previously won two Louisiana junior championships and one Louisiana State Women’s Amateur title.
Jackson State golfer Maddy Beeching, who lives in Ridgeland but is a native of Camberly, England, shot a final round 71 to tie Moss for first place the 54-hole tournament. Moss won the playoff with a par on the fourth extra hole to claim the title. Harper Hinkley of Summitt and Mississippi State also shot a final round 71 and finished third, two strokes back. 
Moss held a two-shot lead entering the final round in which she shot 73. She and Beeching shot even par for the tournament.
Moss began her college career at the University of Memphis, before transferring to Stephen F. Austin and then to Mississippi Christian University where she was All-Gulf South Conference as a junior this spring.
Lee Burke of Madison won the 36-hole senior division, shooting 73-73 to edge 12-time State Amateur winner Cissye Gallagher of Greenwood by a single shot. name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska removes thousands from state’s active voter list, erroneously flagging some citizens
description: The state of Alaska has removed an estimated 3,000 to 3,500 Alaskans from the state’s active voter list, claiming they may be noncitizens. The removals leave those residents able to vote only if they provide extra identity information, and removal puts them on track to be purged from the state’s voter roll altogether. Only U.S. […]
text:
Carol Beecher, the new director of the Alaska Division of Elections, answers questions from reporters on Thursday, Feb. 16, 2023. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)The state of Alaska has removed an estimated 3,000 to 3,500 Alaskans from the state’s active voter list, claiming they may be noncitizens.
The removals leave those residents able to vote only if they provide extra identity information, and removal puts them on track to be purged from the state’s voter roll altogether.
Only U.S. citizens may vote in Alaska, according to state and federal law, but many of the removals appear to have affected citizens who were erroneously flagged by the Alaska Division of Motor Vehicles. 
Carol Beecher, director of the Alaska Division of Elections, told state lawmakers on Wednesday that the removals were the result of “old data” given to the division from the DMV, and she isn’t sure why so many Alaskans were flagged as possible noncitizens.
Under Alaska’s “motor voter” program, people are asked if they want to register to vote when they apply for a driver’s license. The registration process requires the applicant to state whether or not they are a citizen. 
Elections officials check the state’s voter roll against DMV records several times per year, searching for people who may be incorrectly registered to vote here. That usually results in “more like 200 names” being flagged for extra attention, Beecher said. 
The latest check found “a lot more names than we were expecting,” Beecher said.     
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

“We believe that when we did the match, that a lot of old data was picked up somehow. So we’re still ferreting through that,” she said. 
Beecher said that although the number of names flagged by the DMV was “very concerning,” the state has an obligation to act on the agency’s report.
“It is not disenfranchising the individual from being able to vote, but it’s a measure the division has to take to make sure that we only have citizens voting,” she said. 
Under its normal procedure, the division sends letters to people who were flagged by the DMV, asking those people if they are citizens.
Thousands of those letters were mailed to affected state residents starting last month, according to Beecher’s testimony and copies provided to the Beacon by affected citizens.
Beecher told lawmakers that anyone deemed a noncitizen by the state simply needs to contact the Division of Elections by phone, email or mail and state that they are a citizen.
“It is not an onerous request from the division to simply contact us and confirm, and that is what we have asked them to do. We don’t require paperwork. We’re not requiring documentation. Nothing like that,” she said.
After Beecher’s statements, the Beacon asked the head of the Alaska Division of Motor Vehicles, Kathy Wallace, and the Commissioner of the Alaska Department of Administration, Paula Vrana, for an interview. The Department of Administration is the DMV’s parent agency.
In response, the division sent a memo saying that in March, “the DOE provided DMV with a list of approximately 15,200 DMV license and identification applicants and requested that DMV provide citizenship information for these records. This was a non-routine request.”
What it gave to the Division of Elections was “only those records where DMV’s latest confirmed status for an individual was other than ‘Citizen.’”
Based on interviews with affected people, the records flagged by the DMV appear to include Alaskans who obtained driver’s licenses as noncitizens, then became citizens and registered to vote, but have not received a new driver’s license since becoming a citizen.
Alaskans respond to being put on the inactive list
Chris Waigl of Fairbanks got her Alaska driver’s license in 2019 and became an American citizen in 2025. She became alarmed after checking her registration status last weekend, only to learn that she was listed as “inactive – non citizen.”
“They were able to correct it there and then after I sent in copies of my naturalization certificate with a date before my voter registration date,” she said by email.
But Waigl went further, contacting four other people who became naturalized citizens at the same time she did. Of those, only one said they were still listed as an active voter.
One of the others, reached by phone, said he was listed as inactive despite registering as a voter at the local DMV office and presenting his citizenship paperwork at that time.
Another naturalized citizen, living in Juneau and unaffiliated with Waigl, said they also were unregistered despite indicating on their Permanent Fund dividend application that they are a citizen.
Several people affected by the removal said they have attempted to contact the Division of Elections but have been unable to reach staff by phone, and that voicemail boxes have been full.
“It’s just ridiculous,” Waigl said.
She said the state’s policy of simply sending a letter is inadequate, particularly because there may be legal consequences if the state or federal government believes someone has voted as a noncitizen.
“Citizenship rights, immigration is something I’m interested in for obvious reasons,” she said.
This isn’t the first time voter registration issues have been attributed to the DMV. 
In 2022, mistakes by the division led to dozens of noncitizens being registered to vote, even if they specifically stated they were nonresidents and ineligible. Some went on to cast ballots in state and local elections.
The scale of the new removals is notable. Last year, a copy of the state’s inactive voter list showed 541 registrations listed as belonging to possible noncitizens. 
If 3,500 people were added to the inactive list by the Division of Elections, that would represent more than a 700% increase.
The removals caused the state’s active voter roll to shrink between June and July, the first time since at least 2020 that has occurred in an election year, state statistics show.
The removals come seven months after Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom, who oversees the Division of Elections, directed the state to answer a request from the U.S. Department of Justice and turn over extended copies of the state’s voter rolls. 
The Justice Department has made similar requests across the country and intends to share the data with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to check for noncitizens who may have voted illegally.
The tool used by DHS is error-prone and has erroneously flagged some citizens, according to an investigation by ProPublica.
States led by Democratic officials have accused the federal government of deliberately attempting to raise fear, uncertainty and doubt about state elections systems in order to lay the groundwork for challenges to the 2026 midterm elections.
“I’m just truly deeply concerned about this process creating even more distrust in our voter rolls, as if there isn’t enough already because of allegations,” Rep. Ky Holland, I-Anchorage, told Beecher on Wednesday.
A memo signed by Beecher and U.S. Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon in December calls for the state to remove voters from the active list if they are specifically identified by the federal government.  
Civil rights groups sued the state in April over the voter list issue. In June, the state filed a motion to dismiss; that motion is awaiting adjudication. 
State legislators asked Beecher on Wednesday if the latest removals were at the behest of the federal government.
No, said Beecher.
“It has nothing to do with that,” she said. “The information that we have received is specifically from DMV. Why the voter list or why the list was so large this time, we’re not completely sure… we are looking into figuring that out.”
But, she added, if the federal government were to request a removal, the state would follow the exact same procedure as it used recently.
“If we were to get information from them, we would take the same steps of moving them into inactive while we investigated,” she said.
