“If someone is exposed to drugs or alcohol before age 14, it’s almost a 50% chance that they’re going to have an issue,” Allen said. “If you can keep them until age 18 from first exposure, it’s like 5%, so the longer we can delay the first exposure to drugs or alcohol, the better off all families are going to be. Our concern is that legalized recreational marijuana means a reduced perception of risk, more kids potentially using and more investments that we’re going to have to make as a state from a treatment standpoint.”
Muhlbauer said young people accessing cannabis is not the “intent” of the Sand campaign, and if elected, Sand plans to regulate marijuana similarly to alcohol.
“The plan is to treat it much like alcohol, limit the marketing, and the advertising and put a framework and structure on it for those people that are already doing it,” Muhlbauer said.
Muhlbauer added that it is a focus of the Sand campaign to ensure young people will not be “enticed” by the legalization of cannabis.
“I’m here today because I realize that behavioral health and substance use is a crisis in Iowa, and we want to do our part as well to make sure that we better treat our youth, so they have a brighter future,” Muhlbauer said.
Mulhbauer cites family connection to Ember facility
Muhlbauer said one of his children was admitted to the facility nearly one year ago during a crisis. Muhlbauer said he only knew of the facility because of a connection and would not have known where to go for help otherwise.
Democrat Dave Muhlbauer, candidate for Iowa lieutenant governor, speaks to reporters July 23, 2026, after touring Ember Recovery in Cambridge, Iowa. (Photo by Kadin Luhmann/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
“Last fall, we were harvesting corn, and later that evening, my wife met me at the door with our kids because we were in a crisis moment,” Muhlbauer said. “The uncertainty of where your family is at, the future of one of your kids, and knowing that they need help, but not knowing exactly where to go, it’s nerve-wracking.”
Muhlbauer said his fears went away when he walked into the Ember Recovery facility, as the comforting environment led him to believe that the family was in “a good place.”
Muhlbauer participated in a tour of the facility, and a roundtable discussion, where he and four others discussed gaps in Iowa behavioral health treatment for children, and what the Rob Sand for Iowa campaign can do to address the issue.
“I’m here today because I realize that behavioral health and substance use is a crisis in Iowa, and we want to do our part as well to make sure that we better treat our youth, so they have a brighter future,” Muhlbauer said.
During press availability after the roundtable, Muhlbauer praised Ember Recovery’s efforts in helping young Iowans.
“The takeaway is the passion. There’s a genuine passion here to help young adults and youth get on the right path and see a brighter future,” Muhlbauer said. “Andrew has a bigger vision of Iowa being in a better place in these crisis areas, and you’re seeing that through their actions that are reaching people, and we’d like to help them reach more people and put us in the right direction.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: GOP delegate accused of seducing girl likely can’t be replaced on ballot ahead of November election
description: The state Republican Party likely can’t replace Del. Elliott Pritt on the ballot in Fayette County even if he resigns from his seat following his arrest for seducing a 15-year-old girl.
text:
Del. Elliott Pritt, R-Fayette, speaks on the floor of the House of Delegates on March 14, 2026. Pritt was arrested July 22, 2026, and faces one count of enticement of a minor. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)The state Republican Party likely can’t replace Del. Elliott Pritt on the ballot in Fayette County even if he resigns from his seat following his arrest for seducing a 15-year-old girl. 
Del. Elliott Pritt, R-Fayette, (Photo courtesy of Carter County Detention Center)
A bill sponsored by a Republican lawmaker, who is also the Republican party chair, that went into effect last year now restricts how the state GOP can deal with Pritt’s seat ahead of the November election.
Pritt, a public school teacher, was arrested Wednesday and charged with enticement of a minor. He appeared before a federal magistrate judge that same day and is now being held in a Kentucky jail. 
The child’s family recently reported to law enforcement that the girl had been sexually abused by Pritt, 36.
A federal criminal complaint said Pritt communicated with the girl online through Robolox and Snapchat before asking her to meet him in his classroom at Oak Hill High School to engage in sexual activity, which occurred on five to 10 occasions. 
Pritt has not yet resigned from the House following a stern request from House Speaker Roger Hanshaw to do so. The West Virginia Republican Party has also called on Pritt to resign from his seat. 
Pritt also hasn’t removed himself from the ballot this November as all 100 seats in the House of Delegates are up for election. It’s a separate process from resigning as a lawmaker.
Pritt was first elected as a Democrat to the House in 2022. He switched to the Republican party in 2023.
He was unopposed in this spring’s primary election. 
Deak Kersey, deputy secretary of state, said that should a candidate withdraw from the ballot, the vacancy on the ballot cannot be filled by the candidate’s political party. 
“This is new for West Virginia elections, passed via (House Bill) 4350 … In that scenario, the vacating candidate’s political party would not have a candidate for that seat on the ballot,” Kersey said in response to questions from West Virginia Watch.
Del. Josh Holstein, R-Boone
The bill was passed in 2024 and went into effect at the start of last year. It was sponsored by Del. Josh Holstein, R-Boone, who also chairs the state Republican Party.
“Should the seat become vacant, by whatever means, the party will follow the usual process for filling a vacancy outlined in WV Code §3-10-5 governed by state law and the bylaws of the West Virginia Republican Party,” Holstein said. “As for ballot replacement, the WVGOP will release details at a later date.”
The Democratic challenger in the race is Matthew Anderson, a special education teacher in Fayette County. 
Del. Mike Pushkin, D-Kanawha
West Virginia Democratic Party Chair Mike Pushkin told West Virginia Watch that the party’s “primary concern remains with the victim or victims of Elliott Pritt.”
“Republicans and Democrats alike have been united in condemning the horrific allegations against him and in calling for his immediate resignation. That must remain the focus,” said Pushkin, who also serves in the House of Delegates as a Democrat representing Kanawha County.
Pushkin voted against Holstein’s bill changing the appointment of candidates after the filing period.
“The law is clear on this matter. In 2024, Del. Josh Holstein wrote, sponsored and championed House Bill 4350, legislation that prohibits political parties from replacing a nominee this late in the election process. Because of the law he authored, the Republican Party cannot replace Elliott Pritt on the ballot,” Puskin continued. “This is not a matter of interpretation or political opinion. It is the law enacted by the Legislature at Del. Holstein’s urging. Those who write our laws have a responsibility to know them and to follow them.”
The Republican party would be able to nominate a candidate to replace Pritt on the ballot due to disqualification — including a conviction of felony — before the 84th day prior to Election Day. Pritt has been charged, but has not been convicted of felony.
“To be disqualified, it must come from a judge (e.g. through a conviction) or the State Election Commission upon written request. The grounds for disqualification are essentially ineligibility,” Kersey said. 
The disqualification has to occur by Aug. 11.
A death of a candidate also permits the party to nominate a different candidate. 
There are currently nine Democratic lawmakers in the House.
Del. Evan Worrell, a member of House leadership, has asked Gov. Patrick Morrisey to call lawmakers into a special session to deal with Pritt’s seat if he doesn’t submit a resignation. Pritt could face possible expulsion from the House in that scenario. 
The Legislature has to be in session in order to vote on any official punishment of Pritt. Hanshaw has already removed Pritt from any duties in the House; Pritt previously served as assistant majority leader.

title: Gerald “Jed” Kenneth Hornung II
description:
Jed lived a life of faith, service, integrity and leadership. He used his many skills and achievements to lead organizations he cared about and to help others. He enjoyed people and could talk to anyone. He was a loving husband, father and grandfather.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Gerald “Jed” Kenneth Hornung II.
text:
Born: 07/31/1929
Oklahoma City, Oklahoma
Died: 07/20/2026
Burlington, Vermont
Details of service:
The family will hold a private burial. There will be a Memorial Service, at a later date. Arrangements are through Day Funeral Home, Randolph, Vermont and Vermont Forest Cemetery in Roxbury.

Gerald Kenneth (Jed) Hornung II, age 96, passed away on July 20, 2026, surrounded by his loving family after a brief illness. Gerald was born in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma on July 31, 1929, the son of Gerald Kenneth Hornung and Hazel Emily Ruedy Hornung.
Jed lived a life of faith, service, integrity and leadership. He used his many skills and achievements to lead organizations he cared about and to help others. He enjoyed people and could talk to anyone. He was a loving husband, father and grandfather.
Jed attended Classen High School in Oklahoma City, where he learned to be a debater and went on to be a National Debate Champion through the National American Legion Oratorical contest. He was then elected the first National President of the American Junior Red Cross, a youth organization with 20 million members during World War II. Later, in 2018, Jed was named an “Everyday Hero” by the Vermont American Red Cross for 70 years of service.
Majoring in Government and Economics, Jed graduated from the University of Oklahoma in 1951. He was elected President of his Senior Class and his fraternity, and was chosen for PE-ET, which annually honors the 10 most outstanding campus seniors. After graduation, he went from being a member of the Air Force R.O.T.C., to active duty in the United States Air Force, becoming a Captain, during the Korean War. In 1952, he married his sweetheart Virginia (Jini) Ann Spain in Frederick, Oklahoma. They would go on to be married for over 74 wonderful years.
After his military service, he attended Law School at the University of Oklahoma. He served as Managing Editor of the Oklahoma Law Review and was elected President of the honor law fraternity Phi Alpha Delta.
Following admission to the Oklahoma Bar Association, he joined the New York City investment banking firm Wertheim & Co. and attended New York University Graduate School of Business. In 1970 he became a Wertheim & Co. General Partner and the Senior Vice President of four Wertheim subsidiaries.
Jed was active in the United Methodist Church all his life. He and Jini had many good friends through their involvement in many churches. After moving to New England, they raised their three children and were active for twenty-two years at the Norwalk, Connecticut United Methodist Church and Jed was a Trustee of the New York United Methodist Conference. In 1978 he became CEO (General Secretary) of the United Methodist General Board of Pensions, one of the largest pension funds in America. Later in Vermont, they were active in the Middlesex, Shelburne, and North Ferrisburgh United Methodist Churches.
He lived a life using his Christian faith, leadership abilities, and investment acumen to volunteer and assist numerous non-profit organizations, seminaries, colleges, and churches. He organized and for 48 years served as President of the Gerald and Virginia Hornung Family Foundation. The Foundation is now managed by Vanguard Charitable.
His fraternity friendships in college led him to become a Director of the Alpha Tau Omega Foundation. He was a founding Director and the first Treasurer of LeaderShape, which now provides ethical leadership training to students of all genders on more than 85 college campuses.
Other volunteer positions included serving as a Trustee for the United Methodist Reporter Foundation, Dallas, Texas; three United Methodist seminaries: Garrett-Evangelical, Evanston, Illinois; Methodist Seminary in Delaware, Ohio, and Asbury Theological Seminary, Wilmore, Kentucky. He did the same for the United Methodist Higher Education Foundation, Nashville, Tennessee.
Jed and Jini lived in Woodstock, from 1988 until 2004. They enjoyed the scenery and many friendships and many volunteer activities. Jed served as Treasurer of the town of Woodstock. He also enjoyed being involved with the Woodstock Historical Society, Senior Center, Rotary Club, and the Woodstock Round Table. He was a Trustee of Green Mountain College in Poultney. He also served on the board of the Calvin Coolidge Memorial Foundation, Plymouth. Jed and Jini moved to Wake Robin in Shelburne in 2004 and enjoyed many friendships and activities there. They both loved to travel and visited many spots in the U.S. and around the world.
Jed had a deep, abiding love for his wife and family, which he expressed often. He is survived by his wife Jini, of Shelburne, his daughter Kimberly Hornung-Marcy and son-in-law Theodore Marcy of Williston, grandchildren Ariel and her wife Kristina Marcy, Jordan Marcy; his daughter Leslie and son-in-law Timothy Wallstrom of Los Alamos, New Mexico, granddaughters Sarah, Rachel, and Miriam Wallstrom, and his son Gerald Kenneth Hornung III and his fiancé Rene Juza of Boise, Idaho, and granddaughter Heather Hornung Smith and her husband Heyden Smith.
Jed was preceded in death by his parents Gerald Kenneth and Hazel Hornung and his brother-in-law Robert Spain.
The family will hold a private burial. There will be a Memorial Service, at a later date. Arrangements are through Day Funeral Home, Randolph and Vermont Forest Cemetery, Roxbury. In lieu of flowers, please consider a donation to the North Ferrisburgh United Methodist Church, the Shelburne United Methodist Church, or the American Red Cross.

title: Glacier National park to plug leaking oil well near Kintla Lake
description: Glacier National Park officials announced they will begin work next week to plug a leaking oil well in the park’s northern region. The Butte Oil Well, near the head of Kintla Lake, was the first oil well drilled in the state of Montana, predating the establishment of Glacier Park. A 2023 monitoring effort of the well […]
text:
Kintla Lake in Glacier National Park. (Courtesy photo)Glacier National Park officials announced they will begin work next week to plug a leaking oil well in the park’s northern region.
The Butte Oil Well, near the head of Kintla Lake, was the first oil well drilled in the state of Montana, predating the establishment of Glacier Park.
A 2023 monitoring effort of the well detected a methane gas leak, likely due to seismic activity in the area, according to a news release from the park. The park said plugging the well will reduce methane leaks, minimize physical hazards, and minimize migration of geological formation fluids and chemicals into the nearby lake.
The project is expected to begin on July 27 and continue through late August.
Throughout the duration of the construction, trail and camping access in the Kintla Lake area will be affected, according to the press release. The Kintla Lake Wilderness Campground is expected to be closed during helicopter operations and active construction. Visitors should check Recreation.gov for availability before planning overnight trips in the area.
The frontcountry campground at Kintla Lake will be open for first-come, first-served camping during construction.
Visitors should also expect increased construction traffic along the Inside North Fork Road between Polebridge and Kintla Lake. Construction equipment and activities may temporarily affect views and natural sounds around the lake.
There will be a series of helicopter flights in July to transport materials and equipment to the project site, which will require further closures along the Kintla-Boulder Pass Trail on July 27 and 28, and two days in August, which will be announced later, the park said.
Glacier National Park has an interactive story map about the history of the Butte Oil Well and the process to plug it up to prevent leaks, which can be accessed online.
The project is being completed through the National Park Service’s Abandoned Mineral Lands program, which addresses historic mining sites and oil and gas well established before lands became part of the National Park System.

title: GOP govs join Trump pledge designed to shield ratepayers from data center costs
text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Thursday announced the addition of Republican governors, legislators, utility services and tech companies into his voluntary pledge aimed at keeping data center construction and operation costs off the shoulders of American consumers. The Ratepayer Protection Pledge, first signed by the president in March, requires companies that build and use data centers to pay for any new infrastructure upgrades and generation resources that serve them. Tech giants Google, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, xAI, OpenAI and Amazon all signed onto the initial pledge. Now, the measure is expanding to include nearly 200 more stakeholders, including multiple governors.Electric companies and other utilities generally pay for infrastructure upgrades with the revenue that comes from what their customers pay. The agreement aims to shift that cost in communities with new data centers directly to the centers’ companies. According to Trump, the initiative will supply 80% of all the power delivered to American businesses and homes.“As new data centers go up, all of the electricity bills for American families will actually come down,” Trump said during a roundtable event at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency on Thursday. He added that Big Tech companies are “happy” to foot the bill for data centers because it will allow them to continue to function and grow.  “I’ve always said that America’s goal must be to dominate the future, and that includes being the No. 1 superpower in artificial intelligence,” Trump said. “This is how we’ll grow our economy, lower the cost of living, protect American consumers and lead the world in AI and high tech.”  Republican Govs. Jeff Landry of Louisiana, Brian Kemp of Georgia, Jim Pillen of Nebraska and Brad Little of Idaho joined the president at the roundtable to promote their commitment to the pledge. Some governors manage the state utility commissions that set electricity prices.  A total of 23 Republican governors signed the pledge, according to an undated document the White House sent reporters Thursday morning. Only Florida’s Ron DeSantis, New Hampshire’s Kelly Ayotte and Vermont’s Phil Scott declined to sign.The executives said large power plants are supplying energy for their states without raising consumer costs, and touted partnerships with companies such as Meta.Landry said his state’s deal with Meta will “save Louisiana $2.6 billion,” helping to strengthen “river liability” and reduce “resiliency costs” for those who live along the Gulf Coast. In Georgia, Kemp said the pledge will support the operation of nuclear power plants while keeping rates low for local communities.Contradicting numbersThe environmental advocacy group Climate Power published a report Thursday that counters the president’s promises of lowered electricity costs for consumers. According to the organization, prices have spiked 18% on average since Trump took office. “While Trump stages PR stunts to save his tanking approval rating, Americans are paying the price for his cost-raising agenda,” Climate Power said in the report. “As gas prices hit $4 per gallon again this year thanks to Trump’s war of choice in Iran, Americans in five states faced rate hikes as high as $9 a month.” 

 






Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, left, listens as U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright speaks during a roundtable event at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency on Thursday, July 23, 2026. (Photo by Amelia Twyman/States Newsroom)

The states it listed were Missouri, North Carolina, Connecticut, New Mexico and Oregon. Beating ChinaThe speakers Thursday, including Trump, governors, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin consistently said the pledge could help win an AI race with China.“Americans are united in their desire to supercharge our economy, to increase our national security by keeping our lead in artificial intelligence over China,” Wright said. They are also “united in their frustration over the ruinous nearly 30% price rise in electricity across the country during the Biden administration,” he added. Trump noted China’s authoritarian government does not require environmental impact studies or other permits.House billEarlier this week, the U.S. House Committee on Energy and Commerce unanimously passed a bill similar to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge to protect Americans from paying higher electricity costs tied to data centers. Sponsored by Reps. Gabe Evans, a Colorado Republican, and Kathy Castor, a Florida Democrat, the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act would require state utility regulators to consider adopting standards for data centers to pay for their own electricity, infrastructure and other developments. “America must build the energy infrastructure necessary to win the global AI race and outcompete adversaries like Communist China—but hardworking families should never be forced to subsidize that growth through higher electric bills,” Evans, who is the chairman of the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Energy, said in a statement Tuesday. Just before it passed, 52-0, the committee narrowed the scope of the bill to focus specifically on data centers. Language in an earlier draft would have applied to power plants with a maximum electricity demand of 100 megawatts or more, according to Politico.  

 






An Amazon Web Services data center is shown situated near single-family homes on July 17, 2024 in Stone Ridge, Virginia. Opponents of data center construction have pointed to the energy and water resources needed to run them, and the strain that puts on communities. (Photo by Nathan Howard/Getty Images)

The Data Center Coalition, an advocacy group representing some of the biggest names in the industry including Amazon, Microsoft and Google, said in a statement Wednesday that it supported the original version of the bill but took issue with the changes. The changes “single out the data center industry, leaving everyday Americans vulnerable to the costs associated with large load growth from other industries as they continue to expand operations in the U.S,” Josh Levi, the group’s president and CEO, said.Progressives push outright banSome Democratic lawmakers, including as Energy and Commerce ranking member Rep. Frank Pallon of New Jersey, have expressed support for the more restrictive idea of a national data center moratorium.Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont have introduced parallel bills in their respective chambers to implement a nationwide AI data center moratorium. Such legislation would temporarily prohibit the construction of new data centers and the expansion of existing ones in the U.S. until Congress addresses the economic, environmental and safety consequences associated with the facilities. Last week, New York became the first state to impose a ban on AI data centers.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: The testing desert: How closing UAA’s testing center isolates Alaskans
description: I didn’t learn about the permanent closure of the University of Alaska Anchorage Testing Center through a campus press release or a community town hall. I learned about it on a quiet summer afternoon while taking my 14-year-old son to sit for an exam for college credit. Watching a teenager step up, take initiative and […]
text:
A student exits the University of Alaska Anchorage consortium library on Sept. 6, 2024. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)I didn’t learn about the permanent closure of the University of Alaska Anchorage Testing Center through a campus press release or a community town hall. I learned about it on a quiet summer afternoon while taking my 14-year-old son to sit for an exam for college credit. Watching a teenager step up, take initiative and unlock his potential early is an incredible feeling—a vivid testament to what is possible when accessible local infrastructure exists to lift our kids up.
But as we were leaving, a staff member warned us to schedule whatever remaining exams we could as quickly as possible. She was exasperated—and rightfully so. She had just been notified via a Friday afternoon email that the center was closing permanently on July 30th, and the entire staff was out of a job. Just like that, with only a few weeks’ notice in the dead of summer, dedicated employees were discarded and an essential public institution was quietly dismantled.
The staffer said that, according to the university’s email, the rationale centers on reallocation: stripping funds from existing student support services to concentrate resources on recruitment, registration and driving up top-line enrollment numbers. But this strategy reveals a shortsighted paradox: What is the point of pouring money into recruiting new students if we gut the very infrastructure required for them to test, advance and graduate?
What makes this closure so catastrophic is that UAA’s Testing Center was never just a room with computer desks. It was Southcentral Alaska’s only comprehensive, all-in-one physical testing hub. Unlike small, specialized private sites that handle only specific vendors, UAA’s facility managed the entire academic and professional spectrum—college course exams, ACCUPLACER placement, statewide professional licensing boards, trade certifications and national standardized tests like the ACT. No other civilian venue in Anchorage possesses the authorization, footprint or operational scope to absorb that workload. Closing UAA doesn’t shift that traffic elsewhere; it destroys the hub entirely.
When pressed on alternatives, the university points to automated online software and military facilities, but both fall apart under basic scrutiny. Automated proctoring like HonorLock relies on a myth of digital equity that Alaska’s infrastructure cannot support. In a state where broadband frequently stutters, a single Wi-Fi drop can void months of hard work. Additionally, invasive AI webcams present an insurmountable barrier for neurodivergent students or working adults in crowded households. Recommending the testing space at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson is equally flawed: JBER sits behind military security checkpoints. Public university infrastructure funded by Alaskan tax dollars should never require a visitor pass, background check or military sponsorship to access. Access to advancement should not be behind a locked gate.
The ripple effect reaches far beyond college classrooms and straight into our regional workforce. By eliminating our central testing anchor, we are stranding local nurses, teachers, contractors and ambitious young Alaskans in an administrative wasteland. Working Alaskans seeking career-advancing licenses now face the absurd prospect of spending thousands of dollars flying around the state—or worse, to the Lower 48—just to sit in a proctored room for a two-hour exam.
Alaska should be opening doors for its people, not slamming them shut on a Friday afternoon. Watching my son earn college credit showed me firsthand what happens when community infrastructure actually supports educational ambition. University leadership and local community partners must halt this closure immediately and establish an accessible, public-facing civilian alternative before the door locks Alaskans out for good.

title: Fewer Florida residents are receiving federal food benefits
description: The number of Florida residents who receive federal food assistance dropped by 23% during the past year, state data published this month show. There were 2,285,099 residents enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) in June, down from the 2,970,283 in June 2025, data maintained by the Department of Children and Families show. That’s […[...]
text:
Florida has seen one of the largest dips in the number of people receiving food benefits in the last year. (Getty Images)The number of Florida residents who receive federal food assistance dropped by 23% during the past year, state data published this month show.
There were 2,285,099 residents enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) in June, down from the 2,970,283 in June 2025, data maintained by the Department of Children and Families show.
That’s about a 23% reduction. SNAP enrollment dropped steadily in each of the past 12 months.
Although significant, the decrease was outpaced by the 26.1% reduction in financial assistance awarded, from nearly $541 million in June 2025 to about $399 million last month.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Enrollment in social services programs such as SNAP is countercyclical, meaning it increases as the economy worsens. But the drop-off in SNAP enrollment occurred even as the state’s unemployment rate increased during the year, U.S. Bureau and Labor Statistics data show.
The number of enrollees in SNAP was dipping before the July 2025 enactment of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act but increased as the law took effect. The law slashes spending on the food security program by $187 billion over a decade.
To accomplish those costs savings, Congress required states with SNAP payment error rates of more than 6% to contribute toward the costs of the food beginning next year.
Under the law, states with error rates of 10% or more would have to contribute 15% toward food costs, which puts Florida on track to have to pay upward of $1 billion to maintain food benefits at existing levels.
Payment error rates measure the accuracy of each state’s eligibility and benefit determinations and include overpayments and underpayments.
The federal law also:

Limited the categories of lawfully present immigrants who could qualify for benefits.
Extend work requirements to older adults aged 55 through 64 and parents with children aged 14 and older.
Eliminated work requirement exemptions for veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and young people who recently aged out of foster care.


SNAP provides nutritional support for low-income seniors, people with disabilities living on fixed incomes, and other individuals and families with low incomes. Although funded by the federal government, SNAP in Florida is administered by DCF’s Office of Economic Self-Sufficiency, which is responsible for determining eligibility.
National trend 
Florida is not the only state to see a reduction in SNAP enrollees, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, but it experienced one of the more noticeable dips.
Nationwide, SNAP participation fell by more than 4.5 million people, or about 11%, since the federal budget bill took effect, the nonpartisan research and policy institute reports. Arizona saw a 44% reduction in its SNAP participation from July 2025 to June 2026 and Louisiana had a 21% reduction.
The center put Florida’s reduction rate at 21% and Oklahoma’s at 18%.
The center relied on data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Federal data differ from state data due to differences in state and federal reporting protocols.
The atrophy in enrollment occurred despite a double-digit increase in the number of requests for assistance, which from June 2025 to June 2026 jumped by 15.2%

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma data shows lack of fully trained teachers entering the classroom
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — State leaders say they’re still pursuing solutions to reverse a yearslong decline in traditionally trained teachers entering the classroom, all while emergency certified educators continue to fill essential teaching roles.  The number of graduates completing Oklahoma teacher preparation programs, including college degrees in education, has fa[...]
text:
Warner Elementary teacher Pam White directs a student to complete a math problem on the whiteboard in her fourth-grade math classroom on Dec. 10 in Warner. Fewer fully certified teachers, like White, are entering Oklahoma public schools today. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — State leaders say they’re still pursuing solutions to reverse a yearslong decline in traditionally trained teachers entering the classroom, all while emergency certified educators continue to fill essential teaching roles. 
The number of graduates completing Oklahoma teacher preparation programs, including college degrees in education, has fallen by about 40% since 2013, state officials told the Oklahoma State Board of Education on Thursday. 
Traditionally certified educators who completed these programs have represented less than half of all first-year teachers entering the state’s public schools since 2018.
To help fill in the gap, Oklahoma districts hire thousands of emergency certified teachers, who might not have traditional classroom training, when a candidate with full or partial credentials is unavailable. Uncertified adjunct instructors, who must have relevant career experience but aren’t required to have a college degree, also have taken on a growing role in public schools.
The state Board of Education has placed increasing scrutiny on Oklahoma’s reliance on emergency certified teachers, who were a rarity a decade and a half ago. The board votes monthly to issue emergency certifications.
“I’m not against it,” said Becky Carson, a retired teacher and one of the most vocal board members on the issue. “I just want to make sure that the educators that we’re putting there are supported and we’re giving them the right training and being able to remove those that might not be (in) the best place for them.”
Oklahoma State Board of Education member Becky Carson speaks during a meeting Oct. 9 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Research shows teacher quality and credentials impact student academic achievement, she said. If Oklahoma wants to rise from the bottom of national education rankings, Carson said, “we have to look at all aspects that could be of a concern that’s putting us there.”
The state issued 3,928 emergency certifications for the 2025-26 school year, state data shows. 
So far, 1,392 more have been approved for 2026-27, said Jeff Smith, program director for teacher certification at the Oklahoma State Department of Education.
More than 470 of those teachers are renewing past emergency certifications, he said. 
The number of applicants seeking renewals — some as many as eight times after failing to pass certification tests or not completing required coursework — has been one of the state board members’ top complaints.
Sixty of the 638 applicants approved Thursday have been issued an emergency certificate more than three times, according to an Oklahoma Voice analysis of state records. Emergency certifications are typically renewed every one to two years, according to state administrative codes.
“Why are we having people that are having to ask for that renewal eight times?” Carson said. “Why aren’t we being able to get them to pass the test if that’s the reason?”
Data agency staff presented at the board’s meeting Thursday showed the stark reality of the pipeline feeding Oklahoma’s teacher workforce.
Emergency certified educators, once considered a stop-gap measure, were the most common of all first-year teachers in 2025. They represented 38.8% of teachers in their first year and more than 5% of all Oklahoma educators, state officials said.
Traditionally certified educators made up 87.8% of the overall teacher workforce in 2025 and only 37.1% of those in their first year, but their numbers could rise in 2026. So far, they represent 45.5% of 2026 first-year teachers, but state data doesn’t yet reflect the full hiring cycle.
Provisional educators, who have completed some requirements but still have testing or coursework to complete, represented 7.6% of all teachers and 24.1% of first-year educators last year.
That presents a striking difference from 2010, when emergency certifications amounted to 0.5% of incoming new teachers. Those with traditional certifications counted for 96.3% of the classroom teacher workforce and 64.7% of first-year entrants. The rest held a provisional certificate.
The data sheds light on an “unfortunate situation” that state leaders must work together to solve, said Rep. Dick Lowe, R-Amber. The state House Common Education Committee leader, who attended the board meeting Thursday, said he’s going to participate in interim studies and a working group with the state Board of Education to explore solutions.
“I think if you look at those numbers, you kind of understand where our test scores are, where they’re at and why they’ve been there,” Lowe said of Oklahoma’s poor academic results.
State Rep. Dick Lowe, R-Amber, attends a special session of the state House at the Oklahoma Capitol on Oct. 3, 2023. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)
The weakening teacher pipeline wasn’t a shock to Carson, she said, given how many educators complain of classroom behavior issues and a lack of support.
State lawmakers in recent years have increased minimum teacher salaries, created scholarship programs for aspiring educators and established other perks in the hopes of combatting the education workforce shortage.
A state initiative known as TeachForward is helping 450 emergency certified educators earn a standard certification within one year, Education Department staff said Thursday. Six Oklahoma universities partnered with the program to offer accelerated coursework and exams at no out-of-pocket cost to participants.
The agency also touted a program it will launch Monday to give 463 early career teachers a week of professional development and mentoring throughout the school year. The program serves first- and second-year teachers with any type of certification.
State Superintendent Lindel Fields expressed enthusiasm for the program’s potential to help retain participating teachers in the classroom long term.
“There’s a lot of talk about recruiting teachers. The real problem is keeping teachers,” Fields said during the state Board of Education meeting. “Everything we can do to help those teachers be successful in this program is super exciting.”

name: VTDigger
title: Ex-Rutland City officer faces allegations of violating anti-bias policy, falsifying report
description:
Nicholas Fontana is the second officer in recent months accused of violating the state-required Fair and Impartial Policing Policy while a member of the department.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Ex-Rutland City officer faces allegations of violating anti-bias policy, falsifying report.
text:
The Rutland City Police Department in Dec. 2021.  File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

A now-former Rutland City police officer is facing allegations from law enforcement authorities that he violated the state-mandated Fair and Impartial Policing Policy and in a separate incident falsified a police report.
In one instance, a state panel overseeing law enforcement in Vermont is set to hold a hearing regarding allegations that Nicholas Fontana improperly asked people in a vehicle for identification and muted his body-worn camera during the encounter.
In the other instance, the Rutland County state’s attorney last month formally called Fontana’s credibility into question after an internal investigation found that Fontana mishandled a reported assault case. 
Fontana is the second member of the Rutland City Police Department accused in recent months of violating the anti-bias policy. 
The Vermont Criminal Justice Council in June issued a written warning to another member of the department — Cpl. Tyler Tavares — as part of a stipulated agreement. Tavares was accused of violating the policy by contacting federal authorities to get immigration details about people in a traffic stop.
Now, the council has set a hearing for September for Fontana over his alleged role in a traffic stop in 2025 when he worked as a Rutland City police officer.
It’s not clear from filings in both cases whether the allegations against Tavares and Fontana stemmed from the same traffic stop, though circumstances described in the records appear similar.
Christopher Brickell, executive director of the Vermont Criminal Justice Council, referred a question Thursday about whether both cases involved the same traffic stop to Christopher Perkett, the council’s associate general counsel. Perkett was out of the office and not available for comment.
Neither Rutland City Police Chief Matthew Prouty nor Fontana, who resigned from the department this year, could be reached Thursday for comment.
According to the hearing notice in Fontana’s case, he arrived at the scene of a traffic stop by Tavares “on or about” Sept. 22, 2025, and activated his body-worn camera.
During the traffic stop, the notice stated, Fontana “intentionally muted” the camera for large portions of the stop, including when he interacted with people in the vehicle.
He also requested identification from the passengers and did not tell them they were not required to provide this information, according to the notice. 
According to the Fair and Impartial Policing Policy, the hearing notice stated, “Absent reasonable suspicion of unlawful activity, Rutland City Police Department employees shall not require that passengers in motor vehicles provide identification or other documents. If requesting such documents, Rutland City Police Department employees will state that passengers are not required to provide them.”
The hearing notice said Fontana also faces an allegation that he violated the Rutland City Police Department’s body-worn camera policy.
The notice said Fontana faces a range of sanctions if the council affirms the allegations against him, from a written warning to a revocation of his police certification in Vermont.
In the other set of allegations against Fontana, the results of an internal investigation prompted Rutland County State’s Attorney Ian Sullivan to write what is known as a Brady letter. Sullivan wrote in that letter June 11 that the internal investigation concluded that Fontana “intentionally falsified” police department records, neglected duties by not following through on a reported assault and had “willfully discarded or destroyed” a witness statement.
Brady letters are filed when an officer’s credibility is called into question and can often effectively end a law enforcement career. That’s because prosecutors may decide not to take cases the officer had investigated due to the credibility concerns raised in the letter.
In his letter, Sullivan wrote that the investigation found that Fontana created a police report that said a witness had not provided a statement.
“This was false,” Sullivan wrote in his letter. “In reality, the witness had provided a written statement to Nicholas Fontana approximately three weeks before he authored the false report.”
Sullivan, in an email Thursday, wrote that the reported assault had since been assigned to another Rutland City police officer, who is investigating.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Stein, Jackson say NC regulators need to hold Duke Energy to federal data center pledge
description: The pledge asks large energy users and utilities to negotiate agreements so large load users, like data centers, are in a separate rate class and agree to cover the costs of their own power and infrastructure.
text:
Duke Energy is seeking permission to merge Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress. (Photo: Duke Energy) North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein and Attorney General Jeff Jackson said Thursday the state Utilities Commission should hold Duke Energy to its promise to comply with the Trump administration’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge by requiring the utility to agree to it in writing.
At an event Thursday at the headquarters of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, President Donald Trump said 23 governors, all Republican, and about 200 stakeholders, including Duke Energy, have signed the pledge to limit data centers from shifting costs to consumers. 
The pledge asks large energy users and utilities to negotiate agreements so large load users, like data centers, are in a separate rate class and agree to cover the costs of their own power and infrastructure. 
Tech companies like Amazon, Google, Meta, and Open AI also joined the agreement. 
NC AG Jackson rejects Duke Energy’s proposed rate increase

Stein said in a statement he’s pleased to see Duke Energy signing onto the pledge, but there’s still work to be done to ensure they abide by it.
“The North Carolina Utilities Commission and Duke Energy must create a legally binding large load tariff to charge data centers their full freight, and they must establish a program that allows data centers to directly select and pay for their generation,” he said. “North Carolinians are struggling to make ends meet, and data centers must pay their own way to protect families from rising electricity costs.”
“Duke just promised the federal government that it won’t shift the cost of data centers onto families,” Jackson said in a statement. “We agree, but a promise in Washington doesn’t lower a power bill in North Carolina. We’re calling on Duke to make that same promise to the Utilities Commission, in writing, where it can be enforced.”
North Carolina’s state leaders have been working on stricter data center regulations for months. In April, Stein asked legislators to modify sales tax exemptions on data centers. In the state budget, lawmakers did repeal data centers’ sales tax exemption on electricity purchases, but left in place exemptions for purchases of equipment and other services. 
Earlier this week, Jackson pushed back on Duke Energy’s proposed residential rate increase.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho sheriff tells legislators decisions on ICE partnerships should be left to local officials
description: An Idaho county sheriff told a committee of state legislators on Thursday that partnership agreements with ICE should be local decisions, not required by the Idaho Legislature or state government.  “Participation in the ICE partnership programs is voluntary and should remain a decision of locally elected officials who are accountable to their communities the[...]
text:
The Idaho State Capitol Building in Boise shines in the sunlight on Jan. 7, 2025. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)An Idaho county sheriff told a committee of state legislators on Thursday that partnership agreements with ICE should be local decisions, not required by the Idaho Legislature or state government. 
Bonneville County Sheriff Samuel Hulse (Photo courtesy of the Bonneville County Sheriff’s Office)
“Participation in the ICE partnership programs is voluntary and should remain a decision of locally elected officials who are accountable to their communities they serve,” Bonneville County Sheriff Samuel Hulse told the Idaho Legislature’s Committee on Federalism during a meeting Thursday at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. 
“What I want to make clear is that it is the responsibility of the federal government to protect our nation from illegal immigration,” Hulse said. “We have a co-responsibility to ensure that they are effective in their jobs, but it is not local enforcement’s job to enforce the immigration policy of the nation.”
 Sheriff urges flexibility on ICE agreement participation after 2026 bill would have added new requirements

Hulse is president of the Idaho Sheriffs’ Association, which opposed a bill that Idaho legislators introduced earlier this year that would have required local law enforcement agencies to enter into partnership agreements with ICE.



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



In March, the Idaho House of Representatives voted 41-27 to pass House Bill 659 to require local sheriffs and police departments to sign 287(g) agreements with ICE, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. 
But the Idaho Senate never took up the bill, and it died when the 2026 legislative session adjourned. 
On Thursday, Hulse told legislators that capacity issues at local county jails and local budget constraints are two reasons why a local law enforcement agency may not be best served signing a formal partnership with ICE.
“Idaho counties, tribal governments and local law enforcement agencies should have the flexibility to determine whether participation aligns with their operational capabilities, public safety priorities and the needs of their communities,” Hulse said. “While this has been a hot-button subject for the Idaho Legislature recently, this approach reflects Idaho’s longstanding commitment to local control, recognizing that government is most effective when the decisions are made by those closest to the people they serve.”
Hulse told legislators that Idaho sheriffs already voluntarily cooperate with ICE in several ways without signing a formal 287(g) agreement. He said examples include providing ICE with inmate booking information and allowing federal authorities to interview and take custody of individuals.  
“This existing collaboration ensures federal immigration enforcement responsibilities are fulfilled without requiring local agencies to assume those duties directly,” Hulse said. “Mandating 287(g) participation fails to recognize the diversity of Idaho counties. Sheriffs must prioritize core public safety responsibilities and the decisions to enter into federal agreement must remain a local one.”
State Rep. Dale Hawkins, R-Fernwood, takes his seat for the Idaho House’s Local Government Committee meeting on March 16, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Rep. Dale Hawkins, a Republican from Fernwood who co-sponsored House Bill 659, told Hulse that his bill included a provision that would have allowed local law enforcement officials to exit the ICE partnership if it couldn’t comply with the agreement or meet all of the standards.
“It did give that exit, and all they had to do was say, ‘this is why we can’t,’ and they wouldn’t have had to (do it),” Hawkins said. 
This isn’t the first time Hulse has spoken out to Idaho legislators. In December, Hulse wrote to Gov. Brad Little and Republican legislative leaders warning them that discontinuing behavioral health programs represents “a significant public safety concern,” the Sun previously reported. Hulse said that the state’s budget challenges were “self-inflicted,” and the result of an “overaggressive tax reduction stance.”
Although the Idaho Legislature is not in session, a handful of joint committees and interim committees do meet periodically throughout the year. The Idaho Legislature is scheduled to reconvene in January for the 2027 legislative session.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Mike Lindell wins Trump endorsement, immediately criticizes mass deportation campaign
description: In another surprising twist in the race for the Republican nomination for governor, Mike Lindell released an 18-page, five-pronged plan to reform the federal immigration system by creating a path to temporary legal residency for working immigrants.  In an interview with Washington Examiner, Lindell, the Trump-endorsed pillow mogul, said he believes in second[...]
text:
MyPillow founder Mike Lindell speaks to Steve Bannon during a livestream in front of his new Minnesota governor campaign bus on Dec. 11, 2025. (Photo by Michelle Griffith/Minnesota Reformer)In another surprising twist in the race for the Republican nomination for governor, Mike Lindell released an 18-page, five-pronged plan to reform the federal immigration system by creating a path to temporary legal residency for working immigrants. 
In an interview with Washington Examiner, Lindell, the Trump-endorsed pillow mogul, said he believes in second chances for people whose only offense is entering the country without authorization. 
“I met with the illegals down in San Diego,” Lindell said. “I met with a lot of them and I heard their stories.” 
The proposal, described in the document as a “fiscally responsible, legally grounded, and operationally achievable alternative to mass deportation,” quickly drew the ire of right-wing media outlets and one of Lindell’s primary opponents, who referred to the document as an “amnesty” plan.
“I am shocked to see something like that coming out from a Republican candidate,” Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth, who is running against Lindell in the primary election, said in a Thursday interview on WDAY radio. “It flies in the face of what President Trump has done.”
Another problem for Lindell: The Minnesota governor has no control over immigration policy. 
Lindell’s proposal involves immediately deporting all undocumented immigrants with a felony or gross misdemeanor conviction, while  creating a 120-day window for undocumented immigrants to apply for a new “worker visa card,” which would grant temporary legal status contingent on continued work and no criminal convictions. 
After the deadline to apply for a visa passes, businesses employing undocumented workers would face criminal penalties, and those workers would be subject to deportation. 
Lindell also proposes requiring employers to report all cash payments to employees and imposing an English-language requirement for drivers’ licenses.
The plan would have no path to citizenship, and immigrants would be ineligible for the social safety net programs their tax dollars fund, including Social Security and Medicare. It would codify undocumented people as permanent outsiders, but end the brutal deportation campaign. 
The proposal flies in the face of Trump’s mass-deportation agenda, just one week after Trump endorsed Lindell, pushing him to the top of primary polls.
The plan never mentions the state of Minnesota. 
In the hours since news of his plan broke, Lindell seemed to backtrack, denying that his plan is in any way an amnesty. 
He also posted on X his support for Trump’s mass deportation agenda: “As always, I stand with President Trump and fully support his policies to deport illegal aliens from the United States,” in apparent contradiction of the plan he released just hours before. 
Primary Election Day is Aug. 11.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi opioid settlement addiction response projects could face further delays
description: Doug Miracle, right, chairs Mississippi's Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Council for Attorney General Lynn Fitch at a meeting on July 21, 2025.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Members of Mississippi’s Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Council are scrambling to ensure millions of dollars they oversee can actually be used for awarded addiction-response projects. 
State lawmakers earlier this year awarded around $50 million in opioid settlement money — payments made by the companies that contributed to the overdose deaths of more than 10,000 Mississippians. The contracts between the state and the awardees say that the selected organizations will be reimbursed for every three months of work. 
The agreements were supposed to go into effect on July 1, but some organizations that were selected to receive the money haven’t signed them yet because the upfront project costs would be too high. 
The Legislature awarded the north Mississippi community mental health center Communicare $5.2 million to build a new pediatric emergency and long-term residential treatment center in Panola County — the first of its kind in the state. But Melody Madaris, the executive director of Communicare and a member of Mississippi’s Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Council, told other members at a meeting on Tuesday that with the current contract setup, her organization couldn’t start work on the center. 

“There’s no way that our agency can purchase that building and wait for the reimbursement for an entire quarter,” she said at the meeting. “If we were capable of doing that, we would’ve already done it.” 
Madaris told Mississippi Today after the meeting that she has yet to sign Communicare’s opioid settlement contract because of this dilemma. Mississippi Deputy Attorney General Doug Miracle, who filled in as council chair for Attorney General Lynn Fitch on Tuesday, told the other members that less than half of the grant agreements Fitch’s office was responsible for had been signed and returned by applicants. 
Sen. Nicole Boyd, a Republican from Oxford and a council member, said she also heard from recipients that waiting three months could prevent them from ever starting their addiction response work. 
“It’s a difficult issue when it’s quarterly, especially these small nonprofits that we want to be able to work with,” Boyd said at the meeting. “They’re doing great stuff, many of them.”
Nicole Boyd, a Republican state senator from Oxford, at Mississippi’s Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Council meeting on July 21, 2026 Credit: Allen Siegler / Mississippi Today
The $50 million of legislative awards is the first time Mississippi elected officials have used the portion of opioid lawsuit money the settlements say must be used to address addiction. It’s the only state in the country that hadn’t spent any of that share by 2024, according to a KFF Health News investigation. 
Boyd said she was getting texts from people with applicant organizations about the reimbursements as the meeting was happening.
“I think it is a larger problem than the council realizes at this point,” she said to the other members. 
In a roll call vote, the majority of members agreed to allow opioid settlement grant recipients who applied in 2025 to propose alternative fund disbursement arrangements to their contracts, and the council would review each of those requests at the next meeting, which Deputy Attorney General Doug Miracle said would take place in the next two weeks. 
Miracle voted against the motion. He told members that opening up changes to the council-approved contracts for this cycle could further delay Mississippi from using opioid settlement money to address addiction, including for the applicants who can manage the 90-day reimbursement arrangement.
“The packages went out,” he said. “People have been told what the rules of the road were, and they’re returning them.”
Council members did not specify how applicants should go about requesting these changes. 
The Attorney General Office Communications Director MaryAsa Lee did not respond to an emailed question asking for further clarity. Miracle declined a Mississippi Today interview after the meeting.
